Fait à Banjul, Gambie, lors de sa 74 session ordinaire tenue du 21 février au 7 mars 2023.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received on 10 November 2015, a Communication submitted pursuant to Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) by Maître Lambert Nigarura hereinafter referred to as the Complainant, on behalf of Radio Publique Africaine hereinafter referred to as the R.P.A or the victim against the Republic of Burundi hereinafter referred to as Burundi or the Respondent State.

The Complainant reports that the R.P.A is a victim of its investigative work which displeases the power in place in Burundi. He indicates that the Burundian authorities did not appreciate the R.P.A's broadcast of an audio item which shed light on the murder of three (3) religious sisters on 8 September 2014 and that in addition to that, the live broadcast by the R.P.A of the demonstrations against the third candidacy of President Pierre Nkurunziza aggravated the situation. He argues that the authorities decided to use any means to silence the R.P.A for good.

The Complainant reports that on 26 April 2015, on the first day of the demonstrations broadcast live on the airwaves of the R.P.A and with other independent local radios, the R.P.A received a visit from three ministers, namely the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Public Security and the Minister of Communication. He specifies that these authorities ordered the editorial staff of the R.P.A to suspend the broadcast of the unfolding of the demonstrations.

The Complainant indicates that on 27 April 2015, the National Radio Television of Burundi, in his view, in flagrant violation of the agreement binding it to the private radios, cut the transmitters that enabled the broadcasting of private programmes within the country. The Complainant adds that two days later, a contingent of the police and certain members of the intelligence service invaded the premises of the R.P.A for the second time, equipped with a warrant for the provisional closure of the Radio whereas according to the Complainant, it was not for the Public Prosecutor's Office to seize itself of its own motion of a press offence if there was an offence; that since that date, the R.P.A has been prohibited from broadcasting throughout the Burundian territory and that the Management of the Radio nevertheless complied without resistance.

The Complainant further reports that on 13 May 2015, a group of soldiers who attempted to seize power by force invaded the premises of the R.P.A to demand its forced reopening in order to broadcast their message to the Nation. The Complainant specifies that the security guards alone on the premises were obliged to give the contact details of the journalists; that the putschists went to look for the journalists at their homes and forced them to open the radio to broadcast their message.

According to the Complainant, this forced reopening by the putschists led the authorities to carry out their plan to settle scores definitively with the R.P.A and that it is thus that, in the morning of 14 May 2015, upon the failure of the coup, the loyalist forces attacked the premises of the R.P.A with rockets, destroyed it and set it on fire. The Complainant adds that since that day, the hunt for all the journalists of the R.P.A has begun and that the latter are now scattered in the neighbouring countries.

The Complainant considers that the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) should exempt him from the application of the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies. In this regard, he submits on the one hand, that seizing the Burundian courts would be futile because they are not independent and that, considering the R.P.A to be a "sounding board for the putschists", the Burundian Government has neither the will nor the capacity to deal with this case. On the other hand, the Complainant submits that it is dangerous to use local remedies because since the destruction of the R.P.A, all the staff of the R.P.A live in total hiding, that the journalists are being hunted down, that the Director of the R.P.A is wanted by the Burundian judiciary and the lawyer of the R.P.A was himself named in the judicial investigation report for the sole fact that he spoke out against the third candidacy of President Pierre Nkurunziza.

The Complainant submits that the rights of the R.P.A have been violated but that the Burundian people has by the same means been deprived of its right to information and the right to disseminate its opinions.

The Complainant considers that the Commission now requires that complaints before it be submitted within a period of six months following the exhaustion of local remedies or the date determined by the Commission; he recalls that in the present case, he should be exempted from exhaustion of local remedies and that the last facts date from 14 May 2015.
The Complainant further indicates that no other international dispute settlement mechanism has been seized of the present case for any analysis.
The Complainant has not indicated that he requests anonymity.

On examination of the grounds invoked by the Complainant, the latter essentially alleges the violation of the provisions of Articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) and (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 and 26 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission: • to use its competence provided for in Article 30 of the African Charter so that the R.P.A recovers its rights infringed and provided for by the African Charter (Article 9), as regards the recommendations to be made which will be addressed to Burundi; • to sentence the Respondent State to forthwith compensate Radio Publique Africaine destroyed, in his view, unjustly and illegally; • to find with him that if a State party cannot ensure respect for the rights contained in the African Charter, this constitutes a violation of the said Charter and that consequently it appears that the legislation of the Respondent State does not respect in this regard, the treaty commitments of the country arising from the status of State party to the African Charter.
The Secretariat of the African Commission received the Communication on 10 November 2015.

The Secretariat, by letter of 3 December 2015, asked the Complainant to provide certain clarifications and missing documents. The Secretariat specifically asked the Complainant to indicate the reason why his Communication bears two references at the outset, to indicate who the exact victims are in the present case and whether he is authorised to act in their name and on their behalf and finally to provide a document cited in the content of the complaint but which had not been transmitted to the Secretariat.
By correspondence of 7 and 9 December 2015, the Complainant provided the information and clarifications requested; the Secretariat acknowledged receipt by letter of 18 December 2015.
At its 19th Extraordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 16 to 25 February 2016, the Commission considered the Complaint and decided to be seized of it.

On 8 March 2016, the Secretariat informed the Complainant and the Respondent State of this decision and asked the Complainant to submit his observations on Admissibility within two months, in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

At its 58th Ordinary Session held from 6 to 20 April 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer its decision on admissibility pending the submissions of the parties. On 28 April 2016, the Parties were informed of this decision, one by letter and the other by Note Verbale.
On 2 May 2016, the Complainant submitted to the Secretariat his brief on Admissibility indicating that the hard copy of the file containing other evidence would be sent to it by post.
By letter of 13 May 2016, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt and indicated to the Complainant that it was still awaiting the hard copy file that he had mentioned.
On 11 May 2016, the Secretariat received the hard copy file and acknowledged receipt by letter of 17 May 2016 while indicating to the Complainant that annex number 2 mentioned was not in it.

By email of 20 May 2016, the Complainant indicated that the mention of annex number 2 in the file was a laspus calami and added that the content of the said annex is in fact on the CD attached to the file. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt of this email on 20 May 2016.

On 30 May 2016, the Secretariat transmitted the Complainant's brief on Admissibility to the Respondent State and invited the latter to submit its observations within two months in accordance with Rule 105(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On 19 July 2016, the Secretariat informed the Complainant and the Respondent State that the hearing requested by the Complainant could not be granted to him given the stage of consideration of the Communication. Moreover, the Commission informed the Parties that the decision on Admissibility is deferred to a later Session pending the observations of the Respondent State.

On 23 November 2016, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State that the Commission had decided to grant it an additional thirty (30) calendar days for the submission of its observations on Admissibility. The Complainant was informed of this decision the same day by dated letter.
Until then, the Respondent State has not transmitted its observations on the Admissibility of the Communication despite the numerous reminders made to it.
On 13 April, 5 June, 22 August and 8 December 2017, the Secretariat informed the Parties that the Commission had decided to render its decision on Admissibility at a later Session.

At its 63rd Ordinary Session, held from 24 October to 13 November 2018, the Commission declared the Communication admissible. This decision was transmitted to the Parties and the Complainant was invited to submit his written observations on the merits.
On 10 September 2019, the complainant presented his observations on the merits, which were transmitted to the Respondent State on 7 January 2020, with information to the complainant on the same date.

On 16 March 2020, the Secretariat reminded the Respondent State that the time limit allotted to it to present observations on the merits would expire on 7 April 2020 and that at the 27th Extraordinary Session, the consideration of the communication was postponed for lack of the said observations.

On the margins of the 73rd Ordinary Session, which was held from 21 October to 10 November 2022, an official of the Secretariat met a delegation from Burundi to discuss the status of the cases pending against Burundi. The Burundian delegation was informed of the situation concerning the communications pending against Burundi.

By Note Verbale Ref: ACHPR/1068/2022, dated 31 November 2022, the said List of Communications was then transmitted to the Embassy of Burundi in Addis, Ethiopia on 3 November 2022, for the attention of the Ministry of Justice of Burundi. The list was shared with the Burundian delegation by email on 7 November 2022. This communication is among the communications in which the Respondent State has not submitted observations on the merits.

Despite the sending of the list containing the status of the communications pending before the Commission against the Respondent State, including the status of the present communication, the Respondent State has not deigned to submit a request for an extension of the time limit or to submit its observations on the merits.
The Complainant argues that the Communication complies with all the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.

The identity of the author of the Communication is indicated in accordance with Article 56(1) of the Charter. The Communication having been submitted by Maître Lambert Nigarura on behalf of Radio Publique Africaine whose addresses and contact details are clearly specified in the submissions.

The Complainant submits that the Communication is compatible with the Charter of the OAU/AU or with the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights pursuant to Article 56(2) of the Charter. According to the Complainant, the present Communication is directed against the Republic of Burundi, a State party to the Charter since 28 July 1989. The violations alleged in the Communication infringe the rights guaranteed by Articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) and (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 and 26 of the African Charter.
The said violations postdate the ratification of the Charter by the Respondent State.
The Complainant asserts that the Communication is devoid of any insulting language towards the State concerned, its institutions or the OAU in accordance with Article 56(3) of the Charter.

The Complainant states that the Communication is not based on news disseminated through the mass media in application of Article 56(4). The annex to the Communication indeed contains elements of investigations prepared jointly by representatives of the three powers: executive, legislative, judicial, technical and financial partners and civil society.

The Complainant asserts that as regards the exhaustion of local remedies, according to the Commission's jurisprudence in Communication 328/06 Frente de Libertação do Estado de Cabinda v. República de Angola, 2013, paragraph 44, compliance with this requirement must rest on three criteria, namely that the remedy must be: available, effective and sufficient. The Complainant adds that as results from the Commission's decision in Communication 409/12 Luke Munyandu Tembani and Others v. Angola, the rule of exhaustion of local remedies does not apply if the remedies do not exist, if they are unduly prolonged or if they are rendered impossible. The Complainant submits that the remedies are non-existent because neither he, nor the victim nor the representatives of Radio Publique Africaine could go before the courts without being concerned or without endangering their physical and psychological integrity.

The Complainant also states that the remedies are rendered unavailable inasmuch as the judicial apparatus is said to be in the hands of the executive. He considers that the Commission should exempt him from the requirement of exhaustion of remedies which offer no chance of success in accordance with the Commission's jurisprudence, in the case Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, which considers that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies does not apply when these remedies "are not available or are ineffective. The Complainant mentions that he could therefore be exempted from compliance with this requirement because of the lack of independence of the Burundian judicial system subject to the control of the executive as well as the fears of persecution of the natural persons representing the Complainant.

The Complainant recalls that the requirement imposed by paragraph 6 of Article 56 of the African Charter concerning reasonable time rests on two possibilities: submission of the Communication within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter. The Complainant considers that in the present case, given that he has not exhausted the remedies, the question of the time limit cannot run. He therefore leaves it to the Commission's assessment.

The Complainant finally states that the Communication does not concern cases which have been settled by another international body in application of Article 56(7) of the Charter. According to the Complainant, the allegations contained in this communication have not been brought before any other regional, continental or international body. That being so, he claims that this requirement suffers from no deficiency.

The Respondent State has not submitted its observations on Admissibility despite the multiple reminder Notes Verbales that the Secretariat addressed to it for that purpose; notably the following Notes Verbales: ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/378/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1052/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1372/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1875/16, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/264/17, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/396/17, ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/688/17, and ACHPR/COMM/587/15/BUR/1580/17 respectively of 8 March 2016, 30 May 2016, 19 July 2016, 23 November 2016, 13 April 2017, 5 June 2017, 22 August 2017 and 8 December 2017.

The Communication was submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter which gives the Commission competence to receive and consider "communications other than those of States parties". The said communications must, in order to be declared admissible, fulfil the requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.

Under the provisions of Rule 105(2) of its 2010 Rules of Procedure, the Secretariat transmits to the Respondent State the submissions made by the Complainant for it to respond. In the present case, the Commission notes that the procedural requirements thus recalled have been observed as attested by the numerous Notes Verbales reminding the Respondent State to transmit its observations on Admissibility. On the basis of these findings, the Commission decides to consider the Communication on the basis of the elements in its possession, in accordance with its practice.

This procedural question having been settled, the Commission will turn to the Admissibility proper of the Communication under consideration. On the point of compliance with the requirement set out in Article 56(1) of the African Charter, the Commission notes that the Communication clearly identifies the Complainant and the victim represented whose full contact details and addresses were provided in the submissions filed before it. The Commission therefore considers that the Communication complies with the requirement under examination.

As regards compliance with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Commission recalls that the requirement set means compatibility ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci of the Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter. Thus, the examination of compatibility must consist for the Commission in ensuring that all the grounds and requests contained in the Communication are in conformity with the provisions of the above-mentioned instruments.

The Commission notes that in the present case, the Communication is submitted against the Republic of Burundi, a State party to the African Charter since 28/07/1989 and that the Complainant has standing. Furthermore, the Complainant alleges the violation, on the territory of the Respondent State, of rights protected by the Charter, notably the violation of Articles 1, 7(1), 9(1) and (2), 10, 12(2), 13, 14 and 26. The Commission also notes that the Charter was in force in Burundi at the time of the facts. Finally, it is manifest that neither the grounds nor the requests contained in the Communication infringe any of the principles adopted under the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

On compliance with the provisions of Article 56(3), the Commission notes that the Communication does not contain any term capable of being characterised as insulting or disparaging towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. The Communication therefore fulfils the requirement under examination.

The Commission also notes that the requirement set out in Article 56(4) is complied with since the Communication contains in annex, among others, an official document produced jointly by the institutions of the Respondent State including representatives of the government, of the legislative power, of the judicial power, of technical and financial partners as well as members of civil society.

On the point of the Communication's compliance with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Commission in its practice proceeds to examine, one after the other, the alleged violations.

In the Commission's jurisprudential practice, the objective of the requirement contained in Article 56(5) of the African Charter is to allow the State concerned, in this case Burundi, to settle as a priority, according to its domestic law, the alleged human rights violation before its examination by an international body, to avoid such a body being used as a court of first instance but rather being a body of last resort.

In the present case, the author of the Communication has not submitted any application before the domestic courts of the Burundian State, admitting that local remedies offer no chance of success. The Complainant submits that the control that the government exercises over the judiciary is such as to make the institution not independent and as such, the chances of success of seizures in the context of this case are very slim, which would render local remedies ineffective and unsatisfactory.

In its leading decision on the matter, the Commission specifies the meaning of the provisions of Article 56(5) by deciding in the case Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia that the remedies to be exhausted must be available, effective and satisfactory. It emerges from this decision that a remedy is considered available when it can be used without impediment by the petitioner; it is effective if it offers prospects of success and it is satisfactory when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the complainant.

On examination of the Complainant's submissions, it appears to the Commission that local remedies existed but were not available since the Complainant and/or the victim feared being persecuted in the event of an attempt to seize the courts. There would therefore be risks for the Complainant of being entrapped by the judicial institution under the control of the government given also that Radio Publique Africaine has been silenced, destroyed and set on fire by the loyalist forces of President Pierre Nkurunziza. This position is also motivated by other allegations, namely that the radio's staff live in total hiding, the journalists are hunted down, the director of the RPA is wanted by the Burundian judiciary and the lawyer of the RPA is also feared as he is named in the judicial investigation report for having spoken out against the third candidacy of President Nkurunziza through the campaign "Stop the third term". These facts being, objectively, the possibility of triggering domestic resources is exhausted, therefore the "impediment" criterion is met.

Turning to the questions of effectiveness and satisfaction, they could be addressed only if the remedies are available and seizing the domestic courts would not pose a danger to the Complainant or the victim. In the present case, the unavailability and inaccessibility of the Burundian tribunals and courts entail ineffectiveness. Moreover, remedies must be satisfactory. But in the present case, the Complainant alleges that the remedies could not be so given the influence of the government over the judicial administration; this would therefore be such as not to be able to satisfy the Complainant had he brought a remedy. It therefore emerges that the Commission is of the view that the Complainant and the victim cannot be asked to exhaust local remedies knowing that the authorities concerned are hunting them down with also their influence over the justice system.
From the foregoing, the Commission finds that the Communication complies with the requirements of Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

As regards compliance with the provisions of Article 56(6) it emerges from the evidence advanced by the Complainant on the violations that the last facts date back to 14 May 2015, the Communication having been submitted on 10 November 2015, that is practically six months after the facts.

The Commission, referring to the practice in the inter-American and European human rights systems, decided in the case Majuru v. Zimbabwe that the six-month period can be considered a "usual standard".

The Commission has also accepted in its jurisprudence that the determination of the "reasonable time" must be made on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances of each case. The Commission held that 2 years and 5 months in the case Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan and 1 year and 3 months in the case Dr Farouk Mohamed Ibrahim v. Sudan were not reasonable periods, on the ground that the Complainants had submitted the communication well after the moment that could have been considered reasonable but also gave no compelling reason for the long wait before seizing the Commission.

The Commission notes that practically six months separated the date of the last facts from the date of submission of the seizure. To justify this period, the Complainant advances that the journalists of the RPA, the director and the lawyer of the radio were forced to flee the country for having been against the intention of the Burundian Head of State to seek a third term.
The Commission agrees that the fact of the Complainant and the victim fleeing the country because they were sought by the authorities constitutes a situation capable of delaying its seizure.

The other factor taken into account by the Commission in the assessment of reasonable time is the need to ensure fairness and justice. The Commission resorted to it to motivate its decision in the case Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan. The Commission had then decided that, if the objective of Article 56(6) is to discourage delay in seizing it, it is also its responsibility to offer the Complainant the opportunity to be heard when valid and relevant reasons have justified such a delay. The relevant factor in these circumstances is that of the "need for fair justice".

The Commission, according to the facts set out and the arguments submitted, notes the unavailability of local remedies and their inaccessibility in the present case. In these circumstances, the Commission considers that not admitting the present Communication would amount to denying the victims the possibility of remedying the lack of availability and independence of the courts.

Moreover, Article 56(6) of the African Charter provides that the Commission must consider communications which "are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter".

It emerges from the analysis of Article 56(5) made by the Commission in the preceding paragraphs, that local remedies have not been exhausted in relation to the violations subsequent to the final judgment and, consequently, that the time limit for seizure cannot be calculated "from the time local remedies are exhausted" but rather "from the date the Commission is seized of the matter".

In this regard, the Commission notes that the last violations alleged by the Complainant date back to 14 May 2015, the date on which Radio Publique Africaine was ransacked and torpedoed with rockets by the National Police and the Burundian Intelligence Services during the forced eviction. Neither the Complainant nor the victim had the possibility of seizing the domestic courts without being harassed and their fear of persecution was such that they were forced to flee. Given the circumstances, the Commission considers that the period from 14 May 2015 to 10 November 2015 constitutes a reasonable period for submitting this communication before it.
The Commission concludes mutatis mutandis that the Communication fulfils the requirement set out in Article 56(6) of the African Charter.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7), the Communication must not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata or the authority of the matter adjudged; of non-lis pendens; and of non bis in idem.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the alleged facts have not been brought before any court whether national or international. No international or regional human rights body has examined a complaint concerning the same facts nor has the case been settled before another forum applying the principles recalled above. The Commission therefore finds that the Communication complies with the requirement under examination.
In light of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declared the present communication admissible, in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter.

The Complainant alleges the violation of his right to have his cause heard, provided for by Articles 7 and 26 of the Charter. In the first case, because the competent authorities of the Respondent State did not take adequate measures to prosecute those responsible for the violations committed, thus violating Article 7 of the Charter. In the second case, because the Respondent State has not established independent judicial bodies as provided for by Article 26 of the Charter, namely the fact that the government retains great influence over the judiciary.

To support his statements, the Complainant cites the decisions of the Commission, the Assessment Report on the reform of security and justice in Burundi requested by the government of Burundi from the government of the Netherlands and the UN, which concludes that the judiciary is dependent on the government, which in turn controls the Higher Council of the Judiciary; the lack of budgetary and financial autonomy, given that, besides the fact that it represents 2% of the national budget, it is managed by the Cabinet of the Minister; the fact that the President of the Republic is called First Magistrate of the Nation, which creates a certain confusion in the system; the submission of the Higher Council of the Judiciary to the Minister of Justice, systematically accepting all the proposals for appointment of Senior Magistrates and Heads of Institutions.
He also cited cases of senior officers who committed crimes, but were protected or promoted by the political class, thus blocking the action of justice.

The complainant alleges that on 14 May 2015, the date of the attempted coup d'état against President Pierre Nkurunziza, a contingent of the police and some elements of the army and of the Imbonerakure militia attacked the buildings of the RPA with rockets. During the attack, all the radio equipment was burned and the building was destroyed. He alleges that the premises in question belong to a private individual who was deprived not only of the building, but also of his income. Moreover, he has not started the renovation work on the building for fear of the authorities.

He argues that the Respondent State gave no reason to justify the legitimacy of the destruction of the building and the stopping of the operation of the radio, on the contrary, in the middle of an electoral campaign, the operation of the radio was necessary to ensure the information of the population on the conduct of the electoral campaign. On the other hand, the complainant alleges that the destruction of the radio is disproportionate to the type of weaponry used, namely the burning of the building, followed by the blocking of access to the site.

The Complainant alleges that the destruction of the radio station and the suspension of its activities arbitrarily deprived the journalists of the exercise of their freedom of expression and the people of their right to information provided for by Article 9 of the Charter, as elaborated by the Commission's 2002 Declaration of Principles and Article 19 of the ICCPR.

He alleges that the enforcement measure was not aimed at protecting any legitimate interest, but at victimising the RPA for its editorial line given that since 26 April 2015, the RPA had been broadcasting live demonstrations against President Nkurunziza, which annoyed the latter. Citing the case Media Rights Agenda, Constitutional Rights Project v. Nigeria, he submits that "those who assume public functions must be prepared to face greater challenges than ordinary citizens, failing which public debate is no longer possible."

The Complainant alleges that the attack on the RPA premises occurred shortly after the release of its director who had been provisionally detained after the radio broadcast an audio recording shedding light on the circumstances of the death of three (3) Italian nuns in September 2014. This release, according to the complainant, took place because there was international and diplomatic pressure.

He alleges that, following the broadcast of the demonstrations, the headquarters of the RPA was visited by the ministers of the Interior, of Public Security and of the Media, who ordered the immediate suspension of the broadcast. The next day, the RPA's broadcast was cut and on 29 April 2015, the intelligence services forced entry into the RPA premises, for the second time, this time with the warrant to close the radio for security reasons.
He alleges that a journalist of the RPA ventured to cover an event on 29 January 2016, was brutally detained and tortured throughout the day to be released the next day, then went into exile.

Finally, the complainant argues that even if the possibility of restrictions on freedom of expression is admitted as indicated in the case Constitutional Rights Project, Civil Liberties Organisation and Media Rights Agenda v. Nigeria, they must be necessary and proportionate, which, according to the complainant, was not the case with the attacks against the RPA.

The Complainant alleges that the fact that the journalists of the RPA were forced to leave their country constitutes a violation of Article 12(2) of the Charter, which provides for the right of every individual to leave any country including his own, and to return to his country.

The complainant submits that Article 13 of the Charter confers on citizens the right to benefit from a public service. Consequently, the destruction of the RPA premises and the suspension of its broadcasting constitute a deprivation of the citizens' right to benefit from a public service radio, which is contrary to Article 13 of the Charter.

The Complainant alleges that, although Article 1 of the Charter does not expressly provide for the right to reparations, he submits that it has been used by the Commission to grant reparations to victims, notably in the cases Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe and Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence & INTERIGHTS v. Cameroon. He also invokes the case Zongo v. Burkina Faso, in which the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (African Court) concluded that the violation of an international obligation entails the obligation to compensate the victim in an equitable manner.

He considers that the reparations in question may consist of holding the perpetrators of the violation accountable and repairing the damage suffered by the victims. These reparations may take the form of restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and the right to truth, as well as guarantees of non-repetition. They must also be prompt, complete and effective. He claimed to have suffered moral harm because of "the RPA's inability to broadcast information of public utility and to pursue its independent press activities."

For the above-mentioned reasons, the Complainant requests the Commission to order the Respondent State to: i. present public apologies for the violations committed; ii. pay compensation for the moral harm caused in the amount of USD 500,000; iii. pay compensation for the material damage committed in the amount of 1,144,009 euros.

The Commission is called upon to rule on facts presented by only one of the parties, since the Respondent State, although invited to submit its observations, has not deigned to do so from the admissibility stage until the present stage. This situation does not allow for the greatest clarity on what really happened. However, the non-submission of observations by the Respondent State does not prevent the Commission from basing its decision on the facts presented by the complainant.

Thus, it emerges from the initial observations and the briefs on the merits of the case that the RPA is a private radio whose editorial line is not to the government's taste, which went so far as to suspend its broadcasts to the interior of the country because of its coverage of the murder of nuns, then to suspend its broadcasts entirely for security reasons, the government considering that the RPA incited popular uprising.

According to the complainant, after the attempted coup d'état, the premises of the RPA were attacked by putschist soldiers who brought the journalists out of their homes and forced them to reopen the radio and broadcast programmes in their favour. The government reacted by destroying the radio station and began to persecute the journalists whom it considered to be collaborating with the putschists. Some of them were forced to go into hiding and others to flee the country.

The Commission notes that the Complainant includes in his observations allegations relating to the building which, according to him, belongs to someone else. As the complainant represents only the interests of the radio station and its journalists, the Commission will exclude from its examination the allegations concerning the building where the RPA carried out its activities.

On the basis of the above facts, the Commission will proceed to examine the alleged violations of Articles 7 and 26, 14, 12 and 13 of the Charter as presented by the complainant in the order in which they were presented.

Article 7 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal. 2. No one may be condemned for an act or omission which did not constitute a legally punishable offence at the time it was committed. No penalty may be inflicted for an offence for which no provision was made at the time it was committed. Punishment is personal and can be imposed only on the offender.

For its part, Article 26 of the Charter provides that: States parties to the present Charter shall have the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts and shall allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter.

The Commission notes that these two articles of the Charter, read together, form the core of the right to a fair trial. Article 7 deals with the rights and guarantees of individuals who appear or seek justice before the competent judicial bodies, and Article 26 deals with the obligation of the Respondent State to establish an independent judicial system as well as to allow the establishment of national institutions responsible for the promotion and protection of human rights. In other words, Article 7 concerns the procedural component of the right to a fair trial and Article 26 concerns its institutional aspect.

In the present case, the Commission is called upon to rule on the existence or not of a violation of Articles 7 and 26 of the Charter because of the alleged failure to open an investigation aimed at identifying and holding accountable the perpetrators of the violations and because of the lack of independence of the judiciary. On the alleged lack of accountability

The Commission notes that the right of every citizen to have his cause heard by a court provided for in Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter, implies the right of access to justice to make his cause known. Thus, in the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa (2003), the Commission considered that the right to an effective remedy implies access to justice. Consequently, access to justice is the precondition for justice to be able to hear the cause. On the other hand, the obligation of the State party to identify and hold accountable the perpetrators of violations is provided for in Article 1 of the Charter, which stipulates the following: The Member States of the Organization of African Unity parties to the present Charter shall recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enunciated in this Charter and shall undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them.

The Commission considers that the combined reading of Articles 1 and 7(1) of the Charter results in the right of victims to have access to justice to assert their rights, as well as the duty of States parties to create the conditions enabling citizens to have access to justice, or the obligation of the States parties themselves to initiate the appropriate procedures to establish the perpetrators of violations and hold them accountable before the law.

In the case Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission was categorical in stating that Article 1 "gives the Charter the legally binding character always attributed to international treaties of this type". Consequently, a violation of any provision of the Charter, automatically means a violation of Article 1". This means that the only way for a State party to remedy a violation of the Charter is to take appropriate measures as prescribed by Article 1 of the Charter.

The Commission considers that in the present case, two moments must be distinguished. The alleged violations committed before the attack on the RPA, notably the intimidation of the journalists and the suspension of the RPA's broadcasts to the interior of the country, and those which took place following the attack and after it.

In the first case, nothing in the file indicates that the RPA or the journalists who were victims of the alleged violations lodged a complaint with the competent authorities to denounce the alleged violations and claim justice, nor is it demonstrated that the alleged violations required the opening of an investigation suo moto by the authorities. Consequently, there is no basis for asserting inaction by the authorities.

As regards the second situation, the Commission notes that in the circumstances of the case, the alleged facts occurred in the context of an operation against the putschists who, according to the Petitioner, occupied the RPA premises and forced the resumption of its broadcasts in their favour. The facts presented by the Complainant, notably a report drawn up by the office of the Prosecutor General of Burundi, indicate that investigations were opened targeting the insurrectional movement which began on 26 April 2015. This report dates from August 2015 and already includes the facts relating to the attempted coup d'état, in which the RPA and its journalists are suspected of having participated. It is in this context that a procedure aimed at the extradition from Rwanda to Burundi of certain personalities, including the director of the RPA, Bob Rugurika, and another RPA journalist, Gilbert Niyonkuru, allegedly involved in the attempted coup d'état of May 2015, was initiated on 12 October 2015.

The Commission notes that in addition to the case RMPG 697/MA, there was another investigation (RMPG 697/bis/MA/BV/NTH) which, according to the report of the Commission of Inquiry established by the United Nations Human Rights Council on the situation in Burundi, includes the private media that transmitted the putschists' message, namely Isanganiro, Bonesha FM, RPA and Radio-Télévision Renaissance.

The Commission notes that the report of the Commission set up by the Prosecutor General does not mention the attack against the RPA, but rather the attacks against other private radio or television stations by the putschists. And nothing indicates that the second investigation will be conclusive as to the interests of the RPA and its journalists. In these conditions, it would be in the interest of the RPA and its journalists to initiate a process of denunciation of the violations of which they consider themselves victims, by demanding that the perpetrators of the alleged violations also be identified and held accountable.

The Commission notes however that the climate of insecurity which prevailed in the country after the neutralisation of the putschist forces by the government was not conducive to recourse to justice by the RPA and its journalists, the latter having been forced to flee the country or to go into hiding. Moreover, the situation of insecurity and the ineffectiveness of the judicial system in dealing with the petitioner's claims justified dispensing with the exhaustion of local remedies. In this hypothesis, the absence of the opening of an investigation in the country to determine responsibility for the attack on the RPA premises is not attributable to the management of the RPA or its journalists.

The Commission notes that the attempted coup d'état did not prevent the judicial authorities of the Respondent State from opening investigations aimed at identifying and holding accountable its perpetrators and all the persons involved in the attempted unconstitutional change of government. The Respondent State should also create a favourable climate so that other victims of the attempted coup d'état can also have access to justice in safety to assert their rights, all the more so as the case RMPG 697/MA does not include all the victims of the attempted coup d'état, and the case RMPG 697/bis/MA/BV/NTH does not take into account the interests of the RPA and its journalists.

By failing to include the alleged violations committed against the RPA and its journalists in the cases RMPG 697/MA and RMPG 697/bis/MA/BV/NTH, and by failing to create safe conditions for the RPA and its journalists to have access to justice in order to assert the rights they claim to have been violated, the Commission concludes that the Respondent State has violated its obligation, under Article 1 of the Charter, to adopt legislative or other measures to protect the rights under the Charter as well as the right of the RPA and its journalists to access justice under Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter, in order to seek the protection of their allegedly violated rights.

The Commission notes that the independence of the judiciary is abundantly developed in the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance, which provide, among other things, that "the independence of judicial bodies and judicial officers shall be guaranteed by the constitution and laws of the country and respected by the government, its agencies and authorities".

The Commission recalls that in these terms, States parties are required to establish an independent judiciary, a condition for effective judicial protection of human rights under the Charter. This independence can be measured in an abstract or concrete manner. In the first situation, the Commission examines the conformity of the judicial system of a State party with the relevant provisions of the Charter and the applicable international standards on judicial independence. In the second situation, the Commission examines how, in the context of a concrete case before the national judicial bodies, the lack of independence of the judiciary led to the violation of the rights of a complainant.

In the present case, the second situation does not arise, since the victims did not even try to exhaust local remedies. In the first situation, the Commission considers that the facts presented by the Complainant are not sufficient to assess the independence of the judiciary.
The Commission therefore concludes that the complainant's right to have his cause heard by an independent court has not been violated, since he did not even bring his case before the national courts.

Article 14 of the Charter provides that: The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws.

The Commission notes that the classical notion of the right to property confers three (3) faculties on the owner, namely: the use of the object of the property (usus), its enjoyment (fructus) and the right to dispose of it or to get rid of it (abusus). On the basis of this classical notion, Article 14 prohibits interference with the property of others. This is confirmed in the case Open Society Justice Initiative v. Cameroon, in which the Commission starts from the premise that the right to property is protected by the principle of "peaceful possession and enjoyment of property".

In the case Media Rights Agenda v. Nigeria, the Commission reinforced the idea of protection of property by holding that "the sealing of the premises of several publications carried out without due process constitutes a violation of Article 14 of the Charter". For its part, the African Court, in the case Ajavon v. Benin, held that the Respondent State had violated Article 14 of the Charter "by preventing the complainant from carrying out his activity and deriving income from it".

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant alleges the destruction of the building (property of another) and of the RPA's material, equipment and vehicles as well as the suspension of the RPA's broadcasts. The question is whether there was interference with the property of others and whether this is authorised by the Charter.

The Commission notes that the destruction of a property is the most serious form of interference with the use and enjoyment of a property, since it implies its disappearance or its uselessness for the use for which it was intended. The Commission further notes that the suspension of broadcasting, in light of the above-cited jurisprudence in Media Rights Agenda v. Nigeria and Ajavon v. Benin, also implies another form of interference which violates the right to property, in this case, the right of the RPA to continue to broadcast and to generate income for its beneficiaries.

The question arises, however, whether the interference in question is authorised by law, or whether the restriction of the enjoyment of the right to property is permitted for the reasons described in the aforementioned article of the Charter, that is to say for a public need or in the interest of the community. To this end, it should first be noted that Article 14 of the Charter allows restrictions for reasons of public need or general interest. On the other hand, in the case Open Society Justice Initiative v. Cameroon, the Commission considered that Article 27(2) of the Charter is a general restriction clause which also applies to the other rights and freedoms provided for in the Charter. Thus, the right to property must be exercised under Article 27(2) of the Charter which provides that "the rights and freedoms of each individual shall be exercised with due regard to the rights of others, collective security, morality and common interest."

In the present case, it emerges from the submissions that the destruction of the RPA premises and of the equipment found there occurred in the context of the attempted coup d'état during which the RPA premises were stormed and used by the putschists to, for example, announce the removal of the sitting president, among other acts of propaganda. It must therefore be admitted that the attack took place within the framework of the action aimed at neutralising the putschists, who occupied the RPA by force.

The Commission notes that the protection of constitutional institutions against unconstitutional changes of government is an obligation of the Member States of the African Union, Article 4(p) of whose Constitutive Act provides for the principle of "condemnation and rejection of unconstitutional changes of governments". The African Union's own Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance establishes the principle of the prohibition, rejection and condemnation of "any unconstitutional change of government in any Member State as a serious threat to stability, peace, security and development". The Commission finally notes that the Statute of the Court of Justice and Human Rights, in its Article 28(1)(4), includes "unconstitutional change of government" as an international crime. Indeed, the maintenance of constitutional institutions is a fundamental obligation of the Member States of the African Union.

The Commission notes however that the defence of constitutional institutions must be carried out with respect for the human rights of individuals. It is therefore appropriate to assess whether the means used for the defence of constitutional institutions were necessary, appropriate and proportionate to the objective sought. The Complainant submits that the destruction of the RPA was disproportionate, given the type of weaponry used, which set fire to the building, followed by the blocking of access to the site. The Commission notes that the Complainant, in invoking the disproportion of the means used, implicitly admits that the RPA could be targeted as an enemy target, since it was under the control of the putschists.

The Commission recognises that the destruction of the radio may have been an act of revenge, given that relations between the RPA and the government were already strained, which led to the limitation of its broadcasts, then to its suspension until its forced reopening by the putschists. However, the Complainant's written observations are not sufficiently illuminating to demonstrate that the destruction of the radio was an act of revenge, rather than a legitimate act aimed at dislodging the putschists and depriving them of an important instrument of propaganda in a context of conflict.

The Commission notes that the Complainant attaches to the file the audio of the interview of the former spokesperson of the National Police of Burundi, who became a dissident and is in exile. In this audio, the former spokesperson, invited to speak on the circumstances of the attack by the private media, including the RPA, states: I compare this (attack) to a lion that feels wounded, that is to say, the people who were on the side of the authorities saw, for example, the RPA as a station that served the putschists and it had to be destroyed at all costs along with the other private media. As the coup d'état had not completely failed, the people on the side of the authorities saw the media as being able to serve the cause of the putschists, they were therefore considered as enemies to be brought down.

The Commission notes that this statement does not clearly confirm the intention to punish the RPA. In fact, the statement confirms that the attack was due to the fact that the government forces still believe that the coup d'état could still take place and that the RPA and other radio stations which broadcast in favour of the putschists could still be useful to their cause.

The Commission notes on the other hand that the detailed final report of the Commission of Inquiry set up by the UN Human Rights Council states laconically that "a new phase was reached after the attempted coup d'état. On 13 May 2015, the RPA, which had momentarily resumed its broadcasts during the coup d'état, was attacked and set on fire."

The Commission notes that the non-appearance of the Respondent State does not relieve the Complainant of providing proof of the alleged violations. The Commission therefore considers that, in the absence of precise information on the circumstances of the attack against the RPA and given the fact that this attack took place in the context of an attempted coup d'état where the RPA was under the control of the putschists, it has no reason to consider that the destruction of the RPA was disproportionate to the aim pursued.

The Commission considers however that the legitimacy of the destruction of private property used as a tool to effect the unconstitutional change of government does not prevent the government from assuming strict liability for the damage caused to third parties, in particular to the RPA and its journalists, in terms to be determined in the context of an appropriate procedure to be opened at the national level.

Article 9 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every individual shall have the right to receive information. 2. Every individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law.

The Commission considers that this provision covers the right of everyone to have access to information and to express and disseminate his opinions. This right may be exercised individually or within the framework of a legal person. It implies the obligation for States parties to refrain from impeding the exercise of freedom of expression or unlawfully preventing access to information and to create favourable conditions for its effective exercise.

The Commission notes that, as provided for in the Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information (Declaration of Principles), freedom of expression is fundamental in a democratic society. It is particularly important for the participation of individuals in the conduct of the political affairs of their country, notably in the electoral context. In modern societies, this right is exercised through structures organised in the form of radio or other types of media.

The Commission further notes that it is however a right whose exercise may be subject to regulation by law, including restrictions, provided that they are made in accordance with Article 27(2) of the Charter and the applicable international standards.

In the present case, the question that arises is whether the alleged destruction of the RPA premises and the suspension of its activities resulted in a violation of the journalists' rights to carry out their mission of informing the public and also deprived the Burundian people of access to information, notably in an electoral context, or whether the restrictions imposed by the authorities were legitimate and necessary.

The Commission recalls that the incursions at the RPA took place at two moments. Before the attack and after the attack. Before the attack, it should be noted that the intelligence agents present on the RPA premises, followed by the ministers of the Interior, of Public Security and of Communication, ordered the suspension of the broadcast of the demonstrations. This is proven by the information available on the RPA's website and confirmed by other credible sources.

The Commission notes that the presence of the authorities on the premises of a radio station, outside the framework of a courtesy or working visit, notably of police officers to challenge the editorial line of the station, constitutes a form of pressure incompatible with the principle of freedom of expression and of the press in particular, which is all the more true when the pressure is exerted by a member of the government, as was the case with the three ministers.

In a second phase, marked by the attack, followed by the persecution of journalists suspected of collaborating with the putschists, the Commission notes that everything took place after the seizure of the RPA premises by the putschists, who made it an instrument of the coup d'état. The Commission recognises that information is an important tool of opinion control, mobilisation and propaganda in the context of a conflict between two militarised forces, as was the case in the present communication.

The Commission considers that, in these circumstances, an attack on the RPA's facilities may be justified in order to neutralise an enemy propaganda tool, regardless of whether the surrender of the RPA was forced or not. However, the question arises whether the attack was proportionate to the objective pursued.

The Commission considers that, in a normal situation, a radio station can be neutralised by cutting the airwaves through which it broadcasts, unless it has an autonomous antenna. Consequently, an assault or a raid on the radio would not be necessary to interrupt the retransmission by the putschists. However, if the putschists who occupied the radio were armed and had forced the journalists to resume their broadcasts, by threatening them with their weapons, as the Complainant claims, it is not excluded that the RPA premises were struck and destroyed in an attempt to neutralise the putschist forces found there.

The Commission is aware of the need to exercise redoubled caution when it comes to civilian targets, in this case the building and the journalists who worked at the RPA. It is true that at no point does the complainant allege that the civilians who were in the building were hit, apart from the damage caused to the building and to the radio materials and equipment, which the Commission considers may fall under repairable collateral damage. In these conditions, the Commission concludes that, not having sufficient information on the circumstances of the use of force against the RPA's facilities, it cannot consider this action disproportionate.

For all these reasons, the Commission concludes that the violation of freedom of expression found is only that linked to the undue pressure exerted by the authorities on the journalists of the RPA, namely the intelligence services and the three (3) ministers who were present on the RPA premises.

Article 12 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every individual shall have the right to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of a State provided he abides by the law. 2. Every individual shall have the right to leave any country including his own, and to return to his country. This right may only be subject to restrictions, provided for by law for the protection of national security, law and order, public health or morality. 3. Every individual shall have the right, when persecuted, to seek and obtain asylum in other countries in accordance with laws of those countries and international conventions. 4. A non-national legally admitted in a territory of a State Party to the present Charter, may only be expelled from it by virtue of a decision taken in accordance with the law. 5. The mass expulsion of non-nationals shall be prohibited. Mass expulsion shall be that which is aimed at national, racial, ethnic or religious groups.

The Commission emphasises that this provision essentially covers the right of every person to move freely within a country, including his own, to choose the place of his residence in that country, to leave it and to return to it freely, in accordance with the law and subject to the restrictions referred to in paragraph 2 thereof, mass expulsions being prohibited in all circumstances. In the present communication, the question arises whether the flight of the journalists from their own country, in the circumstances in which it took place, constitutes a violation of their rights.

The Commission notes that the journalists left the country after the attempted coup d'état during which the RPA and its journalists were considered as collaborators of the putschists because the latter used the RPA as a propaganda tool.

The Commission notes that in the case John D Ouko v. Kenya and Monim Elgak, Osman Hummeida and Amir Suliman v. Sudan, it held that the involuntary departure of persons from their country for fear of the authorities constitutes a violation of Article 12(2) of the Charter.

The Commission notes that in the present case, the flight is not due simply to the fact that the journalists concerned are suspected of participating in the subversion of the constitutional order. It would be normal for the journalists concerned to appear before the courts and defend their cause in the context of a fair trial. However, the climate created after the neutralisation of the putschists, which is the reason why the victims in this case were not required to exhaust local remedies, forced journalists to flee the country and others to go into hiding. It should be noted that we are talking about journalists who were already subjected to undue pressure, as mentioned above. If the guarantees of a fair trial had prevailed after the neutralisation of the attempted coup d'état, the flight of the journalists abroad would not have been justified.

From the foregoing, it must be concluded that the departure of the journalists from the country was not in conformity with Article 12(2) of the Charter and that, consequently, their right to reside in their own country, provided for in Article 12(1) of the Charter, has been violated.

Article 13 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every citizen shall have the right to participate freely in the government of his country, either directly or through freely chosen representatives in accordance with the provisions of the law. 2. Every citizen shall have the right of equal access to the public service of his country. 3. Every individual shall have the right of access to public property and services in strict equality of all persons before the law.

The above-mentioned provision covers three distinct situations: the participation of every citizen in the public affairs of his country; the right of every citizen to access the public service of his country; and respective public property and services. In his observations, the Complainant alleges that the destruction of the RPA premises and the suspension of its broadcasting constitute a deprivation of the citizens' right to benefit from the public service of radio, in violation of Article 13(2) of the Charter.

The Commission emphasises that while the parties may make their respective legal assessments of the facts, it is for the Commission, in the spirit of Article 45 of the Charter, to make the final characterisation of the facts when it examines the case before it. In the case Evarist v. Tanzania, the African Court held that "the complainant's allegation does not concern Article 3(2) of the Charter, as he claims, which provides that "Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law", but rather Article 7(1) which states that: "Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard".

In the present case, contrary to what the complainant alleges, the Commission is of the view that the situation described falls under Article 13(1) of the Charter which deals with the participation of citizens in the public affairs of their country, directly or indirectly.

The Commission further notes that principle 1(1) of the Declaration of Principles provides that Freedom of expression and access to information are fundamental rights protected by the African Charter and other international human rights laws and standards. The respect, protection and fulfilment of these rights are crucial and indispensable for the free development of the human person, for the creation and nurturing of democratic societies and for enabling the exercise of other rights."

In the case Gabriel Shumba and Others v. Zimbabwe, the Commission recognised that "the right to participate in government is an integral and inextricable part of democracy, such that a State cannot become a democracy if it does not guarantee the right of its citizens to participate in government through free and fair elections".

The Commission notes that participation in public affairs in modern societies is increasingly done through the press, which is tasked with reporting the sentiments and opinions of the population on the state of governance in the country. In doing so, the press, in this case the RPA, renders a public information service to Burundians. In the particular case of Africa, radio plays an important role in this regard, as it is able to reach more remote regions of the country. Moreover, the more diversified the sources of information, the more the citizen is able to understand and give an informed opinion on the state of governance, and private radio is a fundamental instrument for the plurality of information.

The Commission therefore considers that the coverage of a demonstration by the press, in this case the RPA, is a fundamental mechanism to enable citizens to participate in the public affairs of their country. By exerting undue pressure on the RPA, as indicated above, the government placed an obstacle to the participation of citizens in the public affairs of their country, in violation of Article 13(1) of the Charter.

The Commission reiterates its position that it follows from Article 1 of the Charter that it is necessary to grant reparation when a State party fails in its obligations and this failure results in the violation of the rights of individuals. In the present case, the Commission has found a violation of Articles 1, 9, 12, and 13(1) of the Charter. Thus, the request for reparation will be examined in light of the violations found.

The Commission notes that reparation may take various forms: restitution, compensation for moral and other harm, rehabilitation, satisfaction and measures of non-repetition. In the present case, the complainant requests, on the one hand, reparations of a pecuniary nature for moral and material harm and, on the other hand, reparations of a non-pecuniary nature, in this case public apologies (satisfaction).

The Commission notes that apologies constitute one of the forms of reparation, falling under the form of satisfaction. However, the Commission notes that, given the type of violations observed, this form of reparation does not appear necessary or appropriate, given that the violations occurred in a particular context where the government was trying to defend the constitutional and democratic order against the assault of the putschists. On the other hand, it has not been demonstrated that the Respondent State took advantage of the situation to commit violations that normally require apologies, such as crimes affecting the honour and reputation of persons or groups of persons.

The Commission notes that the complainant requests reparation for moral harm in the amount of 500,000 US dollars (five hundred thousand American dollars). The Commission notes that moral harm arises from the suffering caused by the violations, so that the amount of reparation should depend on the gravity of the suffering to be demonstrated by the victim. In the present case, the complainant does not specify the level of suffering, apart from the flight from the country and life in hiding for those who did not manage to flee.

The Commission considers that at this stage of the proceedings and given the level of information on the circumstances of the violations found, the best forum for the determination of pecuniary reparations for moral harm is the national forum, in the context of a process to be initiated by the victims or by the Respondent State before the competent authorities, aimed at establishing the circumstances of the attack and destruction of the RPA and the consequent suspension of the RPA's operation.

As regards the material damage estimated at 1,144,009 Euros (one million one hundred and forty-four thousand and nine Euros), the Commission also considers that the determination of the amount and of the responsibility for this damage should be made in the context of the procedure to be initiated before the competent national authorities.

In light of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. refrains from examining in abstracto the allegation of violation of Article 26 of the Charter; ii. finds that the Respondent State has not violated Article 14 of the Charter; iii. declares that the Respondent State has violated Articles 1, 9, 12(1) and 13(1) of the Charter; iv. urges the Respondent State to create the necessary conditions for the safe return of the RPA journalists who fled the country following the attack on the RPA premises, as well as for the coming out of hiding of those who remained, where applicable; v. requests the Respondent State to open investigations or to create the conditions enabling the RPA and its journalists, as well as other interested parties, to bring actions before the competent entities in order to determine the circumstances of the attack on the RPA premises and to hold the perpetrators of the violations accountable, where applicable. vi. in accordance with Rule 112(2) of the 2010 Rules of Procedure, Finally requests the Republic of Burundi to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of notification of the present decision, on the measures undertaken to implement it. Done in Banjul, The Gambia, at its 74th Ordinary Session held from 21 February to 7 March 2023.

Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu le 9 juin 2014, une communication introduite par l'Association des chrétiens pour l'abolition de la torture (ACAT-Burundi), l'Association pour la protection des droits humains et des personnes détenues (APRODH), le Forum pour la conscience et le développement (FOCODE), le Forum pour le renforcement de la société civile (FORSC) et Track Impunity Always (TRIAL) ci-après dénommés « les Plaintants » pour le compte de Feu Jean-Claude Ndimumahoro ci-après dénommé « la Première victime » et sa famille ci-après dénommée la « Seconde victime » ou la « famille de la Première victime».

La plainte a été introduite contre la République du Burundi (ci-après dénommée Etat défendeur ou le Burundi), Etat ayant ratifié la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine) le 28 juillet 1989.

Les Plaintants rapportent que la Première victime était un citoyen burundais âgé de 34 ans au moment des faits objet de la Communication ; que la Première victime était un homme marié et père de 4 enfants.

Les Plaintants rapportent que la Première victime était un combattant avec le grade de Major au sein des Forces Nationales de Libération (FNL). Ils expliquent que le FNL était un mouvement rebelle qui a déposé les armes en 2009 et s'est constitué en parti politique. Ils indiquent également qu'après des élections présidentielles et parlementaires largement boycottées par l'opposition, les membres du FNL ont commencé à subir à partir de 2010, une politique de répression, d'exécutions extrajudiciaires et d'autres types d'attaques. Ils rapportent qu'au moment de sa démobilisation et de son intégration au sein de l'armée nationale, la Première victime a été rétrogradée et avait fini par quitter l'armée pour se mettre à son compte en tant que mécanicien. Ils soulignent que la Première victime est restée active au sein du parti politique FNL.

Les Plaintants rapportent qu'en septembre 2011, une attaque armée s'est produite dans un bar et que les FNL ont été accusés d'en être les responsables. Ils précisent que du fait des affinités de la Première victime avec un présumé responsable de ladite attaque, la Première victime a commencé à faire l'objet d'une surveillance rapprochée par des agents de l'Etat, des membres du parti au pouvoir et des Imbonerakure (jeunes qui selon les Plaintants, sont affiliés au parti majoritaire et sont accusés d'avoir commis de nombreuses exactions).

Les Plaintants allèguent qu'au-delà de la surveillance, la Première victime a reçu des menaces de mort à maintes reprises et qu'en mai 2012, leur intensification l'avait contrainte à vivre dans la clandestinité.

Les Plaintants rapportent que le 23 juin 2012, la Première victime avait rendez-vous dans l'après-midi à la gare du Nord de Bujumbura, avec M Bizoza, un de ses amis, ancien membre du FNL devenu policier et garde personnelle du Commissaire adjoint de police de la localité de Gitega, M. Michel Rwembe. Ils informent que parti pour ce rendez-vous, la Première victime n'a plus été revue par sa famille.
Les Plaintants indiquent que le 03 juillet 2012, un cadavre sans tête a été retrouvé et que des informations concordantes ont montré qu'il s'agissait du corps de la Première victime.

Les Plaintants informent que selon des témoins, la Première victime a été embarquée dans un véhicule appartenant à l'Administrateur de Gitega, M. Valentin Nahimana. Ils rapportent que lors d'un procès mettant en cause M. Michel Nurweze, un témoin a attesté avoir été détenu avec la Première victime dans une cellule du Service National de Renseignement (SNR) et qu'ils avaient eu à subir de mauvais traitements. Les Plaintants rapportent que l'administration communale a enterré la Première victime sans que la Seconde victime puisse récupérer le corps et indiquent que la tête n'a pas été retrouvée.

Les Plaintants soutiennent que de surcroît, la Seconde victime a continué à faire l'objet de menaces après l'exécution de la Première victime et que des imbonerakure menaçaient quiconque voudrait accompagner la Seconde victime dans son deuil ; ils rapportent que l'épouse de Première victime a fini par déménager avec ses enfants par peur.

Les Plaintants rapportent que lors du procès opposant le Ministère public à M. Michel Nurweze, la famille de la Première victime a voulu se porter partie civile mais leur requête fut rejetée au motif qu'une instruction relative à la mort de la Première victime est en cours au Parquet. Les Plaintants soutiennent qu'en réalité, aucune enquête effective n'a été menée par les autorités compétentes depuis lors.

Les Plaintants soutiennent que les recours internes se sont avérés inefficaces, insatisfaisants et très dangereux. Ils précisent qu'il n'existe pas au Burundi, un cadre légal et institutionnel de protection des victimes et témoins de violations des droits de l'homme. Ils estiment qu'il y a lieu de demander à l'Etat défendeur de prendre des mesures conservatoires pour protéger la Seconde victime et les témoins contre de probables représailles pendant la période d'examen de l'affaire devant la Commission africaine des droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (la Commission).

Les plaignants allèguent que le sort de la Première victime n'est pas isolé, que l'on dénombre au Burundi, plusieurs cas de violations graves notamment les exécutions extrajudiciaires, les détentions arbitraires et la torture. Ils fondent principalement leurs allégations sur des rapports du Bureau des Nations Unies au Burundi et d'autres organisations qui datent de 2010, 2011 et 2012 et sur des recommandations faites au Burundi lors de l'examen périodique universel en 2013. Ils allèguent que ces cas sont en majorité restés impunis.
