From the foregoing, the Commission concludes that there was an arbitrary and extrajudicial execution of the victim by decapitation, one of the most serious forms of violation of the right to life provided for in Article 4 of the Charter.

Article 5 of the Charter states that: Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited.

The Commission notes that this provision of the Charter aims to protect the dignity of the human person. Indeed, the dignity of the human person will be fully respected only if individuals are able to fully enjoy and exercise all the rights inherent in the human person as set out in the Charter and in other applicable human rights instruments. Consequently, when a person is limited in the enjoyment or exercise of his rights, this ultimately affects, in one way or another, his dignity. Thus, the prohibitions provided for in Article 5 of the Charter aim to preserve the hard core of dignity.

The Commission notes that the question that arises here is whether the core of Article 5 of the Charter has been violated, as the complainant claims. In the case El-Sharkawi v. Egypt, the Commission held that in order to determine whether the alleged abuses, conditions of detention and incommunicado detention of the victim were committed in violation of Article 5, the Commission must first determine whether the alleged acts constitute acts of torture and other ill-treatment and, if so, whether there is sufficient evidence to support these allegations.

In the case El-Sharkawi v. Egypt, the Commission invoked its jurisprudence and the Robben Island Guidelines for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture in Africa, to adopt the definition of torture contained in Article 1 of the United Nations Convention against Torture, according to which "torture" means any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, punishing him for an act he or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed, or intimidating or coercing him or a third person, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind, when such pain or suffering is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity.

In the same decision, the Commission considered that this definition of torture contains four (4) cumulative elements, namely: i) the mental or physical suffering must be severe; ii) the act or omission must be intentionally inflicted; iii) the commission of this act or omission must have a specific purpose; iv) and the act or omission must be inflicted by a public official or with his express or tacit consent.

In the present case, the conditions of detention, the lack of communication with the family, the physical violence, the throwing of food on the ground for the victim to eat, and the fact that the victim was decapitated, indicate the severity of the suffering inflicted; there is also no doubt that these acts were carried out intentionally, by State agents, for a specific purpose, namely to pressure the victim to denounce other FNL members, change party or abandon his activities within the party. If these four elements are present, we must conclude that the victim was tortured.
For the reasons mentioned above, the Commission finds a violation of Article 5 of the Charter.

Article 6 of the Charter states that: Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained.

The Commission notes that this provision of the Charter clearly prohibits detentions that were not carried out in accordance with the law. The Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa set out the obligations of States with regard to the right to liberty and security, including the prohibition of arbitrary detention, the obligation to detain only when the conditions strictly prescribed by law are met, on the order of the competent authorities and in accordance with their decision and for the purposes determined by law, and the obligation to open effective investigations in order to identify the perpetrators, hold them accountable and provide reparation to the victims.

The above-mentioned Article protects two (2) fundamental rights, namely freedom of action and movement and personal security. The first right has several aspects that can be summarised in two: the aspect that includes the right not to be detained or imprisoned by public authorities, except for reasons and under conditions prescribed by law; and the aspect that includes the right not to have one's liberty restricted or to be confined in a certain space, without reasons and under conditions prescribed by law.

As regards personal security, it implies that citizens and all those who have chosen Africa to live in must be able to do so in safety and peacefully, free from threats and attacks emanating from public authorities or private individuals.

Any restriction on these two (2) rights must comply with what is previously established in a given legal norm. These rights are mentioned in the Charter in a simplistic manner and without mentioning the guarantees enjoyed by prisoners (detainees and convicts), which explains why certain underdeveloped penal systems or those less concerned with these aspects contained in most Constitutions of African countries do not sufficiently protect individuals whose liberty is limited, in particular detentions considered arbitrary (unlawful/irregular and indefinite). This is what happened in this case.

The Commission recalls that in the case Constitutional Rights Project/Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, it had observed that "where individuals are detained without charge, [...] this constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of their liberty and thus a violation of Article 6".

In the present case, the detention of the victim that preceded his decapitation also took place outside the legal framework, since there is no trace of a competent authority having ordered his detention. It is for this reason that the Commission considered his execution as extrajudicial. It must therefore be concluded that the victim's rights to liberty and security, as provided for in Article 6 of the Charter, were violated even before his decapitation.

Article 7 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal. 2. No one may be condemned for an act or omission which did not constitute a legally punishable offence at the time it was committed. No penalty may be inflicted for an offence for which no provision was made at the time it was committed. Punishment is personal and can be imposed only on the offender.

For its part, Article 26 of the Charter provides that: States parties to the present Charter shall have the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts and shall allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter.

The Commission notes that Article 7 concerns the procedural component of the right to a fair trial and that Article 26 concerns its institutional aspect, that is, the existence of courts whose independence must be guaranteed by States parties.

The Commission considers that in the context of the present case, the question of access to justice must be analysed in correlation with the Respondent State's obligation to open an effective investigation after learning of the decapitation of the victim. However, the Commission had already concluded that the Respondent State had not complied with its obligation to open an effective investigation after learning of the decapitation of the victim, notably by not allowing the effective participation of the victim's relatives in the proceedings as civil party. Indeed, it is unnecessary for the Commission to revisit this question under Article 7 since it has already been examined under Articles 4 and 5 of the Charter and the conclusions of that examination are also applicable in this case. The Commission considers, however, that a particular aspect concerning access to justice arises at the time when the victim was detained without anyone knowing where he was. Between 23 June 2012, the date of his arrest, and 3 July 2012, the date on which his body appeared decapitated, the victim was objectively prevented by the authorities holding him incommunicado from accessing justice to assert his rights, namely to challenge his arbitrary detention, which could have saved his life.

Under the Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, the victim has the right to be informed, at the time of his arrest, of the reasons for his detention, of his right to have recourse to a lawyer and to be examined by a doctor, as well as of his right to communicate with his family or friends.

The Commission is particularly strict as regards access to justice. For example, in the cases El-Sharkawi v. Egypt and Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, the Commission held that the mere detention of persons without trial or charge constitutes a violation of the right of access to justice. In the present case, the situation is more serious because the victim was detained without his relatives knowing where he was, and outside of criminal proceedings, so that the possibility of accessing justice to protect himself against arbitrary detention was nil, and the relatives could do nothing on behalf of the victim.

As regards the alleged violation of Article 26 of the Charter, the Commission considers that the complainant has not presented evidence demonstrating the lack of independence of the judiciary in his particular case. On the other hand, for the victim, the question of the independence of the judiciary did not arise since he was unable to seize the courts to challenge his detention. Consequently, the Commission finds a violation of Article 7(1)(a), insofar as the victim was detained without knowing where he was and, on the other hand, a non-violation of Article 26, because the question of the independence of the courts does not arise, the victim never having brought the case before the courts.
Article 9(2) of the Charter provides that Every individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law.
Article 10(1) of the Charter states that "Every individual shall have the right to free association provided that he abides by the law."

Article 13(1) of the Charter states that "Every citizen shall have the right to participate freely in the government of his country, either directly or through freely chosen representatives in accordance with the provisions of the law."

The Commission notes that the three (3) Articles of the Charter are linked. The first concerns the right of every person to have opinions and to disseminate them. The second concerns freedom of association and the third participation in the public affairs of the country. In other words, in a democratic society governed by law, freedom of expression is guaranteed and can be exercised individually or within an association, notably of a political nature. By contrast, participation in the political affairs of the country is essentially through membership of a political party.

The Commission notes that, as indicated in the Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information (Declaration of Principles), freedom of expression is fundamental in a democratic society, in particular for the purposes of the direct and indirect participation of citizens in the public affairs of their country through political associations.

In this case, the victim was arrested and decapitated because of his membership of a political party, in this case the FNL, and his opposition to the government. By joining the FNL, the victim was exercising his right to be part of a political association opposed to the government and to exercise his political freedoms through that party, while taking part in the conduct of the public affairs of his country through that party.

The Commission recognises that these three (3) rights are not absolute. However, as regards an arrest followed by a decapitation in the conditions already seen in the examination of the allegations of violation of Articles 4, 5 and 6 of the Charter, the Commission is of the view that there is no question of examining a possible justification of restrictions on Articles 9(2), 10(1) and 13(1) of the Charter.

The Commission finds that not only did the Respondent State not take the measures it should have taken to ensure the victim an optimal exercise of his rights, but it allowed its agents to detain and decapitate him for having exercised his rights. Consequently, the Commission finds that the violation of Articles 9(2), 20(1) and 13(1) of the Charter is flagrant and no longer needs to be demonstrated.
Article 18(1) of the Charter provides that The family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral.

The Commission finds that the idea of forming a family is inseparable from cohabitation, from being together, from sharing the same family home, except in the case of compelling reasons or if the couple itself decides otherwise. In the event of separation for compelling reasons, contact with the family must be maintained. It is no coincidence that the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa provide for the right of detainees to maintain contact with their family. This provision also aims to enable the detainee to remain in contact with his family.

The Commission's interpretation of this provision reaffirms that it imposes on the State a positive obligation with regard to the family. The State has the obligation to help the family satisfy its needs and interests and to protect it against abuses of all kinds perpetrated by its own leaders and organs and by third parties.

The State also has the negative obligation to refrain from violating the rights and interests of the family. Thus, in its action and in order to comply with the provisions of Article 18(1) and (2), the State must take measures taking into account the interests of the family, the right to family life and the safeguarding of its unity.

In this case, the situation is even more serious since the victim's relatives, during his detention, had no idea where he was and how they could obtain news of him in order to exercise their right to visit him. The worst occurred when his body was found decapitated and abandoned in the street. The Respondent State, which should have taken measures to protect the family as it has the duty to do under Article 18(1) of the Charter, allowed its agents to carry out acts that infringed this right in its most serious form, namely the extrajudicial execution of one of its members. The Commission notes that in the cases Article 19 v. State of Eritrea and Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, it considered that incommunicado detention constituted a violation of the right to family.
In these circumstances, it must be concluded that the victim's right to family under Article 18(1), and the right of his family to family life and unity, protected by Article 18(2), were violated.

Article 2 of the Charter states that: Every individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as race, ethnic group, color, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status.

The Commission observes that this provision prohibits persons from being disadvantaged in the exercise of the rights provided for in the Charter on the basis of one or more of the grounds mentioned therein. The Commission further observes that the principle of prohibition of discrimination appears as the corollary of the principle of equality between persons provided for in Article 3 of the Charter. Although the grounds of discrimination provided for in Article 2 of the Charter are illustrative, this provision is clear as regards the prohibition of discrimination on political grounds. However, the question arises as to what discrimination is within the meaning of Article 2 of the Charter.

In the case Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe, the Commission defined discrimination as the application of any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference based on grounds such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, fortune, birth or other status, and which has the purpose or effect of nullifying or impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by all persons, on an equal footing, of all rights and freedoms.

In that decision, the Commission considered that there were three preconditions for discrimination: the impugned measure stipulates a difference in treatment, it has a certain effect and it is based on a prohibited ground.

In this case, the Commission concluded that the detention and decapitation of the victim are attributable to agents of the Respondent State. It should be noted that the victim was a member of the FNL as an armed movement before its conversion into a political party; after the conversion of the FNL into a political party, the victim demobilised from the army of the country to join his former movement, which had become a political party. The complainant's observations, supported by the report of the United Nations Secretary-General submitted to the United Nations Security Council and by documents of Human Right Watch (HRW) and Crises Group describing the persecution of former FNL members, support the idea that the detention and decapitation of the victim were due to the fact that he belonged to a different political party and professed a political ideology different from that of the government.

The Commission notes that the treatment of the victim is differentiated compared to members of other political parties, in particular those affiliated with or associated with the ruling party. This treatment has a certain effect on the life of the victim and led to his detention, torture and decapitation. Finally, the detention and decapitation of the victim were based on the fact that he belonged to a different political party and professed a different ideology, a ground which is expressly prohibited by Article 2 of the Charter.
For the reasons mentioned above, the Commission concludes that the victim's right not to be subjected to discrimination, as provided for in Article 2 of the Charter, was violated.

The Commission notes that the complaint alleges the absence of an official and thorough investigation into the detention and decapitation of the victim. The Commission notes that when the Respondent State became aware of the decapitation of the victim, indicating a situation of extrajudicial execution and a consequent violation of a number of other related rights, namely the rights provided for in Articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9(1), 10(1), 13(1) and 18(1), the Respondent State should immediately have proceeded to open an official investigation, conducted by competent and impartial entities with adequate means, in order to identify, hold accountable and remedy the violations committed.

The Commission's General Comment No. 3 on the right to life provides that the failure of the State to take, in a transparent manner, all necessary measures to investigate suspicious deaths and any execution perpetrated by State agents and to identify persons or groups responsible for violations of the right to life and to hold them accountable constitutes, in itself, a violation of this right by the State. This is all the more true where a culture of impunity is tolerated. Any investigation must be conducted promptly, impartially, thoroughly and transparently.

The Commission recalls that in the case Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions v. Sudan, it held that under Article 4 of the Charter, the right to life is the supreme right of the human being. It is the basis of all human rights and, without it, all other rights are meaningless. ... It is the duty of the State to protect human life against unjustified or arbitrary actions of public authorities and private persons. The duty of the State to protect the right to life has been interpreted broadly as including the prohibition of arbitrary killings by State agents and as controlling and strictly limiting the circumstances in which a person may be deprived of life by State authorities. This includes the need to conduct effective official investigations when persons have been killed as a result of the use of force by State agents, to guarantee the right to life through effective provisions of criminal law aimed at deterring the commission of crimes against the person, and to put in place law enforcement mechanisms for the prevention, suppression, investigation and penalisation of violations of criminal law.

In the case of extrajudicial executions, the United Nations Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-Legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions provide for the obligation to open an investigation immediately, conducted by independent and impartial bodies, endowed with all the means and sufficient powers to gather all the information necessary for the manifestation of the truth, and involving the family of the victim and civil society. If the family contests the investigation, the requested State may set up a commission responsible for An Organ of the The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights31 Bijilo Annex Layout, Banjul, North District,West Coast Region, Gambia,Phone: (220) 230 4361 Fax: (220) 441 05 04Email: au-banjul@afrika-union.orghttps://achpr.au.int/ the investigation. The investigation shall establish the circumstances of the execution, the perpetrators, their responsibility and the reparations to the victims within a reasonable time.

The Commission notes that the immediate opening of a complete and effective investigation was also necessary because of the indications that the victim had been tortured before his decapitation. This is required by the Principles on the Effective Investigation and Documentation of Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and General Comment No. 4 on the right to redress for victims of torture in Africa.

The Commission notes that, according to the Respondent State's observations, a judicial investigation was opened with the Public Prosecutor's Office (RMP No. 41547) and the Gitega High Court (RPC No. 547). However, the complainant considers that this procedure was not effective since the family members were never called to testify. The complainant alleges that the family members, represented by the victim's grandmother, wanted to join as civil party, but that this was refused to them.

The Commission welcomes that contact with the family is one of the principles that should guide post-mortem investigations. In its observations on admissibility, the Respondent State did not respond to the applicant's allegations on the lack of seriousness of the case for the purposes of the exhaustion of local remedies, in particular the fact that the victim's relatives were never called to testify. The Commission notes that in its observations on local remedies, the Respondent State had the possibility of providing more elements to enlighten the Commission on the seriousness of the case, which it did not do.

The Commission considers that in the absence of contrary information, and given the general picture of a systematic failure of justice in the country at the time, of such magnitude as to justify not exhausting local remedies, the Commission has no reason to believe that the investigation opened following the decapitation of the victim was genuinely aimed at identifying the perpetrators of the violations, holding them accountable and providing reparation to the direct and indirect victims.

Thus, the Commission concludes that the Respondent State violated its obligation to immediately open an official and thorough investigation into the circumstances of the detention, the killing and the decapitation of the victim, as required by the provisions of the violated Charter, in particular Articles 4 and 5 of the Charter, as well as the United Nations principles and the Commission's General Comment No. 4 mentioned above.

Article 1 of the Charter states that: The Member States of the Organization of African Unity parties to the present Charter shall recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enumerated in this Charter and shall undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them.

The Commission notes that this provision stipulates the general obligation of States parties to recognise and protect the human rights set out in the Charter. It starts from the principle that human rights are realised at the national level and that States parties bear primary responsibility for them. In addition to the specific obligations related to each right set out in the Charter, Article 2 of the Charter provides for a general obligation that complements the specific obligations. It is on this basis that, in the case Sir Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission stated that Article 1 gives the Charter the legally binding character that is always attributed to international treaties of this nature. Consequently, a violation of any provision of the Charter automatically means a violation of Article 1. If a State Party to the Charter fails to recognise the provisions of the Charter, there is no doubt that it violates this Article.
In this case, the Commission found that Articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9(2), 10(1), 13(1) and 18(1) of the Charter were violated. Consequently, Article 1 of the Charter was also violated.

The Commission reiterates its position that it follows from Article 1 of the Charter that there is a duty of reparation when a State Party fails in its obligations and that failure results in the violation of the rights of persons. The Commission notes that in this case, it has found a violation of Articles 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9(2), 10(1), 13(1) and 18(1) of the Charter. The Commission also notes that, in addition to the existence of a violation, the granting of reparations requires that there be harm, as proved by the complainant, and that this harm result from the violation committed (causal link).

The Commission notes that reparations may take different forms. In the case El-Sharkawi v. Egypt, the Commission, relying on the Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy for Victims of Gross Violations of International Human Rights Law and Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law (2005), stated that full and effective reparations include restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition. The guidelines also specify that compensation should be provided for any economically assessable damage, such as physical or mental harm; lost opportunities, including employment, education and social benefits; material damages and loss of earnings, including loss of earning potential; moral damage; and costs required for legal or expert assistance, medicine and medical services, and psychological and social services.

The Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa (Luanda Guidelines) stipulate that Any person who is the victim of unlawful or arbitrary arrest or detention, or of torture and ill-treatment during police custody or pre-trial detention, has the right to seek and obtain effective reparations for the violation of his or her rights. This right extends to the immediate family or dependants of the direct victim. Remedies include the following measures, among others: a. Restitution to restore the victim to the situation that would have existed if the violation had not taken place. b. Compensation, including any quantifiable damage resulting from the violation of the right and any physical or mental harm (such as physical or mental harm, pain, suffering and emotional distress, loss of opportunities, including education, material damages and loss of actual or potential earnings, harm to reputation or dignity, and costs of legal services or expert assistance, medicines, medical services and others), as well as legal costs, and psychological and social services). c. Rehabilitation, including medical and psychological care as well as legal and social services. In the present case, the complainant requests appropriate reparations to the heirs of the victim, including the payment of monetary compensation for the material and moral damage suffered, as well as orders of restitution, psychological, social and economic rehabilitation, restitution (apologies and firm condemnation of the violations committed and publication of the Commission's decision) and non-repetition, the latter in order to ensure political pluralism. The different forms of reparation requested by the complainant are analysed below.

The Commission notes that the complainant requests pecuniary reparations for material and moral damage. As indicated above, in order to grant reparation, in addition to the existence of the violation, it is necessary to determine the victims, the damage and its link to the violation found. As regards material damage, the complainant presents no material damage that he allegedly suffered and the corresponding evidence. However, he may do so before the competent national authorities. Consequently, the Commission analyses below the other elements necessary for the granting of pecuniary remedies for moral damage.

The Commission notes that there is no doubt that the victim of the violations is the one who suffered them in persona. This is a natural consequence of the ownership of rights. If a person's right is violated, the victim is the holder of that right. However, in international law, the notion of victim is more flexible. For example, in the Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy for Victims of Gross Violations of International Human Rights Law and Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law (2005), the victim is defined as follows: persons who individually or collectively suffered harm, including physical or mental injury, emotional suffering, economic loss or substantial impairment of their fundamental rights, through acts or omissions that constitute gross violations of international human rights law, or serious violations of international humanitarian law. Where appropriate, and in accordance with domestic law, the term "victim" also includes the immediate family or dependants of the direct victim and persons who have suffered harm in intervening to assist victims in distress or to prevent victimization.

Under the Luanda Guidelines, mentioned above, compensation extends to the immediate family or dependants. In the case Zongo v. Burkina Faso, concerning the State's lack of diligence in investigating the death of four (4) persons, including the journalist Norbert Zongo, the African Court held that "it can reasonably be considered that those who acted (directly or through representation) in the front line in this case and who suffered most from this situation are the spouses, children, fathers and mothers of the deceased", who appear in the final decision as indirect victims.

The Commission notes that in this case, the direct victim is the deceased; the indirect victims are his wife, the four (4) children of the couple and the victim's grandmother. It should be noted that the victim's grandfather is the one who raised him and who would have represented the family as civil party in the proceedings opened, if she had been authorised to do so. Moreover, the grandfather testified to describe the circumstances of his detention. He is therefore a person who lived through the events and who was exposed to the suffering caused by the situation. He is therefore entitled to compensation for moral damage.

The Commission notes that the complainant does not specify the amount of monetary reparations requested for moral damage. He simply asks the Commission to order appropriate reparations. The Commission shares the African Court's view on the question of moral damage and its causal link. It should be noted that the African Court's position was inspired by the jurisprudence of its Inter-American counterpart. In the case Zongo v. Burkina Faso, the African Court states that As regards the causal link between the unlawful act and the moral damage suffered, the Court considers that such a link may result from the violation of a human right, as an automatic consequence, without any proof being necessary.

The Commission notes that the African Court considers that once there has been a violation, there is moral damage. In this case, a violation having been committed, the existence of moral damage is therefore legally presumed and the causal link with the violations found is also established. The question nevertheless arises of the extent of the moral damage. In this regard, the Commission considers that the extent of the suffering and the resulting moral damage could be established by medical certificates or other means capable of demonstrating the severity of the suffering of the victim and his relatives, namely trauma, anguish, stress, depression or other mental illnesses resulting from the suffering caused by the violations committed against the victim and the treatment reserved for the family in the course of the process.

The Commission notes, however, that the conditions of the victim's detention, the physical abuse inflicted on him, the torture inflicted and the context of the victim's decapitation and thus of the abandonment of his body in a public place, as well as the fact that his head was not found, and thus not properly buried, demonstrate the level of seriousness of the violations committed and the intensity of the suffering of the victim and his relatives. In these terms, the Commission has no doubt about the suffering of the victim before his decapitation and that of his own family who suffered from not knowing the fate that was in store for their relative until it was surprised by the appearance of a lifeless body and the missing head. Indeed, the suffering of the direct victim and the members of his family in these circumstances is materially immeasurable.

As regards the amount of reparations, the Commission is of the view that it would be prudent for the complainant to claim the amount of reparations he considers appropriate to his case and to justify it. If this is not the case, it makes the Commission's task more delicate but it is not deprived of the power to determine the amount of reparations appropriate to the case. It should be noted that even if the complainant had proposed an amount of reparation for moral damage, the Commission would still have the final say.

The Commission notes that according to its General Comment No. 4 on the right to redress for victims of torture in Africa, "compensation should be fair, adequate and proportionate to the material, moral and other damage suffered." However, in the present case, the Commission is of the view that the determination of the amount of compensation must be entrusted to the competent national courts, which are better placed to assess the details of the damage caused and the amount of compensation to be awarded.

The Commission notes that the applicant requests a thorough and effective investigation into the detention and decapitation of the victim and the other violations committed against him, by independent and impartial judicial bodies, in order to identify and hold the perpetrators of the crimes criminally responsible. The Commission recalls that it has already ruled on this question when examining the allegation of violation of Articles 4 and 5 of the Charter and maintains the conclusion resulting from that analysis, by which it granted the applicant's request for the opening of a thorough and effective investigation, conducted by an independent and impartial body, endowed with the means necessary for its work, and that the victim's relatives be involved, in accordance with national law and applicable international standards on investigations opened following an extrajudicial execution.

The complainant requests restitution as well as measures of psychological, social and economic rehabilitation. The Commission recalls that it has already indicated above that reparations may take these forms. As regards the request for restitution, the Commission stresses that it does not appear appropriate to act on the complainant's request, given that the violations found cannot give rise to restitution, that is, the victims cannot be restored to the situation in which they would have been had the violations not been committed.

As regards psychological, social and economic rehabilitation, the Commission notes that the complainant presents no rehabilitation measure, nor does he provide a framework that could justify the Commission ordering such measures suo moto. Thus, the Commission considers that the monetary reparations ordered above are sufficient to allow for psychological, social and economic rehabilitation.

The Commission notes that this measure is also part of the possible reparations, falling into the category of measures of satisfaction. The Commission considers that the detention, torture, decapitation of the victim and the burial of the headless body in the street constitute situations serious enough to warrant a public acknowledgement of the gravity of the facts, apologies to the family and the publication of the Commission's decision or a summary thereof in one of the most widely read local newspapers or in its entirety on the official websites of the government or the judiciary, as the case may be.

The complainant requests the Commission to order the Respondent State to take measures aimed at guaranteeing that what happened does not recur, with a view to ensuring political pluralism. The Commission notes that this measure is part of the possible reparations. However, the Commission recalls that it has not specifically analysed the measures or shortcomings of the national law enforcement oversight system that led to the occurrence of the violations found, and that it has not been asked to do so. The same applies to the measures relating to the protection of victims. The Commission considers that if it were to order measures aimed at guaranteeing non-repetition and the protection of witnesses, these would tend to be generic and would not be based on specific shortcomings of the system that have been found. For these reasons, the Commission rejects this request for reparation.

In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. The Respondent State has not violated Article 26 of the Charter. ii. The Respondent State has violated Articles 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9(2), 10(1), 13(1) and 18(1) of the Charter. iii. Urges the Respondent State to grant reparations to the wife of the victim, the four (4) children of the couple and the victim's grandfather, for the material and moral damage suffered. iv. Rejects the request for restitution and psychological, social and economic rehabilitation. v. Urges the Respondent State to open an official and thorough investigation, conducted by an independent and impartial body, endowed with the necessary means, with a view to identifying the victims, holding them accountable and granting them reparations, without prejudice to the reparations authorised in the present decision. The victim's relatives should be involved in the process, including civil society, in accordance with national legislation and international standards applicable to investigations conducted following an extrajudicial execution. vi. Urges the Respondent State to present public apologies to the victims and to firmly condemn the violations committed, as well as to publish the present decision or its summary in one of the most widely circulated local newspapers or in its entirety on the websites of the government or the judiciary, as the case may be. vii. The Complaint was submitted by Sudan Democracy First Group, REDRESS, Human Rights Watch, INTERIGHTS and Enough Project (the Complainants), on behalf of Sudanese Civilians in South Kordofan and Blue Nile (the Victims) against the Republic of Sudan (the Respondent State).
The Respondent State is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights 1981 (African Charter), having ratified the same on 18 February 1986.

The Complainants claimed that starting on 5 June 2011, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and militia groups, under the control of the Government of the Republic of Sudan, launched a series of assaults against civilians in South Kordofan. On 1 September 2011, a similar pattern of attacks began against civilians in Blue Nile State.

The Complainants stated that more than 31 attacks have been documented since the assaults began. Among them are the 26 June 2011 bombing of the market in Kurchi, South Kordofan, which killed 13 civilians and injured more than 20 others, most of whom were women and children.

According to the Complainants, eyewitnesses in Tilo, South Kordofan, reported that the SAF sealed the doors of civilian homes and then set fire to the buildings, burning alive the civilians who were trapped inside. Further reports, which are corroborated by satellite imagery, showed that on or about 8 June 2011 the SAF removed the bodies of slain Sudanese Civilians from the Tilo and El Gardud villages in South Kordofan and placed them in mass graves that had been freshly dug for that purpose.

The Complainants claimed that the pattern has been the same in Blue Nile State. On 1 September 2011, SAF forces attacked Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile. Refugees recounted that Government war planes targeted civilian areas and armed soldiers chased, captured, and killed civilians fleeing from the attacks. Agents of the Government reportedly captured and killed some of the civilians. The Complainants submitted that the precise casualty numbers are unavailable, because the Respondent State has prevented independent observers from accessing the war zones in either South Kordofan or Blue Nile.

The Complainants submitted that, as of January 2012, the United Nations (UN) Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that approximately 366,000 individuals had been internally displaced or severely affected by the violence in the two States. Since June 2011, more than 140,000 refugees fled South Kordofan or Blue Nile to either Ethiopia or South Sudan.

The Complainants alleged that the victims do not necessarily find safety in refugee camps. This is because, in November 2011, the SAF bombed the Yida refugee camp in Unity State, South Sudan, which is home to many of those displaced from South Kordofan.

The Complainants further submitted that the Respondent State has justified its assaults under the guise of targeting the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North ("SPLM-N"), an organised armed group that has been active in these two areas.

The Complainants alleged that the assaults on Sudanese Civilians have nothing to do with military operations and that agents of the Respondent State have deliberately bombed civilian homes, schools and medical facilities, causing untold loss of life, massive displacements, injuries and damage to property.

The Complainants further alleged that in addition to civilian dwellings, schools and hospitals, the SAF also targeted fields used for civilian food cultivation. Since these assaults took place during the planting season, the Victims will be left without a harvest, creating grave food insecurity. In certain parts of Blue Nile State, it is estimated that only 15% of arable land was planted. When Amnesty International reportedly visited South Kordofan in August 2011, it found that many of those displaced by the conflict had abandoned their fields during prime cultivation time, and were faced with impending starvation. On 14 February 2012, the UN Security Council warned that if food insecurity in some areas of Southern Kordofan and Blue Nile States were not addressed immediately, it could reach emergency levels.

The Complainants further alleged that the Respondent State has refused to allow international organisations to deliver humanitarian aid, including food and medical supplies, into the affected areas. According to the Complainants, in November 2011, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network estimated that areas of southern Blue Nile and South Kordofan were approaching emergency levels of food insecurity - one level short of famine.

The Complainants alleged that the predominantly Arab Government in the Respondent State has made clear its intention to cleanse South Kordofan and Blue Nile States of the ethnic and racial groups who live there. The Complainants made reference to a video published by Al Jazeera of the governor of South Kordofan, Ahmad Haroun, telling SAF soldiers deployed to the Nuba Mountains, in South Kordofan, to "take no prisoners . . . hand over the place swept, rubbed, crushed."
The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State violated the Victims' rights under Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7(1)(a), 12(1), 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 23 of the African Charter.

The Complainants jointly prayed the Commission: 1. To recognise violations of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 9(1), 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 23 of the African Charter; 2. To request the Respondent State to guarantee all the violated rights detailed in this Submission; 3. To accept a separate submission on remedies and reparation and to allow for a hearing on reparation if it has found the Respondent State to be in violation of the African Charter in order to address the:i. appropriate forms of reparation as provided for by the UN Basic Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Remedy and Reparation for Victims of Gross Violations of International Human Rights Law and Serious Violations of International Humanitarian Law, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition for the victims of these violations, including for the next of kin of those who were unlawfully killed by SAF, PDF, or other state forces and authorities, or who suffered harm as a result of the failure of the state to provide adequate protection against violations and to request the Government of Sudan to give effect to such findings; ii. appropriate collective measures of reparation to repair collective or group harm caused by the Respondent State's campaign of massive and serious human rights violations; 4. In addition, to request the Respondent State to set up an independent inquiry to carry out prompt, effective and impartial investigations into the circumstances of the above mentioned violations, and ensure that where sufficient evidence exists, the perpetrators are brought to justice and held accountable for any violations; 5. To call on the Respondent State to: (a) immediately release all arbitrarily detained civilians and ensure that those detained on a lawful basis enjoy full due process rights; (b) urgently facilitate unimpeded access by humanitarian aid groups to deliver assistance to civilians in all parts of Southern Kordofan and Blue Nile; (c) allow full and effective access for international monitors, including human rights officers, to Southern Kordofan and Blue Nile States; (d) provide appropriate housing and basic needs to the displaced persons in accordance with the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement and the AU Convention for the protection and assistance of internally displaced persons in Africa; (e) ensure the safe return of the displaced persons to their communities after the unrest has ceased; (f) reform its national legislation so that it provides: i. for adequate and effective safeguards against abusive use of force as well as abuse of powers in the course of arrest and detention by government forces, law enforcement and security officials; ii. that arbitrary or abusive use of force as well as violations committed in the course of arrest and detention procedures by government forces and law enforcement officials, including torture and ill-treatment, enforced disappearances and rape, are effectively recognised as a criminal offence under the law in Sudan; iii. For criminal accountability of officials responsible for violations, including by removing immunity legislation for such crimes that officials enjoy under Sudanese legislation. (g) ensure training in international human rights and international humanitarian law to law enforcement and military personnel and National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) agents.
The Secretariate received the Complaint on 21 July 2011 and the Communication was seized during the 50 Ordinary Session held from the 24 October to 5 November 2011 in Banjul, The Gambia.
On 7 November 2011, the Commission issued Provisional Measures and respectfully requested the Respondent State to intervene with a view to preventing irreparable harm being caused to the Victims.

By letter dated 16 November 2011, the Complainant was informed about Seizure of the Communication and a copy of the Provisional Measures was forwarded to the same. A Note Verbale informing the Respondent State about the Complaint was also sent on the same date.
Communication 420/12 was subsequently received at the Secretariat on 23 April 2012.

At its 12 Extra-Ordinary Session which took place from 30 July to 4 August 2012 in Algiers, Algeria, the Commission decided to join Communication 420/12 with Communication 402/11 and consider them together as a single Communication in line with Rule 96(1) of its Rule of Procedure 2010. The Respondent State and the Complainants were notified accordingly.
The Commission at its 12 Extra-Ordinary Session also considered the implementation of its Provisional Measures and decided that the Provisional Measures be resent.

On 21 August 2012, the Secretariat forwarded a Note Verbale to the Respondent State resending the Provisional Measures. It requested the Respondent State to report to the Commission on the actions taken to implement the Provisional Measures issued against it within fifteen (15) days of the receipt of the request for Provisional Measures.

The Commission during its 52 Ordinary Session which took place from 9 to 22 October 2012 in Yamoussoukro, Cote d'Ivoire, took note of the non-response of the Respondent State and decided to bring the matter to the attention of the relevant organs of the African Union (AU) and to proceed to consider the Communication at the admissibility level.
On 7 November 2012, the Complainants' submissions on Admissibility were forwarded to the Respondent State and the State was requested to submit on Admissibility within sixty (60) days.

On 1 March 2013, the Embassy of the Republic of Sudan in Dakar, Senegal, informed the Secretariat that the submissions of the Complainants which they had received were illegible. In response, the Secretariat re-transmitted the submissions on 5 March 2013, and informed the Complainants.

On 9 April 2013 and 10 June 2013, the Secretariat received letters from the Complainants raising preliminary objections relating to the Respondent State's submission on Admissibility and requesting that the Commission proceed to decide on the Admissibility of the Communication solely on the basis of the Complainants' submissions.

On 10 April 2013, the Secretariat received a Note Verbale from the Embassy of the Republic of Sudan in Dakar stating that the Respondent State is still not able to read the Complainants' submissions on Admissibility which were re-sent by the Secretariat on 5 March 2013.
On 21 June 2013, the Secretariat wrote to the Respondent State and the Complainants informing them that the matter will be tabled before the Commission at its next Session.

The Commission took a decision on the Admissibility of the Communication during its 14 Extra-Ordinary Session which took place in Nairobi, Kenya, from 20 to 24 July 2013 and both Parties were informed on 6 August 2013.
The Communication was deferred during the 55 Ordinary Session, and subsequent Extra-Ordinary Sessions of the Commission and both Parties were informed in March and June 2014 consecutively.

On 4 June 2015, the Secretariat sent a Note Verbale reference number ACHPR/COMM/402/11-420//12/SUD/903/15 by post to the Respondent State's Embassy in Senegal notifying the Respondent's State that it has been granted a period of 30 calendar days from the date of the notification within which to file its written observations; and that the Commission will proceed to adopt a decision on the merits if the said observations are not received within the time prescribed.

On 3 November 2016, the Complainants requested the Commission to stay proceedings for a period of 12 months due to the steps that were being taken by the Respondent State to resolve the dispute locally.

With the time for the Respondent State to file its written submissions and after repeated reminders to submit its response to the Complainants' written brief on the merit, the Commission has now proceeded to decide the case on the merit in light of Respondent State's default.

According to the Complainants, in cases of serious and massive violations of human rights, the Commission needs to interpret the requirement of exhaustion of domestic remedies in light "of its duty to protect human and peoples' rights as provided for in the African Charter." Further, "the condition that internal remedies must have been exhausted cannot be applied literally to those cases in which it is neither practicable nor desirable for the complainants or the victims to pursue such internal channels of remedy in every case of violation of human rights. Such is the case where there are many victims."

The Complainants submitted that, in the present case, the Respondent's alleged indiscriminate bombing campaign is estimated to have resulted in "hundreds of thousands" victims, including internally displaced persons. According to the Complainants, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) reported that government authorities and the SAF forces committed mass human rights violations throughout 2012, including indiscriminate daily aerial bombardment by government forces in South Kordofan, the killing and injuring of civilians, and the deliberate destruction of grain and water sources, schools, farms, health clinics and other civilian property.

The Complainants also submitted that significant number of women and girls were reportedly raped by SAF forces while fleeing their homes in South Kordofan's Nuba Mountains and "Sudanese government soldiers" reportedly arrested and detained hundreds of men, women and children, which resulted in the disappearance of some of those detained. In Blue Nile State, the SAF also allegedly carried out a bombing campaign starting in September 2011 which continued through 2012, displacing tens of thousands. Government security, police, and military forces were allegedly responsible for the extra-judicial killings, injury, arbitrary arrest, torture and ill-treatment of civilians in Damazin and other locations.

The Complainants averred that the UN has estimated that there is a total of 665,000 internally displaced persons or severely affected people in South Kordofan (520,000 civilians) and Blue Nile (145,000 civilians). By the end of July 2012, the UN Refugee Agency – the United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) – reported that the total number of persons from South Kordofan and Blue Nile who had fled to neighbouring countries to escape persecution had reached 204,000.

The Complainants argue that there is no judicial system or mechanism in place in Sudan that can cope with the large number of victims in the present case. It would be impracticable to expect victims to exhaust any remedies in Sudan as they are "unavailable in fact".

The Complainants further argued that the Respondent State had ample notice of the human rights violations committed in South Kordofan. In particular, this include the Commission's request for Provisional Measures on 7 November 2011 urging the Government "to intervene in the matter with a view to preventing irreparable harm being caused to the victims". The Complainants noted that the AU, the UN and other international bodies have called on the Respondent State and the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) to end the violations in South Kordofan as early as 10 June 2011 and to end the violations in Blue Nile starting September 2011.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State failed to take any measures to respond to the human rights violations committed in South Kordofan and Blue Nile and there is no indication that the Respondent State had acted upon the information on the alleged human rights violations in South Kordofan and Blue Nile.

The Complainants further argued that remedies for human rights violations as committed in South Kordofan and Blue Nile are ineffective and insufficient in the Respondent State. According to the Complainants, they are not required to exhaust any local remedy which is found to be, as a practical matter, unavailable, ineffective or insufficient. They cite the Commission's decision in Dawda Jawara v The Gambia, which states that: A remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment, it is deemed effective if it offers a prospect of success, and it is found sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint.

According to the Complainants, there are no effective domestic remedies for serious human rights violations such as those alleged in the Communication due to: (i) shortcomings in Sudan's legal framework, and (ii) a general climate of fear fostered by the Respondent State that prevents Victims from seeking remedies against human rights violations committed by government officials.

The Complainants added that broad provisions for immunities for a range of State officials further means that any "remedies" do not offer a prospect of success to victims of human rights violations in Sudan. In the present case, the violations are primarily alleged to have been committed by soldiers of the SAF with the support of the Popular Defence Forces (PDF) and security forces.

Similarly, in Blue Nile, witnesses testified that SAF, militia and national security forces committed human rights violations. The Complainants made reference to Article 52 of the National Security Forces Act 2010, Article 46 of the Police Act 1999 and Article 34 of the Armed Forces Act 2007 which provide immunities for these officials, including soldiers, for any acts committed in the course of their duties. The immunities shield these officials from criminal prosecution and any civil suits unless the head of the respective forces, or in case of the Armed Forces, the President of the Republic, approves such legal action. Specifically, Article 34 (2) of the Armed Forces Act of 2007 provides that: No proceedings shall be taken against any officer, or soldier, who commits an act, which constitutes an offence, which occurs in the course, or by reason of his/her discharge of his/her duties, or carrying out of any lawful order, issued thereto in this capacity thereof, and he/she shall not be tried, save upon permission, issued by the President of the Republic, or whoever he may authorize.

The Complainants averred that any complaint regarding crimes committed by a member of the security forces or soldier cannot therefore be pursued without impediment, as their immunity would need to be lifted for any investigation to proceed. Furthermore, they state that there is no judicial or administrative procedure in place that would enable victims in the present case to compel, the relevant authorities or the President of the Republic, in relation to violations committed by members of the SAF, to waive immunity and undertake a full criminal investigation. The Complainants submitted that waiver of immunity is therefore entirely discretionary and immunity is rarely lifted in practice.

According to the Complainants, the most recent government campaign against human rights activists, lawyers, journalists, marginalised communities and individuals believed to be members of the opposition in Sudan extends to South Kordofan and Blue Nile. The Complainants submitted that the Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre reported on 8 March 2012 that an "unknown number of perceived political opponents, especially intellectuals and educated persons, human rights and pro-democracy activists originating from the Nuba Mountains, are held in government custody for prolonged periods and without judicial review." In April 2012, the International Rescue Committee reported that an increasing number of Nuba women and girls were raped while fleeing their homes in Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan.

Considering that the Complainants raised a preliminary objection that any submissions by the Respondent State on admissibility falling outside the time frames established by the Rules of Procedure should not be entertained, the Commission notes that as a matter of due diligence, a party must be expected to raise issues of a technical nature such as illegibility following receipt of a submission, well within the applicable time period. Accepting such argument after the expiry of the time limit would result in an unmerited substantial extension of the time limit and would allow parties to employ them as delaying tactics.
Having established that the African Commission is competent to entertain the Communication before it, the African Commission will now proceed to analyse Admissibility of the Communication.

Article 56 of the African Charter sets out seven requirements that a Communication brought under Article 55 of the African Charter must satisfy in order to be admissible, which apply conjunctively and cumulatively.

In the present Communication, the Respondent State has not made any submissions. Under such circumstances, as the jurisprudence of the Commission dictates in the case of the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v Republic of Angola, "in the face of the state's failure to address itself to the complaint filed against it, the African Commission has no option but to proceed with its consideration of the Communication in accordance with its Rules of Procedure." In the same decision, the African Commission re-affirmed its position by ruling that "... it would proceed to consider Communications on the basis of the submission of the Complainants and information at its disposal, even if the State fails to submit." Consequently, the Commission will rely on the Complainants' submissions to pronounce on the Admissibility of the Communication.

In the present Communication, the authors have been indicated, the Communication is compatible with the provisions of the African Charter and the Constitutive act of the AU as it outlines a prima facie case of the violation of relevant Articles of the African Charter; it is not written in disparaging or insulting language, and the Communication has not been settled through other international procedures.

With regards to Article 56(5), the Complainants contended that they were not able to exhaust local remedies because domestic remedies were not available, effective and sufficient. It is in light of this submission that the Commission will proceed to determine on the availability, effectiveness and sufficiency of Sudanese local remedies to the Complainants.

The Complainants argued that there is no judicial system or mechanism in place in the Respondent State that can cope with the large number of victims in the present case and that it would be impracticable to expect victims to exhaust any remedies in Sudan as they are "unavailable in fact".

While the exhaustion of domestic remedies must in principle be considered in each individual case, the African Commission's jurisprudence in other cases of serious or massive violations of human rights committed in Sudan attests to the lack of effective remedies available in the Respondent State. In regard to massive human rights violations committed in Darfur, where "tens of thousands of people have allegedly been forcibly evicted and their property destroyed" the African Commission found that "in the present communication, the scale and nature of the alleged abuses, the number of persons involved ipso facto make local remedies unavailable, ineffective and insufficient."

Similarly, the Commission found in Amnesty International, Comité Loosli Bachelard, Lawyers' Committee for Human Rights, Association of members of the Episcopal Conference of East Africa v Sudan where hundreds of people were detained without charge and tortured that the "seriousness of the human rights situation in Sudan and the great number of people involved renders such remedies unavailable in fact, or, in the words of the African Charter, their procedure would probably be unduly prolonged."

In the present Communication, the Complainants contended that the Respondent State's disregard for the rule of law in combination with a general climate of fear fostered by the Respondent State, which includes recent government campaign against human rights activists, lawyers, journalists, marginalised communities and the raids against the populations of South Kordofan and Blue Nile, renders any potential remedy unavailable, as it exposes the Victims who seek to pursue legal avenues to significant risks to their security.

The Commission recognised in Anuak Justice Council v Ethiopia that a remedy may only be deemed available "if the petitioner can pursue it without impediments or if he can make use of it in the circumstances of his case. The word 'available' means readily obtainable; 'accessible' or 'attainable, reachable'". The Commission also held in John D. Ouko v Kenya that domestic remedies need not be exhausted where doing so would put victims at risk of their life.

The Respondent State's campaign against human rights activists, lawyers, journalists, marginalised communities and individuals in South Kordofan and Blue Nile demonstrate the genuine risk to victims seeking to take judicial steps with a view to holding those responsible for human rights violations to account. The Complainants submitted that human rights violations continue to be committed in South Kordofan and Blue Nile on a daily basis with complete impunity. No specific provisions exist in Sudanese law or practice that would provide victims with protection. Under these circumstances, it would be "reversing the clock of justice to request the complainants to attempt to exhaust local remedies." Therefore, for the aforementioned reasons and in line with its established jurisprudence, the Commission finds that domestic remedies were not available for the Victims because of fear for their lives and existing risks to their security.

The Complainants also submitted that local remedies are not effective as there exists broad provisions for immunities for SAF soldiers and Sudanese security forces for any acts committed in the course of their duties. The immunities shield these officials from criminal prosecution and any civil suits unless the head of the respective forces, or in the case of the Armed Forces, the President of the Republic, approves such legal action. Moreover, they claim that there is no judicial or administrative procedure in place that would enable the Victims to compel the relevant authorities or the President of the Republic, in relation to violations committed by members of the SAF, to waive immunity and undertake a full criminal investigation. The waiver of immunity is therefore entirely discretionary.

The Commission has previously held that in light of the immunity provisions under Sudanese law, "it would be a mockery of justice to expect that the Victims would get justice from such a discretionary remedy." The Commission has made its position clear that when a remedy is a discretionary, extraordinary remedy of a non-judicial nature, then the Complainants are not required to pursue it as part of the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies. In Constitutional Rights Project (in respect of Zamani Lakwot and Six Others) v Nigeria and Constitutional Rights Project (in respect of Wahab Akamu, G. Adega and Others) v Nigeria, the Commission ruled that when the remedy is of a discretionary, extraordinary remedy of a non-judicial nature "it would be improper to insist on the Complainant seeking remedies from a source which does not operate impartially and have no obligation to decide according to legal principles. The remedy is neither adequate nor effective".
In line with the above reasoning, the Commission finds that the immunity provisions in Sudanese law render local remedies inadequate and ineffective.

Furthermore, it is the Commission's established jurisprudence that, the exhaustion of domestic remedies is not required in cases where it can be shown that a State failed to remedy a situation despite 'ample notice and time' to do so. In the present Communication, it is clear from the request for Provisional Measures issued by the Commission, the reports of the AU, UN and international NGOs that the Respondent State had ample notice of the alleged human rights violations in South Kordofan and Blue Nile State, and should have accordingly taken the necessary steps to investigate the matter. According to the Commission, the failure to take any action means that domestic remedies are not available or - even if they are - not effective or sufficient to address the alleged violations.

The Commission therefore holds that local remedies in the Respondent State were not available, effective and sufficient to the Complainants and hence the Complainants are waived from exhausting local remedies pursuant to Article 56(5) of the African Charter.
In view of the above, the Commission declares the Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter.

The only submissions on the merits that have been made before the African Commission on this matter are those of the Complainants. Despite several Notes Verbale to the Respondent State to file submissions on the merits, the latter has neglected, failed or refused to do so.
The case of the Complainants before the Commission is summarised in the following paragraphs.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State committed massive and serious violations of the provisions of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 9(1), 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21 and 23 of the African Charter, in no particular order.

The Complainants submitted that the SAF, PDF and other forces of the Respondent State carried out extrajudicial killings of a large number of persons living in South Kordofan and Blue Nile in violation of Article 4 of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State is responsible for torture, ill-treatment, rape and sexual violence committed by various forces of the Respondent State in violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

The Complainants also argued that the forced evictions, the destruction of homes and the poor living conditions endured by thousands of civilians as a result of forced displacement constitute ill-treatment in violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that the arrests of many civilians, especially members of the Nuba ethnic group and others believed to be SPLM/A-North sympathisers, as well as UN peacekeepers and journalists, were arbitrary and constitute a violation of the right to security of the person guaranteed under Article 6 of the African Charter.

The Complainants argued that the SAF and NISS arrested large numbers of members of the Nuba ethnic group, SPLM political and civil society activists, civilians believed to support the SPLM/A-North, UN personnel and journalists.

The Complainants further submitted that the SAF and other forces failed to inform individuals of the reason for their arrest, refused to charge those detained, and neglected to grant them access to a lawyer and to their families.
The Complainants emphasized that those arrested and detained have not been able to challenge their arrest or detention before a judicial officer or judge.

The Complainants submitted that not only have the Respondent State's forces committed, and continue to commit, a wide range of human rights violations against civilians in the context of the conflict in South Kordofan and Blue Nile, but also that the Respondent State failed to take any steps to protect the physical integrity of its citizens, in violation of Article 6.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State failed to provide victims of the alleged human rights violations with access to justice in violation of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter and the Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and legal Assistance.

The Complainants submitted that despite the Respondent State's responsibility for serious and massive human rights violations resulting in a large number of victims in South Kordofan and Blue Nile, the victims have not had any access to a remedy and reparation to date.

The Complainants further submitted that the Respondent State has yet to respond to the Commission's two requests for provisional measures and to take the necessary steps to investigate the alleged violations, prosecute and punish those responsible, and provide reparation to victims in South Kordofan and Blue Nile. The Complainants further submitted that no cases are known where soldiers of the SAF or members of the security forces have been held accountable for human rights violations alleged to have been committed in both States, since the outbreak of hostilities on 5 June 2011 and September 2011, respectively. (v) Alleged violation of the right to information (Article 9(1) of the African Charter)

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State's restriction of the right of individuals to receive information by closing the region of South Kordofan and Blue Nile state to national and international media, and by preventing national media and journalists from reporting on the violations committed by the Respondent State in both states, constituted a violation of Article 9(1) of the African Charter.

The Complainants also submitted that the lockdown of South Kordofan and Blue Nile as well as the de-facto blanket ban on national and international media from accessing both States to report on the conduct of hostilities, ostensibly with a view to prevent reporting on human rights violations by SAF, PDF and NCP forces, are unjustifiable under the African Charter. (vi) Alleged violation of the freedom of movement and residence (Article 12 of the African Charter)

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State, by forcibly displacing civilians and by failing to ensure their safe return, has violated the right to residence and freedom of movement as enshrined in Article 12 of the African Charter.

The Complainants further submitted that many of those displaced as a result of the SAF's indiscriminate bombings were not permitted access to IDP camps but rather forced to return to areas where their lives and safety were considered to be at risk.

The Complainants submitted that the SAF's indiscriminate air and ground attacks on civilian life caused the destruction of churches, houses and other property, the abandonment of homes and the loss of livestock and other resources, and therefore amount to a violation of Article 14 of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that the indiscriminate bombing campaign by the Respondent State led to the widespread destruction of homes and livestock and caused hundreds of thousands of persons to be cut off from drinking water, electricity and any medical aid, and constituted a violation of Article 16 of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of civilians by the Respondent State's indiscriminate bombing campaign and other human rights violations resulted in a violation of the right to protection of the family under Article 18 (1) of the African Charter.
The Complainants submitted that the fear of aerial bombardment by the Respondent State has forced civilians to leave behind family members, including children as well as the elderly.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State's forces and authorities have committed widespread acts of sexual violence specifically targeted at women and girls in violation of Article 18(3) of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that by specifically committing sexual violence against female Sudanese civilians, the violations "are gender-specific in the sense that the victims were subjected to acts of sexual harassment and physical violence that can only be directed to women."

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State is responsible for discriminatory treatment of civilians in South Kordofan, Blue Nile as well as other areas in Sudan on the basis of sex, colour, race and ethnicity, and political opinion in violation of Article 2 of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that the Respondent State's assault on members of the Nuba ethnic group violates their collective rights as a "people" under the African Charter. Specifically, they submitted that the Respondent State is responsible for violations of the Nuba people's right to equality under Article 19; their right to existence and self-determination under Article 20; their right to freely dispose of their wealth and natural resources under Article 21(1) and (2); and their right to peace and security under Article 23(1) of the African Charter.

The Complainants submitted that, due to the history of targeted violations committed by the Respondent State against the Nuba people during the conflict in South Kordofan, militias and government forces in South Kordofan killed individuals because they belonged to the Nuba.
