Toutefois, les droits stipulés à l'article 21 restent encore applicables à l'Afrique post-coloniale en faveur de groupes dans un Etat dans la mesure où ils imposent l'obligation de la part des Etats parties de protéger leurs citoyens de l'exploitation des puissances économiques extérieures. En effet, dans ses Directives générales sur les Rapports Périodiques Nationaux, la Commission avait déjà indiqué que le droit de disposer librement de ses richesses et de leurs ressources consiste à s'assurer que les richesses des pays ne sont pas exploitées par des étrangers sans aucun profit pour les pays africains ou en leur laissant un profit marginal.

De ce qui précède, on peut conclure d'abord que le droit à la libre disposition des richesses et des ressources naturelles est un droit collectif concernant un groupe de personnes ou d'individus. Ceci signifie que les groupes ou communautés doivent être impliquées, directement ou indirectement, dans des décisions relatives à la disposition de leurs richesses. Ensuite, la présomption dans la rédaction de l'article 21 est que la menace contre ce droit viendrait en grande partie de l'extérieur de l'Etat et même du continent soit sous forme d'une influence néocoloniale des Etats non africains ou de sociétés multinationales.

En l'espèce, le Plaignant allègue qu'en refusant d'exécuter les différentes décisions restituant la propriété à la victime, le droit de disposer ou de louer le terrain lui a été nié étant donné qu'il n'a pas été en possession du terrain pendant plus d'une décennie. La Commission a bien évidemment établi que le droit de propriété de la victime sur le terrain en question qui comprend aussi le droit d'en disposer, d'en user et d'en jouir les fruits a été violé. Cependant, il n'est pas prouvé que cette violation a impacté sur le droit à la libre disposition des richesses et des ressources naturelles. En effet, comme déjà indiqué, le droit à la libre disposition des richesses et des ressources naturelles a une nature collective en ce qu'elle protège un héritage commun d'un groupe ou une communauté déterminée.

Ainsi par exemple, dans l'affaire Antonie Bissangou / Congo, la Commission a considéré que les biens mobiliers et immobiliers du Plaignant qui ont été endommagés pendant les événements sociopolitiques qui ont secoué le pays en 1993 ne constituaient pas des richesses et ressources naturelles d'un peuple mais plutôt des biens individuels: Elle a enfin conclu que le Plaignant agissait en son propre nom et non au nom d'un groupe d'individus ou d'une population vivant sur un territoire donné et que, par conséquent, il n'y avait pas de violation de l'article 21.

En l'espèce également, le plaignant allègue la violation de son droit de propriété et n'agit pas au nom d'un groupe ou communauté quelconque. Dans ces circonstances, la Commission ne peut pas établir la violation du droit à la libre disposition des richesses et des ressources naturelles, droit qui est naturellement réservée au peuple.
Il en résulte que l'article 21 (1) et (3) n'ont pas été violés.

Le Plaignant allègue une violation conjointe des articles 28 et 29 (2) (4) (6) de la Charte. L'article 28 stipule que "chaque individu a le devoir de respecter et considérer ses semblables sans discrimination aucune, et d'entretenir avec eux des relations qui permettent de promouvoir, de sauvegarder et de renforcer le respect et la tolérance réciproques". Quant à l'article 29 (2) (4) (6) de la charte, il indique que: " L'individu a en outre le devoir : 2) de servir sa communauté nationale en mettant ses capacités physiques et intellectuelles à son service 4) de préserver et de renforcer la solidarité sociale et nationale, singulièrement lorsque celle-ci est menacée 6) de travailler, dans la mesure de ses capacités et de ses possibilités, et de s'acquitter des contributions fixées par la loi pour la sauvegarde des intérêts fondamentaux de la société".

Ces deux dispositions prônent le devoir de non-discrimination et de respecter les êtres humains. Le devoir de "respecter et considérer" les autres sans discrimination est en même temps une obligation négative de tout individu de "s'abstenir de toute discrimination" et un devoir positif de "maintenir des relations propices à la promotion, à la sauvegarde et au renforcement du respect mutuel et de la tolérance". Quant aux aspects de violation de l'article 29 relevés par le Plaignant, ils font tous référence à un devoir de tout citoyen à l'apport productif dans tous les secteurs de la société afin de réaliser le développement national.

En l'espèce, le Plaignant estime que l'Etat défendeur a violé ces deux dispositions de la Charte car les autorités nationales ont refusé de servir les communautés nationales en mettant leurs capacités physiques et intellectuelles au service de la Communauté et de la victime. La Commission estime que les Etats ne peuvent pas être tenus responsables d'un manquement aux devoirs de leurs citoyens. En effet, par leur essence même, les devoirs des individus sont exigés aux individus en leur capacité personnelle. En ce sens, leur non-respect ne peut pas engager la responsabilité des Etats car ces derniers ne sont pas liés par devoirs individuels. Seuls les devoirs propres aux Etats en vertu notamment des articles 17 (3), 18 (3), 22 (2), 25 et 26 de la Charte ainsi que les manquements à l'obligation de respect et de protection des droits de l'homme en vertu des articles 1 à 24 de la Charte peuvent engager la responsabilité des Etats.
Il en résulte que l'article 28 et 29 (2) (4) (6) n'ont pas été violés

Le Plaignant allègue la violation de l'article 1 qui indique tel qui suit: "les Etats membres de l' Organisation de l' Unité Africaine, parties à la présente Charte, reconnaissent les droits, les devoirs et libertés énoncés dans la Charte et s'engagent à adopter des mesures législatives ou autres pour les appliquer". Il estime qu'en ne respectant pas le droit de propriété de la victime, l'Etat du Cameroun a violé les droits de l'homme fondamentaux de la victime.

La Commission relève effectivement qu'il ressort de sa jurisprudence largement établie qu'une violation de l'une des dispositions de la Charte implique automatiquement une violation de l'article premier. Ainsi par exemple, dans la Communication Kevin Mwangwa Gunme et autres c. le Cameroun, la Commission a réitéré qu'une violation de n'importe quelle disposition de la Charte africaine constitue automatiquement une violation de l'Article premier dans la mesure où cela témoigne de l'incapacité de l'Etat partie à adopter des mesures adéquates pour donner effet aux dispositions de la Charte africaine Elle a, par conséquent, conclu qu'ayant trouvé des violations de plusieurs dispositions au cours de son analyse, l'Etat Défendeur a violé l'Article premier.
Ayant ainsi trouvé qu'un certain nombre de dispositions de la Charte ont été violées, la Commission en conclut que l'article 1 a été violé.

Le Plaignant allègue qu'il a droit à la réparation. En effet, il indique qu'en 2005, il devait faire louer son terrain de certificat foncier No 3639 pour 50 000 000 FCFA par mois, soient 600 000 000 FCFA par an et ceci pendant les 15 ans précédant sa saisine de la Commission. Il réitère que l'opération de location de son terrain a échoué à cause des violations de droits de l'homme de l'Etat défendeur à son égard. Il ajoute que l'intérêt annuel de la banque au Cameroun est de 6.25 % ; et qu'en conséquence ce taux doit être appliqué à toutes les 15 années pendant lesquelles il n'était pas en possession de son terrain.

Pour ce faire, il demande une compensation de 10.000.000.000 FCFA (10 milliards) correspondant au loyer non perçu pendant les 15 années (600 000 000 FCFA par an) et les dépenses engagées pendant cette période. Il prie la Commission de ne pas se référer à sa jurisprudence selon laquelle le montant de la compensation soit déterminée selon les lois nationales du Pays défendeur.

La Commission relève que la Charte africaine est muette sur la réparation en cas de violation des droits y consacrés. Cependant, conformément à sa jurisprudence, elle note que la violation des droits protégés par la Charte ouvre droit à la réparation. Ainsi par exemple, dans la Communication Jean-Marie Atangana Mebaro c. République du Cameroun, la Commission a indiqué que la réparation peut prendre des formes variées selon les droits violés et les circonstances de la cause, allant des actions administratives, législatives et judiciaires à la compensation monétaire.

En l'espèce, la réparation réclamée est de nature monétaire. Ainsi, ayant déjà constaté des violations de la Charte, la Commission est effectivement de l'avis que l'Etat responsable de ces violations a l'obligation d'effacer toutes les conséquences de ses actes et ainsi rétablir la victime dans la situation où elle devrait être si ces actes n'avaient pas été commis. Cependant, le principe étant que la réparation doit être juste, adéquate, efficace, suffisante, appropriée, orientée vers la victime et proportionnelle au préjudice subi, il reste à déterminer le montant réel correspondant au préjudice subi.

En effet, le Plaignant ne fournit pas, avec des preuves à l'appui, des documents indiquant que le terrain en question avait une valeur locative mensuelle de 50.000.000 FCFA et que le taux d'intérêt annuel à la banque est de 6.25% comme il l'indique. En l'absence de toutes ces précisions, conformément à sa jurisprudence bien établie, la Commission renvoie le Plaignant aux juridictions nationales pour assurer l'évaluation du préjudice subi. Dans ces circonstances, la Commission rejette la demande du Plaignant sollicitant la non-intervention des juridictions nationales sur cette question.

Le Plaignant demande également à la Commission de faire des recommandations suivantes : a) Recommander à l'état défendeur d'exécuter rapidement la décision n° 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF du 27 décembre 2010, le jugement n° 56/OSE/PTE/DLA/2015 et l'arrêt définitif n° 062/FD/2015 du Tribunal Administratif du Littoral. La Commission trouve que cette demande est fondée et convenable. En effet, l'un des aspects importants d'un procès équitable est l'exécution des décisions qui en résultent. Leur non-exécution placerait la victime dans la même situation de violation des droits de l'homme qu'avant la décision. b) Recommander l'enquête et la révocation pure et simple de Sanda Michael, Registrar of Lands, Mezam pour son refus catégorique d'exécuter la décision n° 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF du 27 décembre 2010, l'arrêt n° 56/OSE/PTA/DLA/2015 et le jugement du Tribunal administratif du Littoral n° 062/FD/2015, tous deux devenus définitifs, contraignants et irrévocables. La Commission estime qu'il n'est pas de sa compétence d'exiger à l'Etat défendeur une enquête aux fins d'une révocation de son employé pour un manquement quelconque à l'accomplissement des responsabilités liées à sa fonction. En effet, la révocation pour manquement à une exécution d'un ordre hiérarchique ou une décision judiciaire relève du pouvoir administratif et par conséquent de la compétence des juridictions administratifs nationaux. Le rôle de la Commission ne se limite qu'à s'assurer que les victimes des violations des droits de l'homme soient rétablies dans leurs droits conformément à la Charte Africaine. c) Recommander l'enquête, la poursuite et la radiation par l'Etat partie défendeur des Avocats Nchifor Anyam Zacheus et Sanigong Anye Henry qui ont utilisé une fausse procurature et portant le certificat foncier No 3693 pour préparer un faux acte de cession et faciliter ainsi une vente frauduleuse de la propriété du plaignant sur le terrain No 3639 situé à Bamenda, Nkwen Mile. Il en est de même pour l'Avocat Fon Robert qui a préparé l'acte de cession pour transférer la propriété au sieur Fokou alors qu'il a été mis en demeure de prendre connaissance de la décision ministérielle numéro 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/MINDAF/BF du 27 décembre 2010 qui est devenu exécutoire, définitif et irrévocable depuis le 08 juillet 2011 en vertu de l'attestation de non recours et pour la deuxième fois suite au jugement n° 062/FD/15 du 01 octobre 2015 qui a rendu un jugement exécutoire, définitif et irrévocable en vertu du certificat de non pourvoi du 24 novembre 2015. La Commission estime ici également qu'il n'est pas de sa compétence d'intervenir dans les poursuites judiciaires des contrevenants au droit pénal interne des Etats. Ceci relève de la compétence des autorités judiciaires nationales compétentes. La Commission ne peut intervenir qu'en cas des violations des droits de l'homme prescrits dans la Charte. Pour ces motifs, la Commission :
Declare que: i. Les articles 12(1), 21 (1) et (3), 28 et 29 (2) (4) (6) n'ont pas été violés ii. Les articles 1, 2, 3, 7 (1) a et 14 ont été violés

La Commission demande à la République du Cameroun : i. De faire exécuter rapidement la décision n° 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF du 27 décembre 2010, le jugement n° 56/OSE/PTE/DLA/2015 et l'arrêt définitif n° 062/FD/2015 du Tribunal Administratif du Littoral ii. De restituer la propriété à la victime conformément à la décision n° 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF du 27 décembre 2010, au jugement n° 56/OSE/PTE/DLA/2015 et à l'arrêt définitif n° 062/FD/2015 du Tribunal Administratif du Littoral iii. D'accorder une compensation correspondante à la valeur locative de la propriété de la victime et d'évaluer les dommages intérêts y relatives conformément aux lois nationales. iv. De lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée par la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples lors de sa 73 Session Ordinaire tenue à Banjul du 20 Octobre 2022 au 09 novembre 2022

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received a Complaint on 9 May 2016 from Ndikum Law Offices (the Complainant) acting on behalf of Mr. Philip Forsang Ndikum (the Victim)
The Complaint is filed against the Republic of Cameroon (the Respondent State), a State Party to the African Charter.
The Complainant alleges that the Victim bought a property located in Bamenda, Nkwen Mile 3 in 1984 and obtained land certificate No. 3639 in 1995.

The Complainant alleges that in 2005, while the Victim was studying in the United States of America, Mr. Chi Simon Ndiforwa, with the assistance of his legal advisers, lawyers of the Cameroonian Bar (Nchifor Anyam Zachcus and Sanigong Anye Henry), altered the power of attorney with a forged version of the Victim's signature and used this falsified document to obtain a false deed of transfer in order to fraudulently sell the Victim's land.

According to the Complainant, on 26 May 2009, the Judicial Police of Buca of the forensic science department confirmed that the power of attorney had been forged while the Victim was studying in the United States of America.

The Complainant alleges that the Victim asked the Minister in charge of State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure (Minister of Lands) to cancel the transfer of his property, which had been illegally sold to Mr. Ndiforwa. The Complainant alleges that the Minister cancelled the sale of the Victim's land and ordered the Registrar of Lands to enforce the decision by ministerial letter No. 00004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010 (first ministerial order).

The Complainant argues that a new Minister of Lands was appointed and annulled the decision of his predecessor. The new Minister allegedly, by decision No. 004310/Y.7/MINDCAF/SG/D6/S210 of 26 August 2013, attached as evidence, revoked the initial decision, which resulted in the transfer of the Victim's land to Mr. Fokou, who is allegedly a supporter of the ruling Party, the Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (CPDM), and a friend of the Cameroonian President, His Excellency Paul Biya.

The Complainant alleges that in 2015, when the Victim had tried by all means to recover his land without success, he seized the Administrative Court of the Littoral Region, challenging the failure by the current Minister to enforce the Decision of his predecessor. The Victim allegedly asked the Court to order the suspension of the construction work in progress on his property and also to annul the fraudulent transfer of his property. The Complainant states that the Administrative Court of the Littoral Region ruled on 01 October 2015 in favour of the Victim and ordered that land certificate No. 3639 be returned to him.

The Complainant alleges that the Victim forwarded the judgment of the Administrative Court of the Littoral Region to the Minister of Lands; to the State Counsel of the Menzam Division and to the Prosecutor General of the North-West Region. The Complainant alleges that the Minister stated that he does not recognise the judgments of Cameroonian courts and tribunals.

According to the Complainant, under circular letter No. 002109/L.MINUH/A000 of 10 August 2004, the enforcement of judgments is subject to ministerial discretion and therefore, on the basis of the Minister's discretion, the decision was not enforced. The Complainant alleges that making the enforcement of judgments subject to ministerial discretion and the abuse of that discretion violate Article 37(2) of the Constitution, which clearly stipulates the separation of powers between the executive, the legislature and the judiciary.
The Complainant alleges that the Registrar of Lands refused to enforce the judgment, indicating that his superior, the Minister of Lands, had ordered him not to enforce it.

The Complainant states that the State Counsel refused to enforce the judgment, declaring that he does not deal with judgments from the francophone regions of Cameroon. According to the Applicant, Article 29 of Law No. 2006/015 of 29 December 2006 on judicial organisation entrusts the Conseil d'État, under the supervision of the Prosecutor General, with the enforcement of court decisions. The Complainant further states that the Registrar of Lands did not question the position of the Conseil d'État.

The Complainant also alleges that the Victim repeatedly and unsuccessfully petitioned the President of the Bar Council of the North-West Region concerning the unethical conduct of Nchifor Anyam Zacheus and Sanigong Anye Henry, lawyers of the Cameroon Bar, who forged his signature and documents, resulting in the fraudulent sale of his property

The Complainant also alleges that the Victim wrote letters to the President of the Republic of Cameroon (11 April 2016), to the Prime Minister (9 March and 11 April 2016), to the Minister of State, Minister of Justice and Keeper of the Seals (9 March and 11 April 2016), to the Secretary General at the Presidency (9 March 2016), to the Chairman of the Anti-Corruption Unit (9 March 2016) and also to the Secretary General of the Commission on Human Rights and Civil Liberties (9 March 2016). None of them replied to or acknowledged receipt of the Victim's correspondence.

The Complainant alleges that on 26 August 2013, the Administrative Court of the Littoral Region ordered the suspension of all construction work on the property in question and also suspended the decision of the current Minister to annul the decision of her predecessor. None of these measures was enforced, and construction on the property continues.

With regard to the obligation to exhaust local remedies, the Complainant submits that the Victim exhausted all available local remedies as required by Article 56 of the African Charter. The Complainant alleges that the Victim struggled for ten years in Cameroon to try to recover his property, as shown by the decision of the former Minister of Lands and the final judgment, which, together with the certificate of non-appeal, show that all judicial proceedings have been exhausted. The Complainant states that the letters sent to President Paul Biya and other Government officials are proof that local remedies were also exhausted through administrative procedures.

The Complainant states that this complaint has never been submitted to another international dispute settlement body for settlement or decision and that it was filed before the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) within a reasonable time in accordance with Article 56(6) of the Charter.
The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated Articles 1, 2, 3, 7(a), 12, 14, 21(1) and (3), 28 and 29 (2) (4) (6) of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission to: i. Recommend that the State of Cameroon promptly enforce decision No. 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 November 2010, judgment No. 56/OSE/PTA/DLA/2015 and final judgment No. 062/FD/2015 of the Administrative Court of the Littoral. ii. Recommend that the Respondent State compensate the Victim in the sum of 10,000,000,000 (Ten Billion) CFA francs for the expenses he incurred during the ten-year period, including the damage he has suffered and continues to suffer as a result of the loss of his property.
The Secretariat received the Complaint on 09 May 2016 and acknowledged receipt on 13 May 2016.

The Commission was seized of the Complaint during its 20th Extraordinary Session and the decision of seizure was transmitted to the parties on 24 June 2016. The Complainant was further informed that he should submit his observations on the admissibility of the Communication within two (2) months.

The Complainant's observations on admissibility were received at the Secretariat on 19 July 2016 and the Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 27 July 2016. By Note Verbale of the same date, the Secretariat transmitted the Complainant's observations on admissibility to the Respondent State, requesting it to make its submission on the admissibility of the Communication within two (2) months.

By letter and Note Verbale of 22 November 2016, the Secretariat informed the Parties that the Respondent State had been granted an additional thirty (30) days to make its submission on the admissibility of the Communication.

The Respondent State's submissions were received on 05 May 2017 and the Secretariat transmitted the submissions to the Complainant on 15 June 2017. The Complainant was given thirty days to submit his further observations on the State's submissions.
The Complainant's additional observations were received at the Secretariat on 18 September 2017 and were transmitted to the Respondent State on 22 September 2017.
From its 61st Ordinary Session to its 25th Extraordinary Session, the Commission deferred consideration of the decision on admissibility

At its 64th Ordinary Session, the Commission considered the preliminary objection raised by the Applicant concerning the admissibility of the Respondent State's late submissions. The Commission decided to dismiss the preliminary objection and allowed the late observations. In its reasoning, the Commission weighed the implications of accepting or rejecting the State's observations. On the one hand, the State submitted its observations out of time and provided no justification for the delay. On the other hand, the Commission considers that the participation of States in the communication procedure is to the advantage of both parties, as it indicates a willingness on the part of the State to remain seized of this matter. Moreover, although the observations were made out of time, they were submitted after a single extension and within five months of the expiry of the time limit. Given that the Commission had, in previous cases, accepted submissions after a much longer delay, and given the advantage to both parties of participating in the Communication process in the present case, the Commission allowed the State's submissions.

The Communication was declared admissible by the Commission at its 26th Extraordinary Session in July 2019; the parties were immediately informed. Subsequently, the Commission requested them to transmit to the Secretariat their observations on the merits in accordance with the Commission's Rules of Procedure.
The Complainant's observations on the merits were received at the Secretariat on 26 February 2020 and transmitted to the Respondent State on 10 March 2020.
The Respondent State obtained an extension of 30 days which expired on 19 December 2020.

On 11 January 2021, the Secretariat of the Commission received a note verbale from the Respondent State requesting an extension of time so that it could prepare and submit its observations on the merits.

By a Note Verbale of 03 March 2022, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State that the Commission had considered its request and had decided to grant it a final extension of time of 30 days. The same information was transmitted to the Complainant. However, this extension period elapsed without the Respondent State submitting its observations on the merits. On the law On admissibility The Complainant's arguments on admissibility

The Complainant submits that his Communication meets all the conditions stipulated in Article 56 of the African Charter and must therefore be declared admissible. été épuisés; c) post facto local remedies to ensure reparation are ineffective and insufficient; d) the Respondent State failed in its duty to open investigations and criminal prosecutions in relation to the forgery by the lawyers as indicated above; and e) civil and administrative remedies are available, but ineffective and insufficient because the Complainant never had the order of the Prime Minister and the court judgments enforced.

The Complainant further states that, while under administrative law the decisions of the Minister and of the administrative court are enforced with immediate effect, in the present case many months have elapsed without their being implemented, despite the fact that the decision was duly served on Government officials and the Victim's further efforts to secure its enforcement. Moreover, the Complainant alleges that Government officials, including the Minister of Lands, the State Counsel and the Prosecutor General of Mezam, stated that the Victim would never have a remedy against the unlawful appropriation of his land.

With regard to the requirements of Article 56(6), the Complainant submits that the communication was submitted within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of domestic judicial remedies. The Complainant argues that the decisions of the Administrative Court of the Littoral of 20 June 2015 and 1 October 2015 were never appealed by the State and subsequently became binding, final and irrevocable through the inclusion of a certificate of non-appeal at the Supreme Court. The Complainant also argues that the Communication was submitted to the Commission one month after the second series of letters addressed to the Office of the President, and others on 11 April 2016. The Complainant submits that the communication was submitted to the Commission on 9 May 2016 after having exhausted all available judicial, administrative, civil and extrajudicial avenues over a period of eight months of waiting to ensure that he could have the two judgments of 20 June 2015 and 1 October 2015 enforced. He therefore argues that the Communication was submitted within a reasonable time.

The Complainant argues that the Communication does not concern a matter that has been dealt with by the Commission or by any other United Nations body or settled by any other international procedure of investigation or adjudication and that the Commission is the only body seized of this matter.

In its observations on admissibility, the Respondent State states that Article 56 of the African Charter provides for seven conditions of admissibility which must be cumulatively met before a Communication is declared admissible. The State asserts that before filing a complaint, the Complainant must have used all the legal or judicial avenues available at the national level to resolve the problem. The State refers to the Commission's decision in Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, where it held that a remedy is considered available if the Complainant can pursue it without hindrance, that it is deemed effective if it offers a prospect of success and that it is found sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint.

The Respondent State argues that, as the administrative court, in its judgment No. 062/FD/15 of 1 October 2015, had annulled the decision of the Minister of Lands of 23 August 2013 (the second ministerial decision), this judgment made the first ministerial decision, which had been revoked by the second ministerial decision, enforceable again. The State asserts that this proves that local remedies are available in the Complainant's case.

The Respondent State argues that by ministerial decision of 23 August 2016, the land registrar and the divisional head of the surveys service of Mezam were instructed to enforce the judgment of 01 October 2015, thereby ensuring that land certificate No. 3639/Mezam is returned to the Victim. The State further submits that on 23 August 2016, the Minister wrote to the Divisional Delegate for State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure of Mezam, for the attention of the land registrar and the divisional head of service, to order the enforcement of the judgment. The State attached a copy of this second correspondence as evidence.

Furthermore, the State refers to the Complainant's observations, as mentioned in paragraphs 10, 11 and 37 above, to the effect that the Minister of Land Affairs refused to enforce the court's judgment on the basis of circular letter No. 002109/L.MINUH/A000 of 2004, which makes the enforcement of judgments subject to the Minister's discretion. The State submits that the circular letter in no way gives the Minister the discretionary power to enforce or not to enforce the judgments of the Court. The State argues that it rather assigns the monitoring of the enforcement of judgments concerning matters within the competence of the Ministry of Territory to the Minister herself, instead of assigning it to the provincial services of the Ministry, as was previously the case. The State argues that there is also no evidence that the Minister of Land Affairs stated that she did not respect the decisions of the courts.

The Respondent State refers to the Commission's jurisprudence in Communication 258/2002 - Miss A v. Cameroon, in which it argues that, besides the fact that the communication was submitted to the Commission while the case was still pending before the national courts, the Commission stressed the fact that the case was subsequently tried in due form before a court, which shows the availability of local remedies. The State therefore argues that the remedies are available, effective and sufficient, since appropriate measures are being taken at the national level to respond to the Complainant's request.

The State submits that the Complainant therefore did not exhaust all local remedies before seizing the Commission and requests the Commission to declare the Communication inadmissible for non-exhaustion of local remedies in accordance with Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

In response to the Respondent State's observations on admissibility, the Applicant argues that the existing local remedies are ineffective and inadequate and have been unduly prolonged from 2005 to 2017 by legal manoeuvres of the delinquent Government for the sole purpose of continuously violating the Victim's human rights.

The Complainant submits that in addition to the illegal issuance of the land title to Mr. Fokou, and despite an injunction ordering Mr. Fokou to cease all construction work on the property, the work was allowed to continue with impunity and was completed in 2017. The Complainant argues that under the law of the State, remedies are provided, including payment of a fine or a term of imprisonment for "persons who use or occupy land without the prior authorisation of the owner", and further that under the law, the court must order the eviction of the occupant, the owner of the land automatically being the owner of the structures. The Complainant argues, however, that the Victim will never obtain full compensation because Mr. Fokou is treated by the Respondent State as a special citizen who is above the law.

The Complainant submits that the special status of Mr. Fokou is further demonstrated by the fact that on 10 January 2017, the Minister wrote to the State Counsel of the Mezam Court of Appeal to re-examine the case in question on grounds of territorial jurisdiction. The Complainant argues that the purpose of this letter is to refuse to return to the Victim the land bearing land title No. 3639. The Complainant further argues that the "judicial ping-pong between the Minister and the Land Registrar of Mezam demonstrates that this matter depends solely on the discretionary power of the Minister and of the executive".

The Complainant further argues that, the Respondent State's submissions on admissibility having been received five months after the deadline, the Commission should reject those submissions and rule on the merits of the communication.

The Complainant argues in the alternative that the Commission should declare the communication admissible given that domestic legal and judicial remedies have been exhausted. The Complainant refers to a precedent in a similar case in Cameroon in which the Register of Lands reissued the title deed in the name of the rightful owner in less than thirty (30) days after receiving the order of the Minister of Lands to cancel a fraudulent land transaction.

The Complainant further submits that local remedies have been exhausted since the first ministerial decision, which became binding, final and irreversible by virtue of the Certificate of non-appeal since 08 July 2011, and the judgment of 01 October 2015 were not enforced in bad faith. The Complainant argues that in the Victim's case, every order or judgment since 2010 was delivered to the Land Registrar by a bailiff's notification, and yet to date no transfer has been made. Moreover, the Complainant states that the actions taken by the Respondent State after 09 May 2016, the date on which the Complaint was submitted to the Commission, are dilatory tactics that unduly prolong the regular procedure and constitute a continuing violation of the Complainant's human rights.

The Complainant argues that the Respondent State's argument that the judgment of 01 October 2015 and the Minister's letters mentioned in paragraph 42 above are evidence of the availability of local remedies is contrary, as it only confirms that the Complainant has exhausted all the legal, administrative and judicial avenues that exist.

With regard to the Respondent State's argument in paragraph 43 above that the circular letter in no way gives the Minister the discretionary power to enforce or not to enforce the judgments of the Court, the Complainant argues that in the absence of such discretionary power, nothing explains why the Land Registrar did not enforce the first ministerial order, the judgment of October 2015 and the Minister's most recent letter of 23 August 2016 requesting enforcement. The Complainant also argues that the Land Registrar was not sanctioned by the Minister for his failure to enforce the judgment, as provided for by Decree No. 941199 of 07 October 1994, the relevant provisions of which on disciplinary measures the Complainant cited in his observations.

In response to the State's argument that there is no evidence that the Minister of Lands stated that she did not respect the decisions of the courts, the Complainant submitted a letter from the Minister of Justice to the Victim, which indicates that the said Minister advised the Minister of Lands to enforce the decision. The Complainant further argues that the Respondent State has not explained why the Minister instructed the Land Registrar of Mezam in her letter of 23 August 2016 to enforce only the originals of the judgment of 01 October 2015, given that photocopies of the judgment are never used as a basis for enforcement in Cameroon. Finally, the Complainant indicates that the Minister wrote to the State Counsel of the Mezam Court of Appeal to re-examine the case on the basis of territorial jurisdiction. However, the Complainant states that there is no post of "State Counsel of the Mezam Court of Appeal" nor a Mezam Court of Appeal. He also argues that this order by the Minister to re-examine the case raises the question of whether the executive can give instructions to the judiciary, in violation of the principle of separation of powers.

The Complainant cited the Commission's decision in Communication 318/06 - Open Society Initiative v. Côte d'Ivoire, in which it indicated that "concerning Article 56(5), its provisions require the Complainant to exhaust local remedies only if they exist and are effective and adequate and are not unduly prolonged. A remedy is considered available when it offers prospects of success and adequate when it is able to give satisfaction to the Complainant and remedy the alleged violation. Where one of these characteristics is lacking, local remedies cannot meet the requirements stipulated in Article 56(5) of the African Charter."

The Complainant argues that he has exhausted all local remedies which, at the same time, remain unavailable, ineffective and inadequate since their enforcement depends exclusively on the discretionary power of the ministerial/executive organ of the Respondent State. The Complainant states that the object of the dispute was that land title No. 3639 be returned to the Victim, free of all encumbrances, but that this has not happened and appears unlikely, despite the binding ministerial order and court order to that effect, and although the competent authorities were notified accordingly, thus rendering the remedies ineffective, inadequate and unduly prolonged. The Complainant further argues that, according to the jurisprudence established by the Commission in Communication 284/03 - Association Newspapers of Zimbabwe (PVT) Ltd and Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights v. The Republic of Zimbabwe, a three-step test must be applied to determine whether the complainant has exhausted local remedies, after which the Respondent State must demonstrate that the remedies are available, effective and that the complainant did not use them. The Complainant argues that while he has proven the first point, the State has failed to prove the second.

Article 56 of the African Charter sets out seven (7) conditions which must all be met for a communication to be declared admissible. Failure to meet one or more of these conditions renders the communication inadmissible.

With regard to Article 56(1), which requires that the author of the Communication be indicated, the Complainant argues that the authors of the Communication have been identified. The Respondent State has not contested this ground, and the Commission agrees that the author has indeed been indicated. The Commission therefore considers that the Communication complies with Article 56(1).

Article 56(2) requires that the Communication be compatible with the Charter of the OAU or the African Charter. The Complainant argues that the Communication is compatible with the African Charter since it alleges serious violations of Articles 1, 2, 3, 7(a), 12, 14, 21(1) and (3), 28 and 29 of the Charter and that it is directed against the Republic of Cameroon, a State Party to the Charter since 20 June 1989. The State does not contest this assertion; Article 56(2) is therefore complied with.

Article 56(3) requires that a communication not be "written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or to the Organization of African Unity (now the African Union)". The Complainant argues that the Communication is presented in a polite and respectful manner, without the use of offensive and disparaging language. The State does not contest this assertion and the Commission has not identified any disparaging language in the Communication either and therefore considers that Article 56(3) has been complied with.

Article 56(4) of the Charter requires that the communication not be based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media. The Complainant argues that the complaint is based on real facts, as shown by the numerous documents submitted in the evidence file in support of the complaint. The State has not raised any objections in this regard and the Commission considers that the requirements of Article 56(4) have been met.

Article 56(5) requires that complaints be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged. The Complainant argues that he has exhausted judicial remedies, since there was not only a ministerial order in his favour, but also a judgment of the Court in his favour, which the State did not appeal and which was subsequently made binding, final and irrevocable by the inclusion of a certificate of non-appeal at the Supreme Court. The judgment of the Court annulled the second ministerial decision and reinstated the first, thus requiring that the Complainant receive a land certificate for his land which had been initially sold on the basis of forged documents. This decision is supported by the evidence submitted to the Commission and has not been contested by the Respondent State.

After the Complainant has alleged the exhaustion of local remedies, the burden shifts to the Respondent State to show which specific remedies were available and had not been exhausted by the Victim. In this regard, the State submits that there was a judgment of the Court in favour of the Victim, which shows that local judicial remedies are available. However, it is not sufficient for the State to prove that local remedies exist. It must also prove that the Complainant has not exhausted them. The reparation sought by the Complainant is the restitution of the Victim's property. Thus, the State should show the additional avenues of redress available to the Victim, which could reasonably have been expected of him to exhaust before turning to the Commission, in order to ensure the enforcement of the judgment in his favour. The State has not done so.

The Respondent State also gives no justification for the non-enforcement of the judgment between 1 October 2015 and May 2016, or even for the non-enforcement of the first ministerial decision of 2010 during the three-year period preceding its annulment in 2013. This is despite the Complainant's argument that "under administrative law, the decisions of the Minister and of the administrative court are enforced with immediate effect" and that "the decision was duly served on officials", arguments which were not contested by the State. The Commission therefore considers that the Complainant has demonstrated that local judicial remedies have been exhausted.

The Commission takes note of the evidence and arguments presented by both the Respondent State and the Complainant concerning the other correspondence that took place after the filing of the complaint. However, the Commission confirms its earlier position, namely that it is concerned with the facts as they were at the time the Complaint was filed, and that these subsequent developments do not concern it at this stage, since it must determine the admissibility of the case at the time it was filed.

Article 56(6) provides that a complaint must be "submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter". The Commission therefore has discretionary power to determine what a reasonable time is, on the basis of the facts before it. In the present case, the judgment was rendered in favour of the Complainant in October 2015, and he waited until 09 May 2016 to submit the complaint to the Commission, a period of six to seven months. The time for determining a reasonable period must therefore be counted from the moment when the Complainant could reasonably have expected the decision to be enforced. As the Complainant argued in paragraph 38 above and the State has not contested, "in administrative law, the decisions of the Minister and of the administrative court are enforced with immediate effect". Thus, within six months following the decision, the Complainant could reasonably have expected the decision to be implemented, but there was no sign of enforcement. À ce serait une période d'environ six mois, the Commission considers that the Complaint was filed within a reasonable time, and that the Complainant has therefore satisfied the requirement of Article 56(6).

The Applicant indicates that, in accordance with Article 56(7), the complaint has not been submitted to any other international procedure of investigation or settlement. The Respondent State has not provided any argument to the contrary. The Commission therefore considers that the requirement of Article 56(7) has been complied with.
In view of the above, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the Communication admissible

The Complainant alleges that the State of Cameroon, as a party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, is bound to ensure the respect and protection of the human rights of every person residing in its country, whether a national of its country or not, in accordance with the legislation in force which is not contrary to the provisions of the African Charter. The Complainant argues that by failing to respect and protect the right to property, the State of Cameroon violated the Victim's fundamental human rights protected by the Charter.

The Complainant insists that the administrative and judicial procedures established by the Government to ensure the respect and protection of human rights are not functional because the Government of Cameroon has failed to make the system work in favour of the Complainant despite the numerous appeals made by the Complainant to the various administrative and judicial authorities to ensure the application of the law and obtain reparation for the human rights violation perpetrated against the Complainant by the respondent party.

In support of his arguments, the Complainant argues that the State of Cameroon did not prosecute the lawyers/notaries who, together with their client Chi Simon Ndiforwa, affixed their signature to a forged power of attorney and forged deeds and that the State of Cameroon did not sanction the Land Registrar of Mezam for shamelessly refusing the orders and decisions of his Minister. He adds that in addition to this, the State of Cameroon did not sanction the Prosecutor General of the North-West Region and the State Counsel of Mezam.

The Complainant also adds that Article 1 of the Charter is a general provision and therefore invites the Commission to declare this article violated if it finds a violation of any other provision of the Charter.

The Applicant alleges the joint violation of Articles 28 and 29 of the Charter because he considers that the administrative and judicial authorities he seized to enforce his judgment and ministerial decision did not do what was necessary to implement them. In particular, he argues that the State Counsel and the Prosecutor assumed that the Victim was francophone and that, on that ground, the decision in French was never enforced whereas under Article 12(1) of the Charter, the Victim has the right to move from an anglophone region to reside in a francophone region without being discriminated against in any way.

In the Complainant's view, the refusal to enforce a judgment in French because the Victim originates from the French regions of Cameroon infringes his human rights in violation of Articles 2 and 12(1) of the Charter. He adds that the Respondent State violated Articles 28 and 29 of the African Charter since the two authorities refused to serve their national communities by not placing their physical and intellectual abilities at the service of the community and the Victim in particular.

The Complainant argues that the Respondent State violated Article 2 of the Charter. In support of his argument, he states that he was and is treated differently; that the difference in treatment has no objective and reasonable justification and that there is no proportionality between the aim sought and the means employed, comparing the Victim's case with the 30-day rule found in the Lackup Yamteh Jonah case.

In support of his argument, the Applicant reiterates that upon receipt of the ministerial instructions to cancel the fraudulent transfer of land title No. 3639/Mezam of 24 July 1995 from Forsang Philip Ndikum to Chi Simon Ndiforwa in accordance with decision No. 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010, the Registrar of Lands refused to enter the Minister's instructions in land certificate No. 3639/Mezam of 24/07/1995 belonging to Forsang Philip Ndikum as prescribed by law.

More specifically, he insists that the Registrar of Land of Mezam should immediately issue to the Victim a new land title No. 3639 in accordance with the 30-day rule in the Lackbup Yamteh Jonah case. He indicates that in the said case, the Minister of State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure wrote to the Land Registrar of the Littoral Region on 16 February 2015 to cancel a fraudulent land transaction concerning land title number 4451/WOURI. The Complainant indicates that, on 09 March 2015, the land title which was in the name of Mr. Kamdem Kuate Paul was cancelled and a new copy of the land title was issued to the original owner within 30 days.

The Complainant therefore concludes that the Lackbup Yamteh Jonah case shows that less than a month is sufficient to fulfil the terms of the decree setting the conditions for obtaining the land certificate. He insists that he had exhausted all local remedies following ministerial letter No. 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010 which became binding, final and irrevocable since 08 July 2011 following the Certificate of non-appeal and, for the second time, following judgment No. 062/FD/15 of 01 October 2015 which also became binding, final and irrevocable following the "Certificate of non-appeal" of 24 November 2015.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated Article 3 of the Charter. In particular, he states that he was placed in an extremely inferior position before the law, a position that was created to undermine his rights in favour of the political heavyweight Mr. Fokou who is, according to him, the personal friend of His Excellency President Paul Biya, chosen by him to be part of the Central Committee of the ruling Party.

In support of his arguments, he refers to the decision of the Minister of Lands of 16 February 2015 ordering the cancellation of the land title and its eventual transfer to its rightful owner. He indicates that the fact that this decision was enforced within a few weeks is a clear indication that the Complainant's case is treated as inferior to that of the Cameroonian whose decision was quickly enforced and to that of Mr. Fokou.

In the Complainant's view, it is obvious that the interpretation and application of the law to Government officials are different from those applied to the ordinary citizen. To justify his assertion, he indicates that the competent government authorities who are supposed to enforce judgment No. 062/FD/15 of 1 October 2015 totally ignored the existence of the judgment in disregard of the law. He concludes that since the Respondent State has not sanctioned the land registrar, Government officials have a mandate to violate his human rights with impunity.

Moreover, the Complainant alleges that the State Counsel of Mezam flagrantly stated that he was not to ensure the enforcement of judgments from the "francophone regions of Cameroon". According to the Complainant, refusing to enforce a judgment because it comes from a francophone region means that it is inferior to those of Bamenda whose judgments are enforced by the State Counsel. According to him, this implies that those who do not reside in the North-West region are not equal in the eyes of the law compared to those who reside in the francophone regions.

The Complainant alleges that the right protected by Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter was violated because the judgment was not enforced. In the Complainant's view, the trial is complete only when the reparation awarded by the court is promptly enforced without bias. He reiterates that his case was properly heard by the Administrative Court of the Littoral and the judgment rendered in his favour but that, because of the dysfunction of Government services, the judgment has not been enforced since 2015. In this regard, the Complainant argues that the non-enforcement of the court decision places the Victim in exactly the same situation of human rights violation as before the case, which violates the principle of fair trial.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violates the right to property enshrined in the Charter in Article 14. He indicates that the land under certificate No. 3639 belongs to the Victim. He argues that under Cameroonian land law, proof of ownership is a land certificate and that the same law lays down the procedure for acquiring land certificates and the procedure for cancelling land certificates.

In particular, the Complainant argues that the aforementioned law specifies that the land certificate can be withdrawn in case of error by Government services in its issuance when the Minister has verified its authenticity. The same law indicates that a withdrawn land certificate must be transferred to its original owner free of charge. The Complainant submits that under this law, the Minister ordered the transfer of the land title to the Victim. He insists that the transfer of the land, as ordered by the Minister, was supposed to be immediate and free of charge but that the Minister of Lands annulled the decision of his predecessor without any legal basis.

According to the Complainant, the Victim's right to property was grossly violated in that the Government was aware of the expropriation of his property despite decision No. 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010, judgment No. 56/OSE/PTA/DLA/2015 and judgment of the Administrative Court of the Littoral No. 062/FD/2015.

In support of his allegation, the Applicant refers to the Endorois case where the Commission established that the right to property can only be violated when this is "in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws". He asserts that, in his case, however, the expropriated land was used as a warehouse for the distribution of construction materials, which serves not the public or general interest but the selfish interest of Mr. Fokou.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated Article 21(3). In particular, he insists that the right to property is accompanied by three fundamental rights: the right to use, the right to enjoy and the right to dispose. According to him, among all these rights enjoyed by virtue of property, Article 21 of the Charter imposes a special responsibility on States Parties to respect and protect the right to dispose.

The Complainant argues that to enjoy the right to dispose of land or a rental property, the owner must be in possession of all the documents confirming his ownership. According to him, under the legislation in force in Cameroon, the right to dispose of registered landed property is vested in the owner of the property, that is, the person whose name is registered as the owner of the land. According to him, by refusing to enforce the various decisions returning the land to the Victim, the Respondent State has denied the right to dispose of and to rent the land, given that he has not been in possession of the land for more than a decade, even after the ministerial decision and the court judgments to ensure that the Victim's land is returned to him.

As already indicated in the part on procedure, the Respondent State did not submit its observations on the merits although such an opportunity had been offered to it through several reminders sent to it. In these circumstances, and in accordance with its well-established jurisprudence, the Commission has no other choice but to proceed to examine the Communication on the basis of the submissions of the Complainant and the information at its disposal to the extent that they are sufficiently substantiated.

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 2 of the Charter which stipulates that "Every individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as race, ethnic group, color, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status". This provision advocates the right to non-discrimination. In view of the Complainant's allegations, it is important for the Commission to define the content of this right.

The Commission defined discrimination in the case of Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (on behalf of Andrew Barclay Meldrum) v. Zimbabwe, as: "any act which makes a distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference on the ground of race, colour [...] or other status and which has the purpose or effect of nullifying or impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by all persons, on an equal footing, of all rights and freedoms". Discrimination is therefore an unlawful or unjustified differentiation, that is to say one based on one of the distinctions cited in Article 2.

Thus, the Commission considers that for there to be a violation of Article 2 of the African Charter, it must be shown that the victim of the alleged violation was deprived of the enjoyment of a right under the Charter on account of his or her race, ethnic group, colour, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status, national and social status, fortune, birth or any other status.

In the case under analysis, the Complainant considers that he was a victim of discrimination because, upon receipt of the various ministerial instructions to cancel the fraudulent transfer of Land Title No. 3639 of 24 July 1995 from Forsang Philip Ndikum to Chi Simon, the Register of Lands discriminated against the Victim because he refused to enter the Minister's instructions on this title as prescribed by Cameroonian law. He insists that, however, in a similar case of Lackbup Yamteh Jonah, the Minister's instructions were followed and the victim obtained a new land certificate within a period not exceeding 30 days.

It also emerges from the Complainant's allegations that the State Counsel of Mezam flagrantly stated that he was not to ensure the enforcement of judgments from the "francophone regions of Cameroon". Faced with these allegations, which were not refuted by the Respondent State although an opportunity to do so had been offered to it, the Commission concludes that there was a violation of the right to non-discrimination under Article 2 of the Charter.
It follows that Article 2 has been violated

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 3, which reads as follows: "1. Every individual shall be equal before the law. 2. Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law." The right set out in this article comprises two meanings, namely the right to equality before the law and the right to equal protection of the law. The two notions are not defined by the Charter.

However, in the case of Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (on behalf of Andrew Barclay Meldrum) v. Zimbabwe, the Commission indicated that "this article guarantees fair and just treatment of individuals within a legal system of a given country and in which all individuals are equal before the law and enjoy equal protection before the law".

In its first sense, this right means the right of all to equal treatment under the same conditions. Indeed, in the eyes of the Commission, the right to equality before the law means that individuals lawfully residing within the jurisdiction of a State must expect to be treated fairly and justly within the legal system and be assured of equal treatment before the law and equal enjoyment of the rights available to all citizens.

It follows that within the meaning of Article 3(1), the same procedures and principles of law must be applied under the same conditions. Consequently, this provision means that existing laws must be applied in the same way to all those subject to them, which implies that the right to equality before the law does not refer to the content of the legislation but rather to the manner in which that content is applied.

As to the right to equal protection before the law, the Commission indicated in the above-mentioned case that this right means that no person or group of persons must be denied the same legal protection enjoyed by other persons or groups of persons in similar circumstances with respect to their life, liberty, property and pursuit of happiness.

Thus, as described by the Commission in the case of Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Angola, in order for a Complainant to successfully bring a complaint under Article 3 of the Charter, he must prove that the Respondent State had not accorded the victims the same treatment accorded to others or that it had accorded favourable treatment to others in the same situation as the victims.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that the Victim was placed in an extremely inferior position before the law, a position that was created to undermine his rights in favour of the political heavyweight Mr. Fokou, a friend of the President of the Republic Paul Biya. In view of the allegations and the previous considerations on the meaning of Article 3 of the Charter, the Commission is called upon to analyse whether the Victim faced a difference in treatment in similar legal situations. After analysing the arguments and the evidence at its disposal, the Commission indeed observes a difference in the enforcement of decisions concerning cases similar to that of the Victim.

Thus, for example, the Commission notes that in a similar case, the Minister of State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure was seized by Mr. Lackbup Yamteh Jonah to demand the withdrawal of a fraudulent transfer of land title No. 44615/Wouri in favour of Mr. Kandem Kuate Paul. Following an instruction to cancel the said Title by the aforementioned Minister, the Land Registrar of Wouri C produced a registration certificate and an analytical statement which indicate that the total transfer made in the name of Mr. Kandem Kuate Paul is cancelled in favour of Mr. Lackbup Yamteh Jonah.
In this sense, the Commission shares the Complainant's view that this differentiated treatment of a case presenting similar circumstances is a violation of Article 3 of the Charter

Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter stipulates that "Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force". This provision protects the right to have one's cause heard in its aspect of the right to appeal to competent national organs.

In this sense, the right to have one's cause heard includes the right to bring a case before a court as well as the right to appeal against a first-instance decision before higher courts. As the Commission indicated in the case of Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia, the guarantees of this provision go beyond hearings in the normal context of judicial proceedings or decisions. In reality, they encompass the administration of justice since the latter must be organised in such a way as to ensure fairness for all regardless of the identity of the parties to the proceedings and the nature of the proceedings itself.

In this sense, the guarantees of Article 7(1)(a) also include the right to the enforcement of judgments. Indeed, in the case of Antoine Bissangou v. Congo, the Commission indicated that "it would be inconceivable for this article to grant an individual the right to apply to all national courts for a remedy against any act violating fundamental rights without guaranteeing the enforcement of court decisions". Thus, it is understandable that the right to have one's cause heard would remain unguaranteed if the decisions taken by Courts and Tribunals produce no effect.

In the present case, the Commission indeed observes that after noting that ministerial decision No. 00004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010 calling into question the transfer of the Victim's property was not being enforced, the Victim seized the Administrative Court of the Littoral. The latter ruled by judgment No. 062/FD/15 of 1 October 2015 in favour of the Victim by annulling the second ministerial decision transferring the property to Mr. Fokou (decision No. 00004310/Y.7/MINDCAF/SG/S120 of 26 August 2013 of the Minister of State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure).

The Commission notes that at the time of receipt of the communication on 9 May 2016, the decision of the Administrative Court of the Littoral had not yet been enforced. Nor is there, in the subsequent exchanges, from the seizure of the Commission until the time it rules on the merits, any document in the file proving that the aforementioned decision of the Court has been enforced.

In this sense, the Commission shares the Complainant's view that the non-enforcement of the decision of the Administrative Court of the Littoral placed the Victim in the same situation of human rights violation as before the decision; which implies the violation of the right to a fair trial within the meaning of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter.

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 12(1), which stipulates that "Every individual shall have the right to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of a State provided he abides by the law". This provision of the Charter advocates freedom of movement and freedom of residence within a State.

In the case of Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan, the Commission indicated that freedom of movement is a fundamental right granted to every person in States and indispensable to the protection and promotion of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

The Commission considers that by virtue of the right to freedom of movement, every citizen of a State generally has the right to leave and return to that State at any time; but also to travel, reside and/or work wherever he or she wishes in the country without interference from the State. Similarly, in its General Comment No. 5, the Commission indicated that the right to move freely within a State confers on every individual the freedom to move within a State without restriction of his or her movements.

As for freedom of residence, it simply means the right to choose one's place of residence recognised for every person. In other words, as the Commission indicated in its General Comment No. 5, this right includes the prerogative of individuals to freely choose and change their place of residence within the State. Thus, for example, in situations where human rights defenders have alleged that they were forced to leave the country of their residence because of their human rights defence work, the Commission found a violation of Article 12(1).

In the present case, the Complainant considers that the Victim's right to freedom of movement was violated because the State Counsel and the Prosecutor General considered that the Victim was francophone and that as such the decision in French was not enforced whereas, according to him, the Victim has the right to move from an anglophone region to reside in a francophone region without being discriminated against in any way.

The Commission is of the view that the Complainant has not substantiated his allegations with elements that are of a nature to qualify the facts presented as a violation of the right to freedom of movement and the right to freedom of residence. In particular, it has not been shown that the Victim was subjected to constraint of any kind forcing him to leave or not to leave any place, to reside or not to reside in a place he does not want.

In this sense, the Complainant's argument that the decision was not enforced because he was of francophone origin does not meet this requirement because such a constraint is not implied. On the contrary, non-enforcement because of the Victim's origin rather implies discrimination.
It follows that Article 12(1) has not been violated.

Article 14 of the Charter stipulates as follows: "The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws". The Complainant's allegations call for an understanding of the content and scope of this right to property.

In the case of African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights v. Kenya, the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights considered that, in its classic sense, the right to property comprises three elements, namely the right to use the thing that is the object of the right (usus), the right to enjoy its fruits (fructus), and the right to dispose of it, that is, to transfer it (abusus). Furthermore, the Commission found that the right to property encompassed not only the right to have access to one's property and not to invade or encroach on the property of others, but also the right to keep, use and control one's property without distraction, as deemed appropriate.

The Commission therefore considers that in addition to the right to have access to one's property and to prevent the invasion and encroachment of the said property, the right to property also includes the right to peaceful possession and use as well as control of that property, as its owner desires. However, Article 14 provides that the right to property may be subject to restrictions for reasons of public need or general interest in accordance with the relevant laws.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that his right to property was violated because the land title of his property was fraudulently withdrawn from him and that under Cameroonian land law, it should be transferred to its original owner. In the case of Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania, land was considered as "property". With regard to the content of the right to property as explained above, it is important to determine whether the Victim really had the right of ownership over the land in question here and that he enjoyed all its attributes, in particular the right to dispose of it, the right to use it and to enjoy its fruits.

The Commission observes that the land certificate of the land in question in the case under analysis belongs to the Victim Philip Forsang Ndikum. This was confirmed by the first ministerial decision No. 00004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010 indicating that the transfer of land No. 03639 was fraudulent and that this land should return to the Victim free of charge.

The same is true of the decision of the Administrative Court of the Littoral of 1 October 2015 on the appeal brought by the Victim against the second ministerial decision 0004310/Y.7/MINDCAF/SG/D6/S210 of 26 August 2013 annulling the initial ministerial decision and requiring the transfer of the land to Mr. Fokou. The Commission notes that in its decision, the Administrative Court of the Littoral found that the appeal was well-founded and that consequently "decision No. 0004310/Y.7/MINDAF/SG/D6/S120 of 26 August 2013 of the Minister of State Property, Surveys and Land Tenure, reporting that No. 0004855/Y.7/MINDAF/BF of 27 December 2010, is annulled with all legal consequences.

All these decisions imply that the Victim had a right of ownership over the land bearing number 3639/Mezam. However, the Commission notes that since 2005, the year in which this land was sold without the Victim's knowledge, the latter has not continued to enjoy the attributes of his right of ownership of this land. In particular, the Commission observes that the Victim did not have access to the said landed property because the corresponding land title had been taken from him and transferred to another person, but also he could neither use nor control the property as a normal owner.

This results from the decisions taken by various administrative and judicial authorities in relation to his situation from the sale of the land without his knowledge until the time of the submission of his application. This is the case of the first ministerial decision which indicated that the transfer of this land was done fraudulently and that it should return to the Victim, of the second ministerial decision annulling the previous decision and requiring the transfer of the land to Mr. Fokou and of the decision of the Administrative Court of the Littoral annulling the second ministerial decision and confirming that the appeal of Mr. Philip Forsang Ndikum was well-founded. All these decisions show that the Victim did not enjoy any of the attributes of the right of ownership over the land in question.
Nor has it been shown that the withdrawal of the title from the Victim was done out of public need or in the general interest of the community.
It follows that Article 14 of the Charter has been violated.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated Article 21(1) which provides that: "All peoples shall freely dispose of their wealth and natural resources. This right shall be exercised in the exclusive interest of the people. In no case shall a people be deprived of it. However, the Complainant limits himself to merely alleging the violation of this provision without giving details as to the causal link between the facts described and the provisions of this article. In the absence of this justification, the Commission concludes that this article has not been violated.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated Article 21(3) which provides that "The free disposal of wealth and natural resources shall be exercised without prejudice to the obligation of promoting international economic cooperation based on mutual respect, equitable exchange and the principles of international law". This provision advocates the free disposal of wealth and natural resources.

In the case of Social and Economic Rights Action Center (SERAC) and Center for Economic and Social Rights (CESR) v. Nigeria; the Commission indicated that, by this provision, the drafters of the African Charter clearly intended to remind African governments of the continent's painful legacy and to bring cooperative economic development back to its traditional place, that is, at the heart of African society. In particular, the Commission pointed out that this provision dates back to the era of colonialism when colonial powers exploited the natural resources of African countries to the detriment of their peoples, which had the consequence of leaving Africa's populations and natural resources still vulnerable.

However, the rights stipulated in Article 21 remain applicable to post-colonial Africa in favour of groups within a State to the extent that they impose an obligation on States Parties to protect their citizens from exploitation by external economic powers. Indeed, in its General Guidelines on National Periodic Reports, the Commission had already indicated that the right to freely dispose of one's wealth and resources consists in ensuring that the wealth of countries is not exploited by foreigners without any profit for African countries or leaving them a marginal profit.

From the foregoing, it can be concluded first that the right to the free disposal of wealth and natural resources is a collective right concerning a group of persons or individuals. This means that groups or communities must be involved, directly or indirectly, in decisions relating to the disposal of their wealth. Second, the presumption in the drafting of Article 21 is that the threat to this right would come largely from outside the State and even from outside the continent, either in the form of a neo-colonial influence of non-African States or of multinational corporations.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that by refusing to enforce the various decisions returning the property to the Victim, the right to dispose of or to rent the land was denied to him given that he has not been in possession of the land for more than a decade. The Commission has clearly established that the Victim's right to property over the land in question, which also includes the right to dispose of it, to use it and to enjoy its fruits, has been violated. However, it is not proven that this violation had an impact on the right to the free disposal of wealth and natural resources. Indeed, as already indicated, the right to the free disposal of wealth and natural resources is collective in nature in that it protects a common heritage of a particular group or community.

Thus, for example, in the case of Antoine Bissangou v. Congo, the Commission considered that the Complainant's movable and immovable property which was damaged during the socio-political events that shook the country in 1993 did not constitute the wealth and natural resources of a people but rather individual property: It finally concluded that the Complainant was acting in his own name and not on behalf of a group of individuals or a population living in a given territory and that, consequently, there was no violation of Article 21.

In the present case also, the Complainant alleges the violation of his right to property and is not acting on behalf of any group or community. In these circumstances, the Commission cannot establish the violation of the right to the free disposal of wealth and natural resources, a right which is naturally reserved to the people.
It follows that Article 21(1) and (3) have not been violated.

The Complainant alleges a joint violation of Articles 28 and 29(2) (4) (6) of the Charter. Article 28 stipulates that "Every individual shall have the duty to respect and consider his fellow beings without discrimination, and to maintain relations aimed at promoting, safeguarding and reinforcing mutual respect and tolerance". As for Article 29(2) (4) (6) of the Charter, it indicates that: "The individual shall also have the duty: 2. To serve his national community by placing his physical and intellectual abilities at its service; 4. To preserve and strengthen social and national solidarity, particularly when the latter is threatened; 6. To work to the best of his abilities and competence, and to pay taxes imposed by law in the interest of the society".

These two provisions advocate the duty of non-discrimination and of respecting human beings. The duty to "respect and consider" others without discrimination is at the same time a negative obligation of every individual to "refrain from any discrimination" and a positive duty to "maintain relations aimed at promoting, safeguarding and reinforcing mutual respect and tolerance".
