Thus in the public sphere this right refers to the obligation of the State to protect "the physical integrity of its citizens against abuses committed by public authorities".
The Complainants therefore consider that the State failed in its obligation to protect Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo against abuses by public authorities.

In the present case Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo suffered several infringements of his liberty and security. He was the subject of intense threats by State agents, a situation which forced him to live in hiding. He was also arrested and detained in December 2009 arbitrarily without any charge being brought against him, before a second arrest on 26 August 2010 which ended in his extrajudicial execution. The Complainants consider that this arrest was made in violation of the rules provided for by both domestic and international law, as it was made without charge, or presentation of the victim before a court.

They also recall that several positive obligations arise from the right to liberty and security of the person and that under Article 6, the State must protect individuals from infringements of their liberty and security and must also prevent such violations and investigate them when they occur in order to prosecute and punish the perpetrators and grant full reparation to the victims.
Consequently, they request the Commission to find the violation of Article 6 by the Respondent State.

Article 7(1) (a) of the African Charter provides that "[e]very individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises [...] the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force."

The Complainants submit that the African Commission has interpreted this article as recognising for complainants the right to have "unhindered access to a court or competent tribunal to hear their case"

They also assert that the rights protected in Article 7(1) (a) are recognised for persons arrested and detained but also for any other individual, and that the African Commission has considered that when victims are prevented from accessing the courts to have their case heard, State authorities violate Article 7 (1) (a) of the African Charter; the same is true "when the competent authorities place obstacles to the victims' access to the courts, they must be held responsible"

They further add that the obstacles that may prevent victims' access to the courts have been identified by the jurisprudence of the African Commission, which has considered among other things that situations or acts of violence committed against victims may render illusory and impossible access to the competent bodies to obtain justice and thus constitute a violation of Article 7 para 1(a) of the African Charter.

Article 26 of the African Charter imposes on States "the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts", an essential component for guaranteeing victims an effective remedy before domestic judicial institutions.
The Complainants submit that the African Commission has already found a violation of Article 26 in connection with Article 7 para 1 (a), when the impartiality of the courts was not guaranteed.

In the present case, although a judicial file was apparently opened, no effective and complete investigation was conducted. It therefore appears that local remedies were set in motion, but in vain as they proved ineffective and unsatisfactory because they did not make it possible to shed light on the circumstances of the death of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo

The Complainants consider that the absence of action by Burundian justice stems from the "general climate of impunity" prevailing in Burundi with regard to serious human rights violations. They also cite the report of the Commission of Inquiry on extrajudicial executions and acts of torture set up in June 2011 which, although having acknowledged the commission of homicide, denied that these were extrajudicial executions.

Moreover, the question of the independence of justice in Burundi has been raised on several occasions including during the Estates General of Burundian Justice held from 5 to 9 August 2013 which highlighted the need to reform the system to ensure its independence, notably by formulating recommendations concerning the independence of justice from the executive, a central subject of concern during the discussions. Indeed, among the main conclusions was the reform of the Higher Council of the Judiciary, the presidency of which is vested in the President of the Republic, and the election of the President of the Supreme Court who is appointed by the President instead of being elected. The Complainants consider that the conclusions of the Estates General of Justice found a lack of independence from the executive.

Finally, the Complainants maintain that the State agents alleged to be responsible in this case are the perpetrators of numerous serious human rights violations and particularly benefit from this generalised impunity.

In view of the absence of results from the procedures opened and of the more general contextual elements presented above, the Complainants respectfully request the Commission to find the violation of Articles 7a1 (1) (a) and 26 of the African Charter
Under Article 9 (2) of the African Charter, "[e]very individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law",

According to the Complainants, freedom of expression, one of whose natural components is freedom of opinion, has been defined by the Commission as "a fundamental human right, essential to an individual's personal development and political consciousness" and vital "for his participation in the conduct of the public affairs of his country". Thus, it is established as an inherent foundation of any democratic society. They add that the Commission recalled in this regard that the legitimate exercise of human rights does not pose any problem for a democratic State governed by the rule of law"
Moreover, the protection of freedom of political opinion through Article 9 of the African Charter has been confirmed by the jurisprudence of the African Commission.

They also report that the Commission has already had occasion to find that the execution of political opponents constitutes a total restriction on freedom of expression resulting in a violation of Article 9(2) of the African Charter. Indeed, it considered that inflicting ill-treatment for the mere reason that an individual seeks to "disseminate political opinions and views [...] unfavourable to the Respondent State" constitutes a violation of freedom of expression. The same goes for the persecution of persons belonging to opposition parties, amounting to a violation of Article 9. The Complainants consider that the same jurisprudence should be applicable with regard to persons who have expressed critical opinions towards the political authorities.

In the present case, the death threats and then the execution of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo occurred because of criticisms made against the national police and public denunciations for corruption. They therefore request that the Commission find the violation of Article 9(2) of the African Charter.

Article 18 para 1 of the African Charter provides that "The family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral".

The Complainants submit that the African Commission has considered that the separation of family members resulting from arbitrary and incommunicado detention constitutes a violation of the right to family life and thus of Article 18 para 1 of the African Charter.

They also submit that the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee has specified the scope of the right to protection of the family provided for in Article 23 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Concluding notably in the case of Marcel Mulezi v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, that the death of the author's wife as a result of ill-treatment inflicted by State agents constituted a violation of this provision.

Likewise, the execution of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo entailed a break-up of the family unit and an infringement of the psychological health of the family members while placing it in a situation of economic precariousness having lost its main provider. It also deprived his children of their father. Moreover, the authorities' refusal to return the deceased's remains to them made the family's mourning more difficult.
Consequently the Complainants respectfully request the Commission to find the violation of Article 18 para 1 of the African Charter with regard to the relatives of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo.

As the procedure indicates, despite the time far beyond the time limits prescribed by the Commission's Rules of Procedure and the reminder addressed to it, the Respondent State did not transmit its observations on the merits.

Article 4 of the African Charter provides that "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right". This inviolable nature of the right to life also emerges from the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) which provides that "Every human being has the inherent right to life. This right shall be protected by law. No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his life".

The right to life is a fundamental right, it is the basis of all other rights, the "linchpin of all other rights. It is non-derogable and applies to all and at all times" General Comment No. 6 of the Human Rights Committee indeed provides that: "(...) It is the supreme right from which no derogation is permitted even in time of public emergency which threatens the life of the nation (art. 4).
The realisation of this right presupposes a particular commitment of the State to take the necessary measures to guarantee its effective protection.

In Noah Kazingachire, John Chitsenga, Elias Chemvura and Batanai Hadzisi (represented by Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum) v. Zimbabwe, the Commission held that international human rights law requires that the State respect and ensure the right to life and that it has the obligation to prevent the unjustified death of its citizens. It must ensure that its organs respect the life of persons within its jurisdiction.

In its General Comment No. 3 on the right to life, the Commission expressly specified that States are responsible for violations of this right committed by all their organs (executive, legislative, judicial), and other administrative or public authorities, at all levels (national, regional or local). It also concluded in Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe, that the failure of the State to take transparently all necessary measures to investigate suspicious deaths and any execution perpetrated by State agents and to identify persons or groups responsible for violations of the right to life and to hold them accountable constitutes, in itself, a violation of this right by the State.
In the case of infringements of the right to life where all means are not implemented to punish the perpetrators, this amounts to an encouragement of future crimes.

In the present case, the extrajudicial nature of Mr Ndikuriyo's death is clearly established by the fact that although he was in a car with other persons at the time of the ambush, he was the only one to lose his life, all the other persons came out unscathed without a scratch including the allegedly attacked vehicle which showed no bullet impact, nor the slightest scratch. To this are added the inconsistencies highlighted in the versions of the authorities' representatives, the absence of an investigation to identify the alleged perpetrators and the refusal to return the remains to the family so that it could bury him with dignity.

In its General Comment No. 3 on the right to life, the Commission stresses that it is incumbent on States to develop and implement a legal and practical framework to respect, protect, promote and fulfil the right to life. States must adopt measures both to prevent arbitrary deprivations of life and to conduct prompt, impartial, thorough and transparent investigations into any such deprivation that may have occurred, holding those responsible accountable and providing an effective remedy and reparation to the victim or victims, including, where appropriate, to their families and dependants.

In the present case, it is clearly established that the State made little of this case by not condemning the acts of the police, whose representative disparaged the memory of the deceased and refused to return the body to the family.

Yet the failure of the State to take transparently all necessary measures to investigate suspicious deaths and any execution perpetrated by State agents and to identify persons or groups responsible for violations of the right to life and to hold them accountable constitutes, in itself, a violation of this right by the State. This is all the more true where there is a tolerance of the culture of impunity.

In the present case, the inaction of the State in not implementing its procedural obligations can be likened to an implicit complicity in the acts perpetrated that resulted in a violation of the right to life.
Consequently, the African Commission concludes that the Respondent State violated Article 4 of the African Charter.

Under Article 5 of the African Charter "[e]very individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited."

In the case of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo it is alleged that the latter was subjected to torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as well as serious infringements of his right to dignity and legal personality as enshrined in Article 5 of the African Charter. Acts of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment are also alleged against his family.

It is also emphasised that the State failed in its obligation of protection by not having taken the necessary measures to prevent the occurrence of acts of torture against Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo and his family, by not putting in place "effective solutions in a transparent, independent and effective legal system" and by not pursuing effective and independent investigations relating to these allegations.

On the question of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the United Nations Convention against Torture of 10 December 1984 defines as an act of torture and barbarity "any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person.... for such purposes as obtaining from him ... information ...; intimidating or coercing him or a third person...". Jurisprudence has given a definition of the incriminated conduct by providing that "torture or acts of barbarity presuppose the demonstration of a material element consisting in the commission of one or more acts of exceptional gravity which go beyond mere violence and give rise to the will to deny in the victim the dignity of the human person"

In Spilg and Mack & DITSHWANELO (on behalf of Lehlohonolo Bernard Kobedi) v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt, the Commission emphasised actions that cause severe physical or psychological suffering (or) humiliate the individual (...).

The Commission also established in its decision World Organisation Against Torture and Africa Zone League for the Defence of the Rights of Children and Pupils (on behalf of Céline) v. Democratic Republic of Congo that to be characterised as torture, the acts perpetrated must not only be severe pain or suffering, but above all caused by or at the instigation of a public authority, with the purpose of punishing or obtaining information or a confession, the said pain or suffering being physical or mental.

Moreover, the Human Rights Committee has consistently recognised in its jurisprudence that "the anguish and distress that the disappearance [...] caused to his entire close family" constitutes a violation of Article 7 of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights with regard to the victim's relatives. In Chitay Nech et al. v. Guatemala, the Inter-American Court also held that the suffering and anguish of the relatives of the victim of a serious human rights violation entails a violation of their right to integrity.

In the present case the Complainants submit that Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo was a victim of extrajudicial execution on 25 August 2010 which represents an irremediable infringement of his life and his physical and psychological integrity. Moreover his remains were left on site for an entire night and were not handed over to his family so that it could bury him with dignity; thus denying his human essence which implies a violation of his legal personality. They add that the family of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo is the collateral victim of the 2acts of torture and intimidation suffered by the latter. Indeed, the multiple intimidations that led the victim to take refuge in hiding caused anguish and fear for his family, which was worried about the victim's security but also about its own security as it dreaded possible reprisals from the persons who were after Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo. Finally the brutal death of the victim created an emotional distress having a negative impact on the members of his family

From the analysis of the facts, it is clearly established that the increasingly pressing death threats against him, as well as the various acts of harassment and intimidation, generated emotional distress which drove the victim to live in hiding for fear for his life. In International PEN, Constitutional Rights Project, Civil Liberties Organisation and Interights (on behalf of Ken Saro-Wiwa Jnr.) v. Nigeria, the Commission considered that Article 5 prohibits not only torture, but also cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. This includes not only acts that cause severe physical or psychological suffering, but also those that humiliate the individual or force him to act against his will or conscience.

It cannot validly be maintained that living in hiding is a choice made lightheartedly and it can in no way be considered that this state of affairs has no impact on the physical and psychological condition of the person who experiences it. Indeed, the fear and anguish induced by acts of intimidation can be considered mental torture.

Moreover, when one considers the thinly veiled threats uttered by the authorities against the victim's family, notably by the Director General of the Police who had declared on the radio that the body would not be returned to the family and that the victim "had got only what he deserved", coupled with the refusal to authorise the family to organise a decent burial for the victim, the finding of inhuman and degrading treatment with regard to the victim and his family is hard to contest.

In its General Comment No. 4 on the right to redress for victims of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the Commission specifies that a person is considered a victim regardless of whether the perpetrator of the violation is identified, apprehended, prosecuted or convicted and regardless of any familial relationship between the perpetrator and the victim. The term "victim" also includes members of the immediate family or dependants of the direct victim and persons who, in intervening to assist a victim or to prevent a person from becoming a victim, have suffered harm.

As regards the dignity of the human person, it is not only a fundamental right in itself, but it constitutes the very basis of fundamental rights. It is in view of the capital importance it holds that the Preamble of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 begins in these terms "Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world". This therefore presupposes that any act likely to harm human dignity constitutes a violation of the fundamental rights of the human person, thus psychological harassment, discrimination, defamation, slanderous denunciation, insults can be considered as acts which infringe the dignity of the human person.

Yet anonymity, the absence of a burial or the impossibility for the family of accessing the place of burial raise the question of the accompaniment of the dead. In Africa, particularly, burying one's dead is honouring them, it is part of the most important rites of life and respect for the dead is a matter of the sacred order. To deny the right to bury a relative with dignity is like denying the human essence and disparaging the value of the latter and what he represents for his family. This may also constitute an insult and moral suffering for the family.

By refusing deliberately to return the body of the deceased to his family, the State representatives violated respect for human dignity which in African culture also applies to the dead. Moreover, the deliberate nature of this act demonstrates the manifest determination of the State representatives to hurt the family and to infringe its honour and that of the deceased, knowing the importance that burial and mourning rites occupy in our African societies.

From the foregoing, it is clearly established that acts of mental torture were perpetrated against Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo and his family. It also appears that a manifest violation of the dignity inherent in every human being was committed. The Commission therefore considers that the Respondent State failed in its obligations under Article 5 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights and finds the violation of this article.

Article 6 of the African Charter provides that "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained".

The Commission established in Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan that individual liberty is a fundamental condition which everyone can generally enjoy. To be deprived of it is a fact that appears to have a direct and undesirable effect on the enjoyment of several other rights, including the right to life and to a family.

In the present case the violation of Article 6 relates mainly to the failure of the State to ensure the security of the person of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo, who suffered several infringements of his liberty and security, and was the subject of intense threats by State agents, who forced him to live in hiding for fear for his life. He was also arrested twice, one in 2009 and the second in 2010 which ended in his death. The circumstances previously cited led to fear and anguish coupled with physical and psychological insecurity, with regard to the victim, undoubtedly causing a violation of his right to security of his person.

The failure of the State to protect the victim while he was under its protection may constitute an aggravating circumstance as it led to an irremediable situation, that is to say the death of the victim. This is all the more glaring when one notes that Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo was the only victim of the supposed ambush.

Indeed, the State is the primary guarantor of the security of persons under its responsibility, particularly when these persons cannot ensure their own protection. The Commission moreover clearly established this in Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe, when it concluded that an act attributable to a third party may well engage the responsibility of the State when the latter failed to prevent the occurrence of the violation (...).

Thus, by not acting in accordance with the precautionary principle which requires taking all necessary measures to ensure the protection of the victim who was already vulnerable, the State made itself complicit if not responsible for the acts restricting the liberty of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo as well as for the infringements of his physical integrity that resulted in his death.

The Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa (Luanda Guidelines) define the term "arrest" as the act of apprehending a person for the alleged commission of an offence or by the action of an authority competent to arrest and detain a person as authorised by law. They further specify that everyone has the right to liberty and security of the person. Detention must always be an exceptional measure of last resort. No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful arrest or detention.

In its General Comment No. 35 on Article 9 (Liberty and security of person) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the Human Rights Committee established that security of person concerns protection against bodily and psychological injury, or bodily and mental integrity. It also considered that deprivation of liberty represents a more severe restriction on movement (...).

If in Abdel Hadi, Ali Radi & Others v. Republic of Sudan, the Commission recognised that deprivation of liberty is one of the legitimate forms of control by the State over persons within its jurisdiction. It specified however that any arrest or detention must be carried out in accordance with the procedure established by domestic law, failing which such an arrest would be considered arbitrary. In the case of the first arrest of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo no charge was brought against him, this state of affairs made him vulnerable and the intimidations that followed forced him into hiding for fear for his life. It can therefore be concluded that this arrest was arbitrary.
Consequently, the Commission finds that the State violated the principles of Article 6.

Article 7(1) (a) of the African Charter provides that "every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force (...)"

Article 26 for its part obliges States to "guarantee the independence of the Courts and shall allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter."

As emphasised by the Complainants in their submissions, the violation of Articles 7(1) (a) and 26 of the African Charter may be found in situations where the impartiality of the courts is not guaranteed notably owing to the appointment of judges by government and political authorities.

Moreover the analysis of its jurisprudence provides examples of obstacles that may prevent victims' access to the courts and/or the partiality of the courts. Notwithstanding this state of affairs, it is for the Commission to establish in light of the facts and arguments submitted to it whether in the present case the same conclusion may apply.
The Commission will first proceed to the analysis of the facts to determine whether there has been a violation of Article 7 (1) (a) and then look into the alleged violation of Article 26.

Concerning the violation of Article 7(1) (a); the right to have one's cause heard presupposes that the measures necessary for the resolution of the harm suffered are concretely implemented with a view to restoring the victim in his right. In the present case, apart from the opening of a file by the Public Prosecutor's Office following the arrest of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo in 2009, no other action was taken. It must be concluded that the cause was not heard despite the steps initiated. The Complainants' arguments submitted in this regard in support of the admissibility of the present communication clearly demonstrate this.

Then, on the basis of the jurisprudence established by the United Nations Committee against Torture, the State has the obligation to investigate in cases of serious human rights violations such as torture. Moreover, in its general comment on the right to life, the Commission recommends that States adopt measures both to prevent arbitrary deprivations of life and to conduct prompt, impartial, thorough and transparent investigations into any such deprivation that may have occurred, holding those responsible accountable (...). Consequently a proven violation of the right to life should be subject to the same obligation and consequently the diligence of justice should prevail. This diligence could translate into adequate protection given to the victim and the speed of the investigation into the causes of his death, but above all in the search for those responsible for his extrajudicial execution for which no prosecution has been initiated.

In the case of Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence and Interights v. Cameroon, the Commission places particular emphasis on the obligation of the State to "carry out investigations" and to "take consequential measures" to prevent the violation but also to remedy it. The obligation to investigate and prosecute is reiterated in Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan, where the Commission concluded that the absence of investigation in cases of arbitrary and extrajudicial executions amounts to a violation of the right to life.

In the present case, the Complainants submitted that the victim's Lawyer Me Nyamoya was arrested for having denounced the facts that happened to the victim, and that the police officers who, like the victim, were actively claiming their rights were also put in prison. Moreover, anyone showing an interest, closely or remotely, in this case was subjected to threats, this is notably the case of the President of APRODH who received direct threats from the Minister of the Interior forbidding him to continue to speak about the victim's case. It is therefore clearly established that everything was done so that the victim's cause would not be heard.

Following the analysis of the Complainants' arguments against the backdrop of established jurisprudence, the Commission concludes that there has been a violation of the provisions of Article 7(1) (a) of the Charter

Concerning the alleged violation of Article 26, relating to the requirement of independence of the courts, it should be analysed in combination with Article 7(1) (d), which relates to the principle of impartiality provided for in Article 7 1(d) of the African Charter; even if the latter was hardly invoked by the Complainants, the Commission considers it necessary to associate it with the present analysis. Thus, if sometimes the necessary impartiality of the judge is designated by the term "independence", impartiality is much closer to the personal independence of the magistrate as opposed to the collective independence of the judiciary. Independence boils down to a "status" and impartiality to a "state of mind".

In its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, the Commission goes in the same direction by indicating that the guarantee of a fair trial presupposes the existence of an independent and impartial judicial body. This presupposes that the independence of judicial bodies and that of judges must be guaranteed by the constitution and laws of the country and created by law to render decisions on matters respected by all; government, institutions and authorities. Moreover, magistrates must settle the cases of which they are seized without restrictions and without being subject to undue influence, inducements, pressures, threats or interventions, direct or indirect, from anyone or for any reason, in order to guarantee their impartiality.

In the present case, the Complainants argue that numerous cases of flagrant human rights violations involving State agents including acts of torture or infringements of life, are not subject to rigorous follow-up by the justice system and in the rare cases that have resulted in an outcome, the sentences or the compensation of the victims are insignificant in view of the harm suffered. They also mentioned the lack of independence of the judicial system from the executive power, which represents a major obstacle to the fight against impunity.

If in its decision World Organisation Against Torture and Africa Zone League for the Defence of the Rights of Children and Pupils (on behalf of Céline) v. Democratic Republic of Congo, the Commission had held that the mere lack of effectiveness of the procedures concerned cannot suffice to establish the lack of independence of the courts which necessarily presupposes elements of external interference, particularly in the absence of evidence supporting this allegation, in the present case, the conclusions of the Estates General of Burundian Justice held from 5 to 9 August 2013 highlighted the need to reform the system to ensure its independence, notably from the executive, a central subject of concern during the discussions.

As regards the generalised impunity in Burundi notably on the issue of extrajudicial executions, the United Nations Commission of Inquiry on Burundi in its 2017 report noted long delays in judicial proceedings, the holding of certain sensitive trials within prison premises, with a deterrent effect on the presence of observers, as well as summary trials under the "flagrante delicto" procedure. It also stressed that the lack of independence of the judicial system observed for a long time in Burundi has aggravated the impunity prevailing in the country. Cases of impunity in Burundi, particularly as regards extrajudicial executions, have been reported by several reports of international NGOs including by the United Nations
On this basis the independence of justice can therefore be questioned. The Commission is therefore of the view that there is a violation of Article 26 of the Charter.

On the basis of the provisions of Article 9(2) of the African Charter which provides that "[e]very individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law". The Complainants submit that freedom of opinion has been defined by the Commission as "a fundamental human right, essential to an individual's personal development and political consciousness" and vital "for his participation in the conduct of the public affairs of his country". Thus, it is established as an inherent foundation of any democratic society. They add that the Commission recalled in this regard that the legitimate exercise of human rights does not pose any problem for a democratic State governed by the rule of law"
They also maintain that the protection of freedom of political opinion through Article 9 of the African Charter has been confirmed by the jurisprudence of the African Commission.

Principle No. 2 on non-interference with freedom of opinion of the General Principles contained in the Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa of 2019 provides that Freedom of opinion, including the right to hold and change any opinion at any time and for any reason, is a fundamental and inalienable human right indispensable for the exercise of freedom of expression. States shall not interfere with anyone's freedom of opinion.

In the Commission's earlier Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression in Africa of 2002, States are expressly requested to ensure that defamation laws do not permit the punishment of persons for accurate statements, opinions or statements regarding public figures which it was reasonable to make in the circumstances and that public figures must tolerate a much greater degree of criticism.

In its General Comment No. 34 on Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights on freedom of opinion and freedom of expression. The Human Rights Committee considered that to criminalise the holding of an opinion is incompatible with paragraph 1 of Article 19. Harassment, intimidation or stigmatisation, including arrest, detention, trial or imprisonment, on account of the opinions that the person may hold constitutes a violation of paragraph 1 of Article 19.
The Comment also indicates that any form of effort to coerce the holding or not holding of any opinion is prohibited.

Consequently the detention of the police officer Jackson Ndikuriyo without charge in December 2009 after he publicly maintained that corruption was rife within the Police, as well as the intimidations and harassment to which he was subjected including his extrajudicial execution, can reasonably be considered as being the consequences of the exercise of his freedom of expression.

Indeed as submitted by the Complainants, the intimidations and other threats against the victim had the sole purpose of silencing Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo. Yet if it is accepted that the right to hold an opinion and to express it is guaranteed by the African Charter, restricting the exercise of this right by any means may reasonably be considered a violation of Article 9(2) of the said Charter.
In conclusion of the analysis of the facts and of the various legal texts relevant to the question, the Commission considers that there has been a violation of Article 9(2).

The Complainants submit that the rights of the family of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo were violated, owing to his extrajudicial execution but also to the acts of torture, acts of intimidation and harassment to which he was subjected.

Article 18(1) of the African Charter enshrines the family as the natural unit and basis of society and consequently it must be protected by the State which takes care of its physical health and moral.

The Commission has clearly stated that the separation of family members constitutes a violation of the right contained in Article 18(1); it has also recalled that the State has a positive obligation with regard to the family, which it must assist in meeting its needs and interests and protect this same institution from abuses of any kind by its own agents and organs and by third parties. In the exercise of its positive obligations, the State exercises a negative obligation which is that of preventing the occurrence of any act aimed at violating the rights thus enshrined.

The Declaration of Basic Principles of Justice for Victims of Crime and Abuse of Power, adopted by the General Assembly in its resolution 40/34 of 29 November 1985, considers as "victims" persons who, individually or collectively, have suffered harm, including physical or mental injury, emotional suffering, economic loss or substantial impairment of their fundamental rights, through acts or omissions that are in violation of criminal laws operative within Member States. These may include the immediate family or dependants of the direct victim.

Beyond the provisions contained in the African Charter it is unanimously accepted that the family constitutes the foundation of society, particularly in Africa where it has a sacred character. Thus, ensuring the protection of the family is preserving the balance of the nation. It is therefore essential to ensure that this protection is done according to the established norms.

In the present case, the family of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo suffered acts of mental torture, inhuman and degrading treatment, intimidations and harassment suffered by the victim which also affected it. Then, it suffered the anguish and emotional distress caused by his death. To this are added the worries for its physical but also economic security with the death of the victim who provided for the needs of the family. Moreover, his children found themselves orphans, deprived of one of their parents. This may constitute a violation of Article 18(3) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, which provides that no child shall be deprived of maintenance by reason of the marital status of the parents. The mother of his children now being a widow, the maintenance and future of the latter is now uncertain with the loss of the one who ensured financial security.

It is now appropriate to analyse whether or not the State failed in its positive obligation towards the family. The positive obligation presupposes compliance with a negative obligation by the State which consists in ensuring that there is no violation of the rights and interests of the family. The physical and moral security of the family implies the protection of economic and social rights for its realisation. The death of the victim broke the unity of the family that the State must protect under the provisions of Article 18(1) of the Charter.

In view of the foregoing there is no doubt that the State was not able to protect the life of the victim causing an irreparable loss for his family but also broke its unity. The Commission therefore finds the effective violation of Article 18(1) by the Respondent State.

Article 1 of the African Charter requires States Parties to the African Charter to recognise the rights guaranteed therein and to adopt legislative and other measures to give effect to these rights, duties and freedoms.

The Commission's jurisprudence has established that any violation of one of the provisions of the African Charter automatically entails the violation of Article 1. In other words, if a State Party fails to ensure respect for the rights contained in the African Charter, this constitutes a violation of the African Charter.

In this regard, and having found that the Respondent State violated several articles of the African Charter, namely Articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) read together with 26, 9(2) and 18(1), the Commission concludes that the Respondent State violated Article 1 of the African Charter.

Furthermore, this responsibility is automatically engaged as soon as it is concluded that a right protected by the Charter has been violated. In view of all the foregoing, the Commission concludes that there has been a violation of the provisions of Article 1. The Commission, For these reasons,
Finds that the Republic of Burundi violated the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) read together with 26, 9(2) and 18(1) of the Charter.

Consequently: i. Requests the Republic of Burundi to conduct a thorough investigation, through independent judicial bodies, into the execution of the victim and the other violations suffered; ii. To put in place mechanisms to combat the generalised impunity regarding extrajudicial execution and infringements of the right to life; iii. Further requests the Republic of Burundi to grant the Victim's beneficiaries adequate and sufficient reparation as well as the necessary medical and psychological assistance, if still applicable; iv. To ensure the full application of Law No. 1/04 of 27 June 2016 on the protection of victims, witnesses and other persons at risk; v. Requests the Republic of Burundi to adopt all necessary measures so that such acts do not recur and to ensure that the law on political parties respects democratic principles and political pluralism; vi. Finally requests the Republic of Burundi to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of notification of the present decision, on the measures undertaken for the implementation of these recommendations. Adopted during the 72nd Ordinary Session in camera of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held virtually from 19 July to 2 August 2022

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat), received a Complaint on 26 October 2018 from Femi Falana (the Complainant), on behalf of 53 Cameroonian refugees and asylum seekers (the Victims) who were deported from Nigeria on 26 January 2018.
The Complaint is submitted against the Republic of Cameroon (the Respondent State), State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).
The Complainant submits that at the request of the Respondent State, authorities in Nigeria illegally and unfairly returned the Victims to the Respondent State.

The Complainant alleges that the "returnees are mostly leaders of the people of Southern Cameroon... who have been living in Nigeria with their families for years." He states that some of them have been granted political asylum while others were asylum seekers in Nigeria.

The Complainant avers that on 7 January 2018, the Victims assembled in Abuja to discuss the problems being encountered by several Cameroonian asylum seekers in Nigeria. He adds that before the meeting started, security personnel from Nigeria arrested the Victims and took them to an underground detention centre in Abuja.

The Complainant submits that while in detention, the Victims were denied access to their family members, lawyers and doctors. The Complainant states that, further to instructions from the Victims, he represented them before the Federal High Court in Abuja, contesting their arrest and detention.

The Complainant avers that while the case was pending before the Court, their lawyers received information of the plan to deport the Victims to Cameroon, and they rushed to the Federal High Court in Abuja to stop the "illegal plan." He adds that they also reached out to the Comptroller-General of Immigration, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Nigeria.

The Complainant alleges that despite a letter from the UNHCR reminding Nigeria of its legal obligation under international law not to deport the Victims, the Respondent State “pressurized” Nigeria to hand over the refugees. He states that Cameroonian security agents forcefully took the Victims on 26 January 2018, and that the Victims are being held in incommunicado detention.

The Complainant avers that Nigeria does not have an extradition agreement with Cameroon, and that the deportation therefore occurred outside the ambit of the extradition laws of Nigeria and Cameroon. He further avers that the Respondent State violated the Victims’ right to enter, reside, seek and obtain asylum in Nigeria, in violation of the African Charter and other legal instruments to which the Respondent State is party.

The Complainant submits that the Victims “are the leaders of the movement agitating for the creation of the republic of Ambazonia from Cameroon”. He further submits that in 2002, they filed a suit at the Federal High Court in Abuja to determine whether the people of Southern Cameroon are entitled to self-determination, which the Court decided to refer to the International Court of Justice.

The Complainant alleges that although the Victims are civilians, they are being tried before a military tribunal. Further, he states that the Government without any investigation, announced that the Victims would be tried for terrorism. The Complainant adds that a Special Military Tribunal has been specifically constituted for the purpose of prosecuting them.

The Complainant alleges that the trial commenced on 10 January 2019, and that their lawyers who are based in Nigeria have been denied access to them as well as the opportunity to defend them. However, in a subsequent submission, the Complainant indicates that he is representing the Victims before the Special Military Tribunal in Cameroon.

In his latest submission, the Complainant avers that only ten (10) of the Victims were charged before a Special Military Tribunal, while the remaining Victims have not been charged with any offence, although they are being held incommunicado since January 2018.

The Complainant submits that in two separate judgments delivered on 1 March 2019, the Federal High Court in Abuja declared that the deportation of the Victims from Nigeria was illegal and unconstitutional, and requested the Nigerian Government to pay them compensation and bring them back to Nigeria. The Complainant concludes that domestic remedies available in Nigeria have been exhausted.

The Complainant submits that being refugees and asylum seekers in Nigeria, the Victims are not required to exhaust domestic remedies in Cameroon. He further states that "the quasi-judicial process in Cameroon is weak, unfair, corrupt, politicised and manipulative," and that the instant case is of a "“come for your assured judgment" which is akin to judgment without justice".
The Complainant alleges violation of Articles 5, 6, 7, 11, and 12 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Commission) to: a. Find a violation of Articles 5, 6, 7, 11, and 12 of the African Charter; b. Undertake an in-depth study, based on the "series of serious" and "massive" violations"; c. Urgently hold an extra-ordinary session to address the illegal and unfair return of the Victims, and the continuing violations of their rights; d. Conduct an official visit to the Respondent State with the relevant rapporteurs and put pressure on the authorities to immediately release the Victims from unlawful detention and end the "politically motivated trial" of naturalised Nigerians, refugees and asylum seekers; e. Find that the continued detention, mistreatment and unfair trial of the Victims by the Respondent State amounts to cruel and degrading treatment; f. Pursuant to Rules 84 (2) and 118 (3) & (4) of the Rules of Procedure, refer the matter to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Court); g. Adopt Provisional Measures to:• immediately stop the "mistrial" of the Victims before a military tribunal and return them to Nigeria to re-join their families, pending a decision on the Communication; and • Provide assurances and guarantees about the safety of the Victims.

The Secretariat received the Complaint on 26 October 2018. Between 16 November 2018 and 22 July 2019, multiple correspondences were exchanged between the Secretariat and the Complainant, for requisite clarifications and addition information, in accordance with the applicable Rules of Procedure of the Commission.

During its 65 Ordinary Session, the Commission examined the Complaint and decided to be seized thereof and to grant the requested Provisional Measures, but declined the request for referral of the Complaint to the African Court.

On 11 November 2019, the parties were notified of the Commission's decision, with a request to the Complainant to file written arguments and evidence on the Admissibility of the Communication within two months of notification in terms of Rule 105(1) of the 2010 Rules of Procedure. The Provisional Measures issued by the Commission were also sent to the State and the Complainant respectively on 11 November 2019 and 22 November 2019.

Between the 27 Extra-Ordinary Session and its 72 Ordinary Session, the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication, during which period the Secretariat informed the parties by correspondence of 8 May 2021, that the Commission was yet to make a determination on the Communication, but that the deadline for submission on the Admissibility of this Communication expired on 11 January 2020.

Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2010) establishes that when the Commission has decided to be seized of a Communication, it shall request the Complainant to present arguments on Admissibility within two (2) months.

Rule 113 provides that when a deadline is fixed for a submission, either party may apply to the Commission for extension of the period stipulated. The Commission may grant an extension of time for a period not longer than one (1) month.
To date, and more than two (2) years after the stipulated deadline, the Complainant has not (i) made any submissions on Admissibility and (ii) has not requested for an extension of time to submit.

The Commission considers that the Complainant's failure to submit observations on Admissibility within the prescribed timeline or at all, or indeed to seek an extension of the time as provided by the Rules of Procedure, amounts to want of diligent prosecution of this Communication. Consequently, in line with its jurisprudence, the Commission finds that the Complainant has shown no interest in prosecuting this Communication.

In view of the above, the Commission decides to strike out the Communication for lack of diligent prosecution. Done in Banjul, The Gambia, during the 73 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, 20 October to 09 November 2022

Como resultado do tratamento infligido, o queixoso alega ter sofrido inúmeros golpes e outras lesões. Acrescenta que lhe taparam a boca para abafar os seus gritos de dor e pedidos de socorro.

O queixoso afirma ainda que mostrou ao Ministério Público os seus ferimentos na cabeça, braços e pulsos. Estas circunstâncias também foram comunicadas à Administração Interna que foi à prisão para o interrogar sem notificação prévia à equipa de defesa do queixoso. As autoridades declararam que os ferimentos sofridos por ele eram lesões auto-infligidas e não foi iniciada nenhuma investigação.

O queixoso salienta que, até agora, a sua equipa de defesa não conseguiu obter cópias de quaisquer testes e relatórios médicos realizados pelas autoridades cabo-verdianas desde que foi detido na Ilha do Sal, em Cabo Verde.

O queixoso afirma que durante a sua prisão, houve uma grande preocupação de que a combinação de estresse extremo, a proibição de contacto com outros prisioneiros, o confinamento numa cela de 2x2 metros, a falta de electricidade durante 23 horas por dia, a falta de saneamento, a falta de acesso a medicamentos e uma dieta pobre e inadequada podem causar problemas de estômago, tendo em conta que tem cancro do estômago que estava em remissão.

O queixoso afirma ainda que apesar da decisão do Tribunal de Justiça da CEDEAO datada de 2 de Dezembro de 2020, que solicita ao Estado Requerido que cumpra medidas provisórias, incluindo a substituição da medida coerciva da vítima à prisão domiciliária e lhe permita o tratamento médico necessário às suas próprias custas, foi negado ao Professor de Medicina, Dr. Sikora o acesso ao seu paciente, ao chegar à prisão a 20 de Dezembro de 2020 e apesar de ter a acreditação oficial.

O queixoso declara ainda que todos os pedidos feitos por ele relativamente ao acesso a tratamento médico adequado e a um médico qualificado independente especializado em oncologia foram ignorados pelas autoridades de Cabo Verde.
O queixoso afirma que a 25 de Janeiro de 2021, foi finalmente transferido da cadeia para a prisão domiciliária. No entanto, as visitas continuam a ser proibidas ou excessivamente controladas.

O queixoso declara que a 15 de Março de 2021, o Tribunal de Justiça da CEDEAO, pelo seu Acórdão, ordenou Cabo Verde que libertasse o queixoso com efeito imediato; que interrompesse a execução de todos os procedimentos e processos de extradição do queixoso para os Estados Unidos da América; e que indemnizasse o queixoso pelos danos morais sofridos como resultado da sua detenção ilegal.

O queixoso afirma ainda que a decisão continua sem qualquer aplicação a nível interno de Cabo Verde. Ele afirma que, pelo contrário, as autoridades judiciais, administrativas e executivas de Cabo Verde afirmam que Cabo Verde não é obrigado a aplicar as decisões do Tribunal de Justiça da CEDEAO e a respeitar o direito internacional dos direitos humanos.

O queixoso assevera que a 16 de Março de 2021, apesar do Acórdão vinculativo do Tribunal da CEDEAO, foi adoptado um despacho pelo Supremo Tribunal de Justiça de Cabo Verde autorizando a sua extradição para os Estados Unidos da América.

Por último, o queixoso alega que foi interposto um recurso extraordinário perante o Tribunal Constitucional a 26 de Maio de 2021 mas que este já ultrapassou-os prazos em que era obrigado a responder. Contudo, a extradição está iminente e pode ocorrer a qualquer momento a partir de agora. No entanto, o Estado Requerido recusou-se a divulgar qualquer informação relativa à data da extradição alegadamente por razões de segurança.

O Queixoso viria a ser extraditado e entregue às autoridades dos EUA em 16 de Outubro de 2021, não obstante a decisão do Tribunal de Justiça da Comunidade Económica dos Estados da África Ocidental e as Medidas Provisórias de suspensão da sua extradição solicitadas pela Comissão.
Os Queixosos alegam a violação dos artigos 4.º, 5.º, 6.º, 7.º, 12.º, 16.º e 18.º da Carta Africana dos Direitos do Homem e dos Povos (Carta Africana).

Os Queixosos pedem à Comissão que: a) Declare a violação da Carta Africana e, especialmente, dos artigos 4.º, 5.º, 6.º, 7.º, 12.º, 16.º e 18.º; b) Garanta o reconhecimento, pelo Estado Requerido, da sua responsabilidade internacional; c) Assegure a apresentação, pelo Estado Requerido, de um pedido de desculpas público pelo grave sofrimento infligido ao Queixoso; d) Assegure a publicação, pelo Estado Requerido, a nível interno, da decisão da Comissão sobre o mérito; e) Obtenha garantias, por parte do Estado Requerido, da não repetição, e especialmente, em termos de respeito aos direitos consulares e ao estatuto diplomático dos agentes internacionais; f) Assegure o reembolso, pelo Estado Requerido, das despesas legais da sua prisão domiciliária e representação legal perante os tribunais de Cabo Verde; g) Assegure o pagamento integral, pelo Estado Requerido, da indemnização de 200.000 dólares devidas nos termos do acórdão do Tribunal de Justiça da CEDEAO de 15 de Março de 2021.

A Queixa foi submetida ao Secretariado em 11 de Agosto de 2021. Em 12 de Outubro de 2021, a Comissão aceitou a Queixa e, por ofício de 12 de Novembro de 2021, solicitou o Queixoso a submeter suas alegações escritas sobre a Admissibilidade e o Mérito da Comunicação no prazo de sessenta (60) dias.

Por Nota Verbal da mesma data, dirigida ao Presidente da República de Cabo Verde, a Comissão solicitou ao Estado Requerido medidas provisórias visando a suspensão imediatamente da extradição do Queixoso para os Estados Unidos da América e a tomada de medidas necessárias para assegurar ao mesmo o acesso a cuidados de saúde adequados e eficazes.

Em 10 de Março de 2022, em resposta ao pedido de informações submetido pelo Queixoso sobre a situação de medidas cautelares solicitadas pela Comissão ao Estado Requerido, o Secretariado informou o Queixoso que não tinha recebido nenhum relatório do Estado Requerido sobre a execução da medidas provisórias solicitadas.

Na correspondência referida supra, o Secretariado lembrou ao Queixoso que lhe tinha sido concedido sessenta (60) dias para submeter as suas alegações escritas sobre a admissibilidade e o mérito da Comunicação e lhe instou a informar a Comissão se quer submeter alegações escritas adicionais ou se quer manter as alegações iniciais feitas na Queixa.

Até a presente data, o Queixoso não submeteu as alegações escritas sobre a Admissibilidade e o Mérito da Comunicação, nem respondeu ao pedido de esclarecimento da Comissão sobre se quer submeter as alegações escritas adicionais ou se vai manter as alegações.

A Comissão nota que o artigo 116(1) do Regulamento de 2020 prevê que quando a Comissão declarar aceite uma Queixa, ela solicita ao queixoso que apresente observações e provas sobre a admissibilidade e o mérito da Comunicação no prazo de sessenta (60) dias. Nos termos do artigo 98.º do mesmo Regulamento, a Comissão pode prorrogar este prazo, a pedido de qualquer das partes na Comunicação.

Na presente Comunicação, o Queixoso não apresentou as alegações escritas sobre a admissibilidade e mérito no prazo estipulado, nem solicitou a sua prorrogação, não obstante ter sido alertado pelo Secretariado nesse sentido através da correspondência de 10 de Março de 2022 (ver o parágrafo 30 da presente decisão).

A Comissão nota que, apesar das diligências do Secretariado, o representante do Queixoso não se dignou colaborar na conclusão do procedimento visando viabilizar uma decisão sobre a admissibilidade e seguimento do procedimento para a fase seguinte, sobretudo depois da extradição do Queixoso para os Estados Unidos da América a 16 de Outubro de 2021.
Pelo exposto, a Comissão considera que não existem motivos para manter a Queixa no seu rol.

A Comissão recorda que já havia pronunciado no mesmo sentido nas Comunicações 594/15 – Mohammed Ramadan Mahmoud Fayad Allah v República Árabe do Egito; 612/16 – Ahmed Mohammed Ali Subaie v República Árabe do Egito; 412/12 – Journal Echos du Nord v República do Gabão e Comunicação 387/10- Kofi Yamagnane v Togo.

À luz do que precede, a Comissão ordena a exclusão da Queixa do seu rol. Adoptada durante a Septagésima Terceira Sessão Ordinária da Comissão, que decorreu em Banjul, Gâmbia, de 21 de Outubro a 9 de Novembro de 2022.

Le 13 février 2018, le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu une Plainte introduite par Monsieur Jean Ping (ci-après dénommer « la Victime ») représenté par Maître William Woll, avocat au barreau de Paris, France (ci-après dénommer « le Plaignant »).
La plainte est soumise contre la République du Gabon, Etat partie à la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (La Charte Africaine) qu'elle a ratifié le 20 février 1986.

Le Plaignant conteste la réélection de Monsieur Ali Bongo au poste de Président de la République du Gabon lors de l'élection présidentielle du 27 août 2016 et dont les résultats ont été proclamés par le Ministère de l'Intérieur, le 31 août 2016 au soir.

Le Plaignant indique que, le 27 août 2016 se sont tenues les élections présidentielles sur tout le territoire gabonais. Il s'agissait d'un scrutin majoritaire à un tour. Ces élections ont vu s'affronter dix candidats dont le Plaignant et le Président de la République sortant, Mr. Ali Bongo Ondimba.

Le 30 août 2016, huit Provinces sur les neuf que compte le Gabon, ainsi que les représentations diplomatiques gabonaises, ont publié leurs résultats, donnant 169599 voix à Mr. Ping et 108659 voix à Mr. Bongo (la différence des voix était de 60940 voix et en faveur de Mr. Ping). Cependant, les résultats de la province du Haut-Ogooué, dont Mr. Bongo est originaire, n'ont pas été publiés. Cette province compte 71.714 inscrits et, selon les copies de 182 sur 297 des procès-verbaux, Mr. Ping aurait obtenu 4.144 voix et Mr. Bongo 27.409. Les 115 autres procès-verbaux n'ont pas été produits.

Le Plaignant rapporte que le 31 août 2017, le Ministre de l'intérieur a proclamé la réélection de Mr. Bongo, et les résultats donnés concernant la Province du Haut-Ogooué se présentaient comme suit : Inscrits : 71.714 ; Votants : 71.667, Abstentions : 47, Bulletins blancs ou nuls : 367, Suffrages exprimés : 71.300, Ali bongo : 68.064 voix et Jean Ping : 3.071 voix. Ces résultats contredisaient le décompte effectué par Mr. Ping à partir des 182 procès-verbaux dont il dispose concernant cette Province.

De plus, les procès-verbaux de la ville de Moanda faisant partie de la Province du Haut-Ogooué enregistrent, par exemple, 392 bulletins blancs et nuls et 5.225 abstentions, très loin des chiffres annoncés par le ministre pour toute la province. Malgré les demandes de la France, les Etats Unies et l'Union Européenne de publier les résultats par bureaux de vote, cela n'a jamais été fait.

Aux dires du Plaignant, après l'annonce des résultats, des manifestants étaient descendus dans la rue le 31 août, et l'Assemblée nationale avait été incendiée. La Garde Républicaine avait dispersé les manifestants avec des tirs à balles réelles et au moins 1.000 personnes avaient été arrêtées, dont des partisans de Jean Ping, mais aussi des pilleurs et des simples citoyens.

Selon le Plaignant, dans la nuit du 31 août au 1 septembre 2016, le quartier général de la Victime avait été pris d'assaut à l'arme lourde à 1h00 du matin par les forces de sécurité, la garde présidentielle, la police et des mercenaires. On avait dénombré au moins 27 morts et des dizaines de disparus. Durant l'assaut, des ambulances avaient été disposées à proximité et s'emparaient des corps des victimes afin de les évacuer et au petit matin, il n'en subsistait aucune sur place.

Le Plaignant affirme que le 2 septembre 2016, environ un millier de personnes avaient été arrêtés et parmi elles le député démissionnaire Mr. Bertrand Zibi, fervent soutien de Mr. Ping et Mr. Landry Washington Amiang, proche de Mr. Ping de nationalité américaine et résidant aux Etats Unis, arrêté à son arrivée à Libreville. A ce jour ces deux personnes sont toujours détenues.

Le Plaignant rapporte également la coupure totale des connexions internes entre le 1 et le 5 septembre 2016 avant d'être partiellement rétablie et l'accès aux réseaux sociaux interdit pendant plusieurs semaines.

Le Plaignant rapporte également que Mr. Abel Mbonne Nzondou avait saisi la Cour Constitutionnelle d'une requête en réformation, dans laquelle il contestait les résultats du 3 arrondissement de Libreville, en expliquant que la présidente de la Commission électorale locale de ce bureau de vote avait disparu toute une nuit durant, avant de réapparaître « sous la protection de l'armée ». Monsieur Mbonne s'est désisté plus tard (le 18 septembre).

Le Plaignant affirme que la Victime avait déposé une requête en réformation de l'élection présidentielle auprès de la Cour Constitutionnelle gabonaise, seul organe de recours compétent en la matière, en date du 8 septembre 2016. Mr. Gérard Ella Nguema Mintoghe quant à lui avait introduit une requête en réformation en demandant que deux des membres de la Cour, proches de MM. Ping et Bongo se récusent, à savoir Mme Mborantsuo, présidente de la Cour et mère de deux demi-frères de Mr. Bongo et Mme Afriquita Dolorès Agondjo, nièce de Mr. Ping.

Le Plaignant affirme également que le 23 septembre 2016, la Cour Constitutionnelle avait rendu deux décisions (050/CC et 052/CC), dans lesquelles elle rejetait la demande de récusation formée par Monsieur Mintoghe (050/CC). conformément à sa jurisprudence bien établie sur cette question, ainsi que la demande de recomptage des voix, formulée par MM. Ping et Mintoghe. Dans sa décision 052/CC, la Cour Constitutionnelle a confirmé la réélection de Monsieur Bongo avec 172.990, 50,66 de voix contre 161.287 pour Mr. Ping.

Le Plaignant indique que le 03 novembre 2016, Mr. Ping avait introduit une requête en révision des décisions numéro 050/CC et numéro 052/CC précitées auprès de la Cour Constitutionnelle. Il avait notamment invoqué la possibilité offerte par l'article 87 de la loi organique sur la Cour Constitutionnelle qui autorise la révision dans les cas suivants : s'il y a eu fraude des parties de nature à avoir déterminé la conviction de la Cour ; s'il y a eu faux témoignage reconnu par décision de justice ; si la décision considérée a été rendue sur des pièces fausses ; et si, depuis la décision, il a été recouvré des pièces décisives détenues par l'adversaire. Le 15 novembre 2016, par décision numéro 060/CC, la Cour Constitutionnelle avait rejeté ce dernier recours. De ce fait ; le rejet de la seconde requête de la Victime, marque l'épuisement des voies de recours internes.

Le Plaignant rapporte que le 20 septembre 2016, Mr. Bongo avait adressé à la Cour Pénale Internationale (CPI) une requête dans laquelle il accusait Mr. Ping de « crimes contre l'humanité » et d'inciter la population à commettre un « crime de génocide ». Cette affaire n'a pas été réglée car la Cour Pénale Internationale n'a pas pour mission de régler un conflit post-électoral.

Le Plaignant rapporte également que le 4 novembre 2016, dans la résolution CADHP/Res.359 (LIX) 2016, la Commission Africaine avait dénoncé les violations des droits de l'homme perpétrées au Gabon. Il indique aussi que dans le pré-rapport établi par la Mission d'observation de la gestion du contentieux électoral sous l'égide de l'Union africaine dont les auteurs sont deux membres des Cours constitutionnelles togolaise et tchadienne, il avait été écrit qu' : « au total les procès-verbaux de la province du Haut Ogooué sont si bien rédigés, ordonnés et par ailleurs, la coïncidence entre le nombre d'inscrits, celui des suffrages exprimés et l'attribution quasi-totale de ceux-ci à un seul candidat qu'ils paraissent invraisemblables ». Ils avaient ajouté que « les procès-verbaux que nous avons examinés exclusivement laissent apparaître une constante avance du candidat Jean Ping sur le candidat Ali Bongo Ondimba ».

Le Plaignant ajoute également que, dans son rapport présenté au Conseil de Sécurité le 28 novembre 2017, le Secrétaire général des Nations Unies avait consacré plusieurs paragraphes à la situation post-électorale gabonaise et confirmé l'attaque du Quartier général de la Victime par les forces de sécurité le 1er septembre 2016, l'arrestation et la détention de certains membres de l'opposition et de militants de la société civile, la restriction de la liberté d'expression à travers la suspension des services internet, l'envoi des SMS et l'accès aux réseaux sociaux, les morts, un nombre indéterminé des blessés et de plus de 900 arrestations.

Le Plaignant rapporte que de nombreuses anomalies lors du scrutin mais aussi dans la proclamation des résultats le 12 décembre 2016, ont été relevées par le rapport la mission d'observation électorale de l'Union européenne présente au Gabon, notamment «le fait que les nombres de non-votants et de bulletins blancs et nuls soient plus élevés dans une seule Commission Electorale Locale (Monnda) que les totaux de deux catégories de résultats sur l'ensemble de la province ce qui signale des anomalies pendant la phase de consolidation des résultats». La mission avait aussi dénoncé le flou des règles de la procédure à suivre par la Cour Constitutionnelle qui ouvraient la place à l'arbitraire et conduisaient à l'absence de tout recours utile pour les candidats malheureux.

Le 2 février 2017, le parlement européen avait adopté une résolution dans laquelle il relevait que «les résultats officiels de l'élection présidentielle manquent de transparence et sont extrêmement douteux, ce qui a pour effet de remettre en cause la légitimité du président Bongo» et avait par ailleurs déploré que «le refus de la Cour Constitutionnelle de procéder au recomptage des voix et de comparer les dépouillements avant la destruction des bulletins».

Le Plaignant affirme que le 27 mars 2017, le pouvoir gabonais a suspendu administrativement la Convention nationale des syndicats du système éducatif (CONASYED) qui soutenait Mr. Ping, motif pris de troubles manifeste à l'ordre public, d'entrave à la liberté de travail, de violences et de voies de fait.

Le Plaignant rapporte que plusieurs proches de Mr. Ping ont été arrêtés au cours de l'année 2017. Il s'agit notamment de Mr. Alain Djally, lieutenant de l'armée de l'air gabonaise, de l'activiste Hervé Mombo Kinga, du ministre Frédéric Massavala, porte-parole de la coalition et de Mr. Pascal Oyougou, membre du cabinet de Mr. Ping. Excepté Mr Dally, tous les autres sont toujours détenus. D'autres arrestations ont été faites suite à une marche organisée par les partisans de Mr. Ping. Par ailleurs les arrestations sont devenues systématiques depuis des mois, ainsi que les enlèvements.

Le Plaignant affirme que ses partisans ont été empêchés d'aller l'accueillir à l'aéroport alors qu'il revenait d'une tournée diplomatique en France et dans d'autres pays européens, et qu'ils avaient été réprimés à coup de gaz lacrymogène et de violence. Par ailleurs, les 2 et 8 septembre 2017, il été refusé à Mr. Ping de quitter le territoire sans aucune motivation légale.

Aux dires du Plaignant, le 14 septembre 2017, le Parlement européen avait adopté une seconde résolution dans laquelle il condamnait «fermement les menaces permanentes, les agressions, le recours à la force ainsi que les restrictions sévères et les intimidations à l'encontre des opposants, des défenseurs des droits de l'homme et des journalistes au Gabon.» Il demandait également aux autorités gabonaises «de respecter le droit de l'opposition à manifester pacifiquement, de libérer immédiatement toutes les personnes encore détenues illégalement, de mettre un terme à tous les actes de harcèlement, d'intimidation et de persécution contre les opposants, et de prendre des mesures concrètes pour garantir la liberté d'expression».

Le Plaignant rapporte que dans le cadre du démarrage du dialogue politique Intensifié en septembre 2017, les travaux entre les officiels gabonais et l'Union européenne avaient essentiellement été consacrés aux réformes électorales (3 octobre) ; au rôle de la Cour Constitutionnelle dans le processus électoral (6 octobre) et aux droits de l'homme, sujet central du partenariat entre le Gabon et l'Union européenne (18 octobre). A cet effet, l'Union européenne avait réitéré son appel et son appui à l'organisation d'une enquête indépendante sur les violences post-électorales.

Le Plaignant soumet que le 12 janvier 2018, ayant annoncé son départ pour la France, en vue de rencontrer son avocat, Mr. Ping a reçu une convocation pour audition émanant de Mme. Marie-Christine Lebama, juge d'instruction et épouse de Mr. Jacques Lebama, membre de la Cour constitutionnelle. Ladite convocation était assortie d'une interdiction de quitter le territoire gabonais.
Le Plaignant affirme que cette affaire n'a pas été soumise à un autre organe international de règlement des litiges ou de compétence similaire.
Le Plaignant, allègue la violation des dispositions des articles 7 et 13 de la Charte africaine.

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission d'adopter les mesures conservatoires en ordonnant l'état du Gabon : a. d'organiser de nouvelles élections présidentielles partielles dans la seule province de Haut-Ogoué ; b. de suspendre les fonctions de président d'Ali Bongo dans l'attente des résultats de ces élections partielles ; c. de confier, par intérim, le pouvoir présidentiel à l'actuelle président du Sénat, Madame Lucie Milebou-Aubusson, conformément à l'article 13 de la Constitution gabonaise ; d. de respecter la liberté d'expression politique de Monsieur Ping ainsi que sa liberté de circulation incluant celle de quitter le territoire du Gabon et d'y revenir ; e. de libérer les proches soutiens de Monsieur Ping qui sont emprisonnés uniquement en raison de leurs opinions politiques : Messieurs Zibi, Amiang, Mombo Kinga, Massavala, et Oyougou.
La Plainte est parvenue au Secrétariat de la Commission le 13 février 2018. Le Secrétariat en a accusé réception le 22 mars 2018.

Lors de sa 62 Session ordinaire du 24 avril au 9 mai 2018, la Commission africaine a examiné la Communication et décidé de l'admettre. La commission a également octroyé des mesures conservatoires en conformité avec l'article 98 de son Règlement intérieur.

Le 23 mai 2018, le Secrétariat de la Commission a informé le Plaignant et l'Etat défendeur sur la décision de l'admission et les mesures conservatoires, notamment la demande formulée à l'endroit de l'Etat Gabonais de garantir la liberté d'expression politique de Monsieur Ping ainsi que sa liberté de circulation dans l'attente de la décision de la Commission sur la Communication. Pour les autres demandes de mesures provisoires, la Commission ayant estimé qu'elles relèvent du fond de l'affaire et ne peuvent de ce fait, faire objet de mesures provisoires.

Par la même note verbale, le Secrétariat a invité le Plaignant à présenter ses preuves et ses arguments sur la recevabilité dans le délai de 2 mois suivant la notification, conformément à l'article 105 (1) de son règlement intérieur.
Le 23 juillet 2018, le Secrétariat de la Commission a reçu les arguments du Plaignant sur la recevabilité.
Le 29 octobre 2018, le Plaignant a requis que soit appliqué l'article 58 de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples

Le 1 février 2019, le Secrétariat a transmis à l'Etat du Gabon le mémoire du plaignant sur la recevabilité en l'invitant à transmettre ses conclusions dans le délai de deux mois à compter de la réception de la notification, conformément à l'article 105 (2) du règlement intérieur de la Commission.

Par la même note verbale, le Secrétariat a prié l'Etat Gabonais de bien vouloir l'informer des dispositions prises en vue de la mise en œuvre des mesures conservatoires qu'elle avait requises dans la même Communication.
Le 21 mars 2019, le Secrétariat de la Commission a reçu de l'Etat défendeur son mémoire en défense qui a été transmis au Plaignant le même jour.
Le 4 mai 2019, le Secrétariat de la Commission a reçu du Plaignant des observations additionnelles sur le mémoire en défense de l'Etat défendeur sur la recevabilité.

Le plaignant soutient que la quasi-totalité des conditions de recevabilité telles que requises par l'article 56 de la Charte sont manifestement réunies sans même qu'il soit nécessaire d'argumenter longuement. Selon lui, seule la condition relative au « délai raisonnable » de saisine depuis l'épuisement des voies de recours internes nécessite d'être élucidée.

Le Plaignant soutient que la condition de l'identité de l'auteur est manifestement remplie car, selon lui, l'identité de l'auteur est bien connue. Il indique qu'il s'agit de Jean Ping (la Victime) représenté par Maître Woll (le Plaignant). Il ajoute qu'il est né le 19 novembre 1942 à OMBOUE (Gabon). Le plaignant souligne également que l'auteur est ancien diplomate, ancien président de la Commission de l'Union Africaine.

Le Plaignant soutient que la Communication est compatible avec la Charte car non seulement elle est dirigée contre un Etat (Gabon) qui a ratifié la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples, mais également elle concerne des violations perpétrées alors que l'Etat gabonais était déjà liée par la Charte. Il souligne, enfin, que la Communication dénonce la violation des articles 7 et 13 de la Charte.

Le plaignant soutient que sa plainte ne contient aucun terme outrageant ou insultant. Il réitère surtout que l'auteur et lui ont pris le soin extrême de ne pas utiliser le moindre terme qui pourrait être outrageant ou insultant à l'égard du Gabon, de ses institutions ou celles de l'Union Africaine.

Le Plaignant soutient que seules 17 pièces sur les 77 que contient le dossier font état d'informations reléguées par la presse nationale et internationale, et que par conséquent, il devient clair que les informations fournies ne sont pas exclusivement issues des moyens de communications de masse.

La Plaignant soutient qu'il a épuisé toutes les voies de recours internes. Il indique que le contentieux en question concerne les résultats des élections proclamées par le Ministère de l'intérieur et que le seul organe de recours compétent en la matière est la Cour constitutionnelle du Gabon. En particulier, il affirme avoir introduit le recours en réformation de ces résultats auprès de cette Cour et que cette dernière a pris deux décisions : l'une rejetant tous les arguments soulevés par le plaignant et l'autre proclamant Ali Bongo Ondimba comme Président élu. Il réitère avoir formulé un nouveau recours contre ces deux décisions, un « recours en révision » mais que la Cour Constitutionnelle a rejeté de nouveau ce recours. Il conclut que par conséquent, il n'existe plus aucun autre recours disponible en droit interne gabonais. Affaire non réglée conformément aux principes de la Charte des Nations Unies, de la Charte de l'Organisation de l'Unité Africaine ou des dispositions de la Charte
