Limited resources at the disposal of the State, which has affected progress in the implementation of human rights related programs; iii. Slow pace of institutional reforms to match the constitutional standards and the obligations under the African Charter, which affects the pace of enjoyment and enforcement of human rights in Malawi; and iv. Despite progress in the general awareness of rights in Malawi, there is still lack of public awareness of the human rights among citizens as guaranteed under the African Charter, resulting in a lack of empowered citizens and consequent weak demand for the fulfilment of human rights by the Government.

While recognising the significant efforts made by the Government to promote and protect human rights in accordance with the provisions of the African Charter, the Commission is however concerned about the following:

While the Commission appreciates Malawi’s response to its recommendations in Malawi’s initial and combined Report of 2015, it however notes that, the current Report does not provide specific and comprehensive answers to some of the questions and issues raised by the Commission. In this regard the Report does not for instance, provide comprehensive disaggregated data, including gender disaggregated data on its implementation of the rights guaranteed in the African Charter in order to allow the Commission to objectively assess Malawi’s level of compliance vis-à-vis the obligations contained in the African Charter.
In addition, the Report does not also follow the Commission’s State Reporting Guidelines under Article 62 of the African Charter.

Malawi has not yet ratified some key regional human rights treaties which are critical for enhancing the enjoyment of human rights, including: i. Protocol to the OAU Convention on Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; ii. Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights; iii. Protocol to the OAU Convention on the Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; iv. Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons in Africa; and v. Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa.

Malawi has not yet ratified some key international human rights treaties, including: i. International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families; ii. Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), aiming at the Abolition of the Death Penalty; iii. The Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture; iv. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; v. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; vi. Optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; vii. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure; and viii. Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT).

In addition to the above, Malawi is yet to domesticate some relevant regional and international human rights treaties that it has ratified, notably, the African Charter and the International Convention for the Protection of all Persons from Enforced Disappearance, due to its dual system for domestication of international law under its legal architecture.

The Commission is generally concerned about the lack of information in the Report regarding adequate awareness of the population about their rights, legal procedures and available remedies in respect of their civil and political rights.

The Commission is concerned that: i. Malawi has neither signed nor ratified the OPCAT and there are no indications on the steps taken to ratify the same; ii. Malawi has not expressly criminalized torture under its Penal Code and has not domesticated the UN Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading treatment or Punishment (CAT); iii. The Report does not contain information on measures the Government is putting in place to raise awareness amongst members of the judiciary on their obligation to open inquiries into allegations of torture or ill-treatment particularly when they are raised during trial; and iv. The Report is silent on the remedies that are available for suspects who have been convicted despite alleging that their confessions were obtained through torture.

The Commission is also concerned about: i. The lack of information on legislative and other measures that are in place to ensure adequate redress for victims of torture including compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition; and ii. The lack of definitive data in the Report on the number of victims of torture including on persons with albinism, and measures adopted to ensure adequate redress for victims of torture including compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition.

The Commission is concerned that: i. Malawi has observed a moratorium on the death penalty since 1994.In this regard, while noting the positive steps taken, there remains concerns as to prison conditions for death row detainees, and deaths of persons in prison custody; and ii. Lack of data on the re-sentencing hearings for individuals who had previously received the automatic death sentences in light of the 2007 Malawi High Court Kafantayeni decision, which prevents the Commission from making an objective assessment of the process.

The Commission is concerned about the: i. Conditions of the current prison facilities, as they continue to house inmates of all categories; ii. Lack of data in the report on rehabilitation, recreation and education programs and facilities available to prisoners; iii. Lack of information regarding the number or quality of meals for inmates; as well as information regarding sanitary facilities and the availability of antiretroviral drugs for inmates with HIV-AIDS; iv. Lack of statistics on deaths in prisons and places of detention; v. Lack of information on the continuous training of law enforcement officials in matters relating to the protection of human rights; and vi. Lack of information regarding the number of female Officers recruited in the Police and in the Penitentiary/Correctional Services.
The Commission is concerned that Malawi has not adopted a Refugee Policy and that the National Migration Policy which incorporates aspects of refugees, is still pending approval by Cabinet.

While the Commission appreciates the post Cyclone Idai Emergency Recovery and Resilience Project, the Commission is concerned that this project only targets five (5) out of fifteen (15) districts and two (2) cities affected, resulting to unequal distribution of resources and remedies to the victims in other affected areas.
The Commission is concerned with the fact that the draft Bill for older Persons has not been enacted into law, while the 2012 Disability Act is still under review.
The Commission is also concerned with the lack of disaggregated statistical data for older persons in the Report.

Malawi has still not conducted the Study recommended by the Commission in the Concluding Observations of the State Report of 2015, aimed at establishing the existence of Indigenous Populations in the country.

The Commission is concerned that the Delegation did not respond to the Commission’s inquiries about the Kayelekera uranium mine which was temporarily closed in 2014 and remains so for the foreseeable future. Information about legislative measures taken by the State to ensure the smooth transition of affected communities from economic dependence on the operations of the Kayelekera mine remains pending.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission makes the following recommendations to Malawi:

Malawi should: i. Continue the regular submission of Periodic Reports on the implementation of the African Charter in compliance with Article 62 of the African Charter; ii. Provide, in its next Periodic Report, up-to-date statistics and data on all relevant sectors as well as on activities of institutions with a human rights mandate; and iii. Inform the Commission, in its next Periodic Report, of the measures taken to address the issues of concern and to ensure the effective implementation of the recommendations contained in these Concluding Observations relating to the African Charter.

Efforts should be made by Malawi to ratify the following Instruments: i. The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Older Persons in Africa; ii. The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa; iii. Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aiming at the abolition of the Death Penalty; iv. Protocol to the OAU Convention on Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; v. Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights; vi. International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families; vii. The Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture; viii. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; ix. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; x. Optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and xi. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure.

Malawi should include in its next report, information regarding adequate awareness of the population about their rights, legal procedures and available remedies in respect of their civil and political rights.

Malawi should in its next review period: i. Enact laws to define and expressly criminalize torture in accordance with the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and the Commission’s Robben Island Guidelines; ii. Initiate programs for training law enforcement agents on the Robben Island Guidelines; iii. Ensure that victims of torture and other ill-treatment, including persons with Albinism have the right to all forms of redress including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition in accordance with General Comment No. 4 on the African Charter on Human and People Rights; and iv. Adequately resource the IPCC to enable it discharge its mandate effectively.

Malawi should: i. Improve prison conditions to house more inmates; ii. Create programs and respective spaces for the rehabilitation, education and recreation of prisoners; iii. Provide information on existing sanitary facilities in prisons, as well as information on the distribution of antiretroviral drugs to inmates with HIV-AIDS; iv. Take necessary measures to record and publicize deaths that occur in prisons and places of detention; v. Include matters relating to the protection of human rights in training of law enforcement officials; and vi. Provide Lack information on the number of female Officers recruited in the Police and in the Penitentiary/Correctional Services.

Malawi should: i. Adopt an official moratorium on the death penalty as a positive step towards the definitive abolition of the death penalty; and ii. Provide in its next report, measures taken by State to investigate cases of deaths in prison custody and ensure the trial and punishment of perpetrators where investigation reports suggest unnatural deaths.
Malawi should adopt a Refugee Policy and the Government should ensure that the National Migration Policy is approved by Cabinet.

Malawi should extend opportunities and benefits provided by the post Cyclone Idai Emergency Recovery and Resilience Project to all districts in the region, and ensure that redress to victims of the cyclone is all-inclusive.

Malawi should: i. Enact the draft Bill for older Persons, as well as the 2012 Disability Act which is still under review into law; and ii. Include disaggregated statistical data for older persons in its next periodic Report.

Malawi should provide information in its next periodic Report on the legislative and other measures taken by the State to compensate communities affected by the closure of the Kayelekera uranium mine.

Malawi should undertake the Study referred to in Paragraph 43 of the Initial and Combined Report under reference to ascertain the existence of indigenous populations and communities in the country as recommended by the Commission.
Regarding the implementation of the Maputo Protocol, the Commission notes the following positive aspects:
The Commission notes that there are many positive aspects regarding Malawi’s compliance with its obligations under the Maputo Protocol which it ratified on 20 May 2005.

The Commission commends Malawi for submitting its second Periodic Report in accordance with Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol which is well- articulated and in line with the Guidelines for State Reporting under the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission commends Malawi for the following Laws: i. The Prevention of Domestic Violence Act; ii. The Marriage Divorce and Family Relations Act; iii. The Gender Equality Act and the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; and iv. The Customary Land Act.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Its commitment to the promotion and protection of the rights of women through the enactment of a number of progressive laws aimed at reversing previously discriminatory laws, norms and practices in the country; ii. Adoption and implementation of the Gender Equality Act Implementation and Monitoring Plan for gender equality, integration, influence, empowerment, dignity and opportunities for men and women in Malawi (2016 – 2020); iii. Implementation of Section 11 of the Gender Equality Act which provides that an appointing or recruiting authority in the public service shall appoint no less than forty percent (40%) and no more than sixty percent (60%) of either sex in any department in the public service; iv. Lobbying, advocacy, awareness and sensitization campaigns to reduce gender disparities; v. The Mandatory reporting of Ministries; Departments and Agencies (MDAs) on gender indicators and outcomes of number of women recruited and sent for further studies and trainings through the Organizational Performance Appraisal which MDAs signed with the Office of the President and Cabinet; vi. The public service Sexual Harassment Policy developed to make public service institutions favorable for all gender groups; and vii. Ensuring gender equality and the empowerment of women in the county through several strategies.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Male engagement strategy which identifies and prioritizes interventions for involving men and boys in Gender Based Violence (GBV), Sexual Reproductive Health Rights (SRHR) and HIV-related issues; ii. Measures taken to address GBV, including the setup of one stop centres in hospitals; victim support units at Police stations; community support units and the provision of toll free lines; and iii. The establishment of counselling and rehabilitation centres to redress victims of GBV.

The Commission notes with satisfaction: i. The express prohibition of harmful practices as provided for under the HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; ii. Initiatives to combat harmful traditional practices, including activities which clarify toxic cultural and social norms; iv. The 2018 Strategy to end child marriages which is providing guidance in the implementation of interventions targeting girls especially those in rural areas; v. Engagement and lobbying with community leaders including chiefs and religious leaders to become champions for ending child marriages and promoting girls’ education; vi. The minimum age of marriage at 18 under the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act; and the amendment of the Constitution to increase the age of a child as well as the age of consent to marry to 18; vii. The express view by the Malawi Law Commission that Marriage below the age of 18 is a health hazard and that early marriage has negative development implications; and viii. The National Strategy which aims at eradicating child marriage by 2022.

The Commission notes: i. Section 24 (1) (b) (i) of the Constitution which recognises that women can own property separately or jointly and that they are entitled to a fair distribution of the marital property upon dissolution of marriage; and ii. Section 74 of the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act which further provides for equitable distribution of matrimonial property.
The Commission commends Malawi for electoral reforms to include gender quotas in the election of Members of Parliament.

The Commission notes with satisfaction: i. Efforts made by the Government to encourage girl children to stay in school remain and continue with their education such the National Strategy on Inclusive Education 2016 to 2020 with initiatives inter alia: inclusive education projects and Keeping Girls in School; and ii. The Re-Admission Policy in 2016 which provides for the readmission of girls back into school after pregnancy during the COVID-19 Lockdown. The policy also enables pregnant girls to sit for exams during their pregnancy.

The Commission notes with satisfaction, the: i. Domestication of the Maputo Protocol through the enactment of various legislations, including the Gender Equality Act, Marriage Divorce and Family Relations Act and HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; ii. Improved status of child mortality and maternal mortality; iii. Measures taken to ensure postnatal care for women including outreach mobile clinics in hard-to-reach areas; information, education and counselling conducted to the communities and antenatal mothers on importance of postnatal care; availability of revised postnatal registers and reporting tools to track performance; and revision of postnatal care guidelines which requires women to be in hospital 48 hours before discharge; and iv. Revision of Post Abortion Care (PAC) Guidelines and community awareness programs on the Guidelines.

The Commission applauds Malawi for: i. The adoption of a National Policy for Older Persons and efforts to establish a Community Elderly Committee; and ii. Plans to introduce Elderly Friendly Health Services which includes geriatric services in existing outreach clinics.
Lack of awareness of the Maputo Protocol results to slow implementation of the Protocol.
In spite of the Government’s efforts to promote and protect the rights of women, the Commission is concerned about the following:

While the Commission appreciates the detailed responses provided by Malawi to the various questions regarding implementation of the Maputo Protocol, the Commission would appreciate more information on the concerns raised by the Commission hereunder.

The Commission is concerned that: i. There is no indication in the Report about how the Government intends to scale up the sensitisation of the gender-related legal instruments and awareness to the grassroots; ii. Gender quotas for political positions and in the private sector still remain problematic; and iii. I mplementation of affirmative action measures for women in the civil service seems to be hampered by patriarchal cultural values which limit women’s access to leadership opportunities.

The Commission is concerned: i. That while the Report states that the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act has been reviewed, there is no indication that the offence of marital rape has been included, and the amended Bill is yet to be presented to Parliament; ii. About lack of data on the registration and acceptance by the authorities of cases for domestic violence; and iii. Sexual harassment especially for women running for public office.
The Commission is concerned that there is no information about other forms of harmful cultural practices in the Report, including widow’s marriage to brother-in-law as an obligation, FGM etc.
While the Commission applauds the protection accorded on the girl child under the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act, it is concerned that implementation of the Act remains a challenge.
The Commission is concerned by the high illiteracy rate among females and stigma towards pregnant girls on their return to schools.
The Commission is also concerned about the high drop-out rate among girls due to lack of toilets in schools for girls to manage their sanitation needs, especially during their periods.

The Commission is concerned that the Report does not provide any information on the Termination of Pregnancy Bill developed by the Law Commission and yet to be deliberated on and approved by Cabinet at the time of presentation of this Report, even though there have been attempts to take the Bill in Parliament as a Private Members Bill.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission makes the following recommendations to Malawi:
The Government should continue to comply with its obligations under Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol, including by implementing the Commission’s recommendations.

The Government should create more awareness on policies and laws in the country that relate to gender parity and ensure that the awareness campaigns are done across the country, including in the rural areas.

The Government should increase its efforts in challenging deeply rooted beliefs and attitudes surrounding women’s appointment in public and political positions, and implement affirmative actions as stipulated in the Gender Parity Equality Act.
The Government should inform the Commission during its next review, about the status of the amended Prevention of Domestic Violence Act.
The Government should create conditions so that, in practice, sexual harassment that inhibits women from running for public office is reduced.
The Government should take steps to pass a law against sexual harassment.

In its next Periodic Report, the Commission would appreciate more information on other forms of harmful cultural practices that exist in Malawi, including the issue of widows being compelled to marry their brothers-in-law.

The Government should use practical and effective legal, policy and programmatic measures to stop early, child and forced marriage. This should include enforcement of criminal liability for perpetrators, addressing poverty and education causes as well as provision of information on reproductive health to avoid early sexual activity and ultimately early marriages.
The Government should include information on the registration and admissibility by the judiciary bodies of cases brought in the context of marital rape.

The Government should take measures to clearly and firmly lower the illiteracy rate among women and girls, and allow girls to remain in schools, including the creation of specific toilets for them in schools.
The Government should provide in its next Periodic Report, information on the status of the Termination of Pregnancy Bill and reasons for delay in its finalization and enactment into law.

The Commission urges Malawi to also provide in its next Periodic Report, detailed information on the effective implementation of the recommendations made in these Concluding Observations relating to the Maputo Protocol. The Commission requests the Government of Malawi to submit its next periodic report within two years from the notification date of the present Concluding Observations. Adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights at the 70 Ordinary Session held from 23 February to 9 March 2022

The Republic of Cameroon is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter) having ratified it on 20 November 1989. It presented its Combined Periodic Reports (4, 5 and 6) under Article 62 of the African Charter and Initial Reports under Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol and Article 14 of the Kampala Convention during the 67 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission), held virtually in November/December 2020.

The Delegation of the Republic of Cameroon (the Delegation) was led by His Excellency Felix MBAYU, Minister Delegate to the Minister of External Relations in charge of Relations with the Commonwealth.

The Report underscores progress made by Cameroon in the area of human and peoples’ rights as well as legislative, administrative and other measures taken to implement provisions of the African Charter, since the presentation of its 3 Periodic Report at the 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia.

The Commission notes with satisfaction the inclusive and participatory approach in the preparation of the Report, in particular, the establishment of an inter-ministerial committee responsible for drafting reports and monitoring the implementation of human rights-related recommendations, with the involvement of the National Human Rights Commission, other institutions of the Republic and representatives of human rights organizations.
It commends the Republic of Cameroon for its Report which includes detailed statistics and relevant analyses of the current human rights situation as well as challenges.

It welcomes measures taken to implement recommendations made by the Commission following the consideration of Cameroon’s 3 Periodic Report at the 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia.

The Commission commends the Delegation of Cameroon for the open and constructive dialogue which prevailed during the presentation of the Periodic Reports and for the quality of the information provided in response to the concerns raised by the members of the Commission.

These Concluding Observations are divided into three parts: a first part on the African Charter followed by recommendations, a second part which focuses on the Maputo Protocol and is also followed by recommendations, and finally a third part on the Kampala Convention with recommendations. Part A: African Charter On Human and Peoples’ Rights - Article 62:

The Commission takes note of the presentation by the Republic of Cameroon of its 4, 5 and 6 Periodic Reports on the implementation of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights during the 67 Ordinary Session held virtually in November/December 2020.

It welcomes the commitment of Cameroon, which is now up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter. Recommendation: - The Republic of Cameroon should include a separate and detailed section in its next Report describing actions taken to implement the recommendations made by the Commission. - Ratifications

The Commission takes good note of the ratification by Cameroon, during the reporting period, of several human rights instruments, both at the level of the African Union and the UN, as well as other sub-regional conventions and bilateral agreements aimed at improving the rights of Cameroonians. : - Ensure that the ratification process of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities is completed and take the necessary steps to ratify the following instruments: o Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa; o Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security; o The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; and - Make the Declaration under Article 36(4) of the Protocol on the establishment of the African Court to allow full access to justice for all Cameroonians. Article 1: Legislative measures to incorporate the provisions of the African Charter into domestic laws

The Commission welcomes the adoption, by the Government of the Republic of Cameroon, of several legislative texts relating to human rights promotion and protection since the presentation of its last Report. Recommendation: The Republic of Cameroon should pursue efforts aimed at incorporating the provisions of international human rights instruments into its domestic laws, notably by finalizing the adoption of the laws on associations, trafficking in persons and human rights defenders. It should also ensure the effective implementation of adopted laws by conducting outcome assessments. Article 25: Duty to promote human rights NHRIs and other institutions

The Commission commends Cameroon on the establishment of the Human Rights Commission of Cameroon (2019) to replace the National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms. Recommendation: - The Republic of Cameroon should ensure that the Human Rights Commission has the necessary financial and human resources to carry out its full mandate as a National Human Rights Institution. Article 2: Right to freedom from discrimination
The Commission takes note of the provisions included in the Criminal Code punishing acts of discrimination.

However, it is concerned about the lack of information on measures taken to educate the population in this respect. Recommendation: - Ensure that awareness-raising campaigns are carried out on the issue of discrimination and that discriminatory acts are effectively punished as provided by law. Article 3: Right to equality before the law and to the equal protection of the law

The Commission notes Cameroon’s efforts to ensure equality before the law for all. Nevertheless, it is concerned about the difficulties faced by some litigants and lawyers before the courts as a result of the lack of adequate measures to take the English language into consideration.

The Commission is also concerned about the continued prosecution of civilians in military courts. Recommendations: - Ensure that measures are taken for all litigants to bring cases before the courts in their preferred language (English or French); and - Ensure that civilians are tried in civil courts for better administration of justice. Article 4: Right to life
The Commission is concerned that the death penalty is still maintained in the law, even as a deterrent, as the possibility is there to use it at any time.

Furthermore, although the State has indicated that it is improving the living conditions of all prisoners, no details on these improvements have been given. - The Republic of Cameroon should take the necessary measures to abolish the death penalty; and - Provide information on the measures taken to improve the living conditions of prisoners, particularly those on death row. Article 5: Prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment

The Commission takes note that the mandate of the CDHC was extended to include the prerogatives of the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture in respect of the State’s obligations under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (OPCAT). Article 6: Right to personal liberty and protection against arbitrary detention
The Commission notes the establishment of a Commission for the compensation of victims of police custody and abusive pre-trial detention.

Yet, the duration of pre-trial detention is still an issue. Recommendation: - Address the recurrent issue of prolonged pre-trial detention by implementing the Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-trial Detention in Africa. Article 7: Right to a fair trial

The Commission notes with satisfaction the changes in the organisation of the Supreme Court pursuant to Law No. 2017/014 of 12 July 2017, which established a Common Law Division under the Judicial Chamber to improve access to justice for litigants with a common law background, as well as the appointment of members of Legal Aid Commissions to the judicial courts.

It also notes that the functioning of legal aid commissions was hampered by financial constraints, which therefore limited its full enjoyment by litigants. - Ensure that the new organisational structure of the Supreme Court is widely disseminated to the public and that adequate support measures are put in place (translators and interpreters); and - Increase the budget for legal aid. Article 9: Right to receive information and freedom of speech

The Commission takes due note of the information contained in the Report on the measures taken to maintain media diversity and to address the challenges of electronic media, including social networks.
The Commission also notes the organisation of various training courses for journalists and media professionals.

However, the Commission notes the need to protect access to the internet for all citizens without restriction, while recognising the importance of regulation. Recommendations: - Ensure the full implementation of safeguards relating to access to information, notably those included in Law No. 2015/007 of 20 April 2015 governing audiovisual activity in Cameroon; - Develop an Information, Communication and Digital Information Act; and - Adhere to the 2019 Declaration on Freedom of Expression. Articles 10 and 11: Right to freedom of association and assembly

The Commission is concerned about the lack of a specific legal framework for the protection of human rights defenders and the multiple reports of arbitrary arrests and other acts of harassment of individuals working to promote and protect human rights, particularly in the context of the socio-political crisis in the northern and eastern regions of Cameroon. - Adopt a specific law on human rights defenders; - Ensure a safe working environment for human rights defenders; - Ensure that the implementation of the law on associations is in line with the Guidelines on Freedom of Association and Assembly of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights; and - Guarantee the right to peaceful assembly without space and time restrictions that render this right meaningless. Article 12: Right to freedom of movement

The Commission notes the various measures taken by the State in terms of support to refugees and asylum seekers as well as the positive cooperation with UNHCR in this respect. Recommendation: - Continue efforts to mainstream local integration as a solution for long-term refugees and not only in the context of a cessation clause; local integration can reduce conventional refugee support costs. Article 13: Right to participate in government
The information contained in the Report demonstrates the will of the Republic of Cameroon to ensure the participation of all population subsets in the management of public affairs.

However, the Commission notes that the figures given for voter registration do not refer to the number of men, thus making it difficult to determine whether gender parity is effectively respected or progress has been made in that respect. - Continue efforts to include all categories while ensuring that quotas are set for this purpose to ensure greater equity; and - Provide figures on the number of women, young people, people with disabilities and indigenous minorities in decision-making positions. Article 14: Right to property/ right to housing Right to property

The Commission takes note of the measures adopted to secure access to land, the regulatory framework to protect the needs of vulnerable groups as reflected in the fight against land grabbing and consultations with customary and indigenous communities, measures to protect against violations of land rights, judicial protection of the right to property and the conditions for compensation in the event of expropriation in the public interest. It also takes note of the establishment of an ad hoc committee in charge of reviewing the proposals of Cameroon’s traditional leaders on the ongoing land, forestry and mining reform.
The Commission hopes that the reform will strengthen existing safeguards and protection of the right to property for all in Cameroon. Right to housing

The Commission takes note of the various actions carried out in terms of housing, notably the implementation of initiatives to increase the supply of building plots and houses and ongoing housing construction projects, including the construction of 100 8 Pages 44 and 45 of the Report. 9 The proposals include: recognition of the right of the village to collective and non-transferable ownership of traditional land, without any special formality; granting ownership to all the villages through a deed signed by the Government; recognition of the validity of customary law in the management of village land; not requiring development of land as a prerequisite to having access to land ownership. 10 Pages 63 and 64 of the Report. units in each of the regional capitals excluding Yaounde and Douala, and the launching of the Cité des Cinquantenaires project.

However, it is not stated in the Report whether some of the housing units under construction will be used for social housing purposes and what percentage will be reserved for persons with reduced mobility. - Implement a social housing policy for the most disadvantaged; and - Finalize the ongoing land, forestry and mining reform and ensure that it reinforces the rights already guaranteed. Article 15: Right to employment

The Commission notes the existence of a Guaranteed Minimum Wage which was revised upwards in 2014, the creation of a significant number of jobs, as well as the incentives to support job creation. During the 2013-2018 period, a total of 20,004 jobs were created in the public sector.

Nevertheless, the Guaranteed Minimum Wage is quite low and has remained the same since 2014 despite inflation and the rising cost of living and this reduces the purchasing power of workers. - Take the necessary measures to increase the amount of the Guaranteed Interprofessional Minimum Wage (SMIG), taking into account inflation and the cost of living, in order to enable workers to have a source of income that will help them attain a decent standard of living; and - Strengthen measures to support the private and informal sector in job creation, including entrepreneurship. Article 16: Right to health

The Commission notes the measures adopted by Cameroon with regard to the right to health, including: - The expansion of the health map and the training and recruitment of various health workers; - The reopening of some midwifery schools that had been closed; - The adoption of Decree No. 2016/6447/PM of 13 December 2016 establishing the terms and conditions for the allocation of bonuses, calculated from all paid services, to medical and paramedical staff working in public health facilities; - The introduction of Guidelines on patient consultation procedures in public health facilities to address the difficulties encountered by patients in accessing health care; - The allocation of funds to health facilities for the delivery of care to poor patients; and the launch of the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) process to provide quality care and equitable access to health services, and protect the population from financial hardship.

However, the Commission notes that the amount of the national budget allocated to health is not indicated in the Report and would like to point out that, according to the Abuja Declaration, at least 15% of the national budget should be allocated to this sector. - Establish monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to monitor the impact and outcome of these measures; - Continue efforts to strengthen the health system; - Report on the progress made in reaching the different objectives listed in the Report, including statistics and indicator data; and - Allocate at least 15% of the national budget to the health sector, as required by the Abuja Declaration. Article 17: Right to education

The Commission notes with satisfaction that 13.34% of the national budget is allocated to education and that various cross-cutting reforms have been undertaken in the education sector, including the adoption of a new textbook policy, curriculum reform and the reduction of economic and geographical disparities, as well as measures to support economic accessibility, such as free public primary education and the promotion of equitable access to education for girls, persons with disabilities and indigenous populations. Recommendation: - Pursue efforts and report on the results obtained following the implementation of the reforms undertaken. Article 18: Rights of the family and vulnerable groups Persons Living With HIV/AIDS

The Commission commends Cameroon, which had an HIV/AIDS prevalence rate of 2.7% as at 1 December 2020, confirming the downward curve of the pandemic (4.3% in 2011, 3.4% in 2018 and 2019). The Commission encourages the State to continue its efforts in prevention and in improving the conditions of persons living with HIV/AIDS. Rights of persons with disabilities: Article 18 (4)

The Commission takes note of the various measures adopted by the State, in particular the formal consolidation of strategic options for the protection of persons with disabilities, access for persons with disabilities to infrastructure, housing, transport and communication, access for persons with disabilities to political, sports, artistic, cultural and leisure activities, physical therapy for persons with disabilities, and the improved management of actions in favour of persons with disabilities.

However, there is no clear information about the actual implementation of these measures and their impact on the lives of persons with disabilities. Furthermore, there is no information on access to housing that meets the needs of persons with disabilities or on measures concerning access to employment. Rights of older persons (Article 18 (4))

The Commission notes the existence of a national policy document on the protection of older persons, which aims to ensure that the concerns of older persons are effectively mainstreamed into the policies, programmes and projects under the various sectors in order to protect them from social exclusion. However, there is no reference to concrete support for older persons, such as benefits, social protection and medical care. - Adopt measures for the effective participation of indigenous communities in decision-making bodies, for example by setting a quota for such participation; - Adopt targeted measures for the protection of indigenous peoples’ land, including through the issuance of a collective title deed that is valid before the courts; - Continue the programme for the professional integration of pygmies; and - Finalize the study on the official definition and identification of indigenous peoples and provide feedback in the next Report. Recommendations: - Provide information on the effective implementation of the measures mentioned in this Report; - Take into account the needs of persons with disabilities when developing housing projects, particularly with regard to social housing units; - Provide details on measures implemented to ensure the well-being of older persons; and - Adopt measures to provide support for the most disadvantaged older persons. Article 19: Right of all peoples to equal rights (rights of indigenous peoples and populations)

The Commission notes the efforts made by Cameroon regarding the protection of the rights of indigenous peoples. However, several measures are still pending and the study on the official definition and identification of these populations is yet to be finalised. Article 20: Right to self-determination
The Commission notes the holding of a national dialogue with a view to putting an end to the socio-political crisis in Cameroon and the efforts made in this regard.
However, it notes that many violations have been committed and remain unpunished to this day.

The Commission also notes that although efforts have been made towards effective decentralisation, much remains to be done to ensure that all regions, without exception, benefit from sound administration and the necessary assistance and support from the State. - Ensure that the means required for the smooth functioning of public services are made available to enable effective implementation of the decentralisation system and a thriving population; and - Roll out the decentralisation policy while respecting the specificities of each region. Articles 21 and 24: The right to freely dispose of natural resources and wealth and the right to a general satisfactory environment
The Commission takes note of the measures adopted to monitor the extractive industries, including the various good governance measures listed in the Report.
It also notes the efforts made to protect the environment through various measures to prevent, mitigate and/or adapt to the adverse effects and risks of climate change.

The Commission takes note of the various information contained in the Report. It however notes that certain information is missing, relating in particular to: - The existence of a licence or mining register that can be consulted online; - An online register of the beneficial owners of companies bidding for, operating or investing in extractive assets, including the identity of their beneficial owner(s), the extent of their participation, and the arrangements for exercising such participation or control; - The details of the Government’s participation in extractive companies; - Major mining exploration activities in Cameroon; - Production in the extractive sector per region, tax-related data per company and the percentage invested in local and regional development; and - Revenue from transport in the mining sector and its distribution among the population. - Strengthen existing measures; - Organise awareness campaigns among the population so that they adopt more responsible behaviour in terms of environmental protection; - Establish a licence or mining register that can be consulted online; - Make available an online register of the beneficial owners of companies bidding for, operating or investing in extractive assets, including the identity of their beneficial owner(s), the extent of their participation, and the arrangements for exercising such participation or control; - Disclose the details of Government participation in extractive companies; - Provide information on major mining exploration activities in Cameroon; - Provide information on production in the extractive sector per region, tax- related data per company and the percentage invested in local and regional development; and - Provide information on revenue from transport in the mining sector and its distribution among the population. Article 22: Right to economic, social and cultural development

The Commission notes the efforts made by Cameroon in the area of social, economic and cultural rights. Recommendation: - Strengthen ongoing actions to effectively achieve the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, namely: No Poverty, Zero Hunger, Good Health and Well-being, Quality Education, Gender Equality, Clean Water and Sanitation, Clean and Affordable Energy, Decent Work and Economic Growth, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, Reduced Inequality, Sustainable Cities and Communities, Responsible Consumption and Production, Tackling Climate Change, Water Life, Land Life, Peace, Justice and Effective Institutions, and Partnerships to Achieve the Goals.
Cameroon ratified the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa on 13 September 2012.
The Commission reiterates its congratulations to the Republic of Cameroon for the submission of its Initial Report, in accordance with the provisions of Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission notes with satisfaction that the Cameroonian authorities prepared the part of the Periodic Report reserved for the Maputo Protocol in accordance with the Guidelines adopted in this regard. - While recalling that this Periodic Report is good practice at the regional level, the Commission encourages the Republic of Cameroon to pursue its commitment to submitting periodic reports, including on the implementation of the Maputo Protocol, in accordance with the relevant guidelines; and - Cameroon should also intensify its efforts to disseminate and popularise the Maputo Protocol at the national level. Articles 2 and 3: Equality and non-discrimination

Despite the existing framework, efforts still need to be made by the Cameroonian authorities to combat discrimination against women, as in other countries in the region, both with regard to the legal system and harmful practices.

Examples include discriminatory provisions in customary laws, wage inequalities and the existence of different conditions for the acquisition, transmission and retention of Cameroonian nationality depending on whether one is male or female. - Reform its laws so as to repeal certain provisions that discriminate against women, such as Sections 1421 and 1428 of the Civil Code relating to the management of family property and the law on nationality, which include measures that discriminate against Cameroonian women with regard to the transmission of their nationality; - Ensure better domestication of the provisions of the Maputo Protocol, in particular, through the inclusion of a definition of discrimination; - Ensure that the provisions of customary laws do not contradict those of the Maputo Protocol; and - Address wage inequalities through appropriate legal provisions and policies. Articles 4 and 5: Violence against women

At its 61 Ordinary Session, the Commission adopted Guidelines on Combating Sexual Violence and its Consequences in Africa. Also, at its 72 Ordinary Session, the Commission adopted Resolution ACHPR 522 (LXXII) 2022 on the Protection of Women Against Digital Violence in Africa, which, among other things, calls on States to review/adopt legislation that aims at combating all forms of digital violence against women. - Ensure the popularisation and dissemination of the above-mentioned instruments; - Amend the Criminal Code to include punishment of marital rape, domestic violence and female genital mutilation; - Ensure effective and optimal implementation of national policies to combat gender-based violence; - Redouble efforts to rehabilitate victims of domestic violence, in particular, by enhancing access to support centres; - Strengthen efforts to combat all forms of violence against women, by encouraging the Judiciary to hear cases; and - Continue efforts to end harmful traditional practices, in particular, through awareness-raising campaigns aimed at informing about the legal system and the related dangers. Articles 6 and 7: Marriage, separation, divorce and annulment

The Commission takes good note of the various programmes focusing on the protection of the family unit in Cameroon, such as the Premarital, Matrimonial and Family Education Programme being implemented since 2013. - Ensure full compliance with the provisions of the Criminal Code, particularly Section 356, which criminalises marriage under the age of 18 and forced marriage; and - Increase awareness on harmful traditional practices that encourage forced or early marriage. Article 8: Access to justice and equal protection before the law

The Commission takes note of the conviction, by the Military Court of Bamenda on 24 July 2018, of a Private First Class to 7 years imprisonment for the rape of a 17-year-old girl, violation of orders and possession of drugs.
Unfortunately, other allegations of rape perpetrated by the military in particular, were also brought to the attention of the Commission.
The Commission is concerned about the lack of information on the number of prosecutions and convictions of perpetrators of violence against women.

Victims’ silence can also be a major obstacle to ensuring access for women to justice and their protection. - Take all necessary measures to encourage and promote women’s access to justice; - Conduct awareness campaigns against the silence, whether chosen or imposed, of victims of abuse; and - Redouble efforts to ensure the prosecution and disciplining of security and law enforcement officers involved in cases of violence against women and girls. Article 9: Participation in political and decision-making processes
The Commission notes the evolution in the representation of Cameroonian women in certain sectors of activity, such as the Judiciary.

On the other hand, Cameroonian women are under-represented, particularly in private sector entities (reports indicate a representation rate of 32%). - Continue efforts to ensure the meaningful participation of women at all stages in the design, preparation, implementation and evaluation of development policies and programmes; and - Increase efforts to strengthen women’s leadership and participation in public and political life. Articles 12-17: Economic, social and cultural rights

The Commission takes note of the efforts deployed by the Cameroonian Government to promote education in general. However, it should be noted that the illiteracy rate in Cameroon is higher among women.
In addition, the conditions under which women and girls work on plantations and in the mining sector, as well as those of women employed as house helps, are deplored in public reports.

Similarly, ensuring access to health care, particularly for women and girls, is a major challenge for the Cameroonian authorities. - Take appropriate measures to ensure equal access for girls and young women to all levels of education and their retention in school; - Ratify the International Labour Organization Convention (No. 189) concerning Decent Work for Domestic Workers (2011); - Extend legal and social protection to include women working in the informal sector; - Improve health infrastructure and access to health care for women in poor rural areas; - Address the issue of the shortage of blood supplies by, inter alia, implementing the 2003 Blood Transfusion Act, as a means to combat maternal mortality; - Guarantee access to contraceptive care and maternal and child health services, particularly for the most vulnerable groups (women from rural and remote areas, refugees and internally displaced women, etc.); and - Ensure that abortion, as provided for in Article 14(2) (c) of the Maputo Protocol, is respected and implemented. Articles 20-24: Categories enjoying special protection

The Commission takes note of the measures aimed at addressing the specific needs of pregnant or breastfeeding women serving a prison sentence (supervision in a dedicated area, medical and psychosocial support). - Pay special attention to the protection of older women and women with disabilities; - Adopt measures to adequately protect the rights of widows in accordance with the Maputo Protocol, in particular, those married under customary law and widows subject to cleansing rituals in some rural areas; and - Adopt measures to strengthen the protection of women’s rights in prison, especially during the current COVID-19 pandemic.

Internal displacement of people is a new reality which sets many challenges for States, as it is becoming more and more recurrent. For a long time, it was due to internal conflicts or as a result of large-scale projects, but it is increasingly due to climate change- induced natural disasters. This has serious consequences for the States, which must respond to the protection and assistance needs of these populations.

The ongoing socio-political crisis in Cameroon has worsened the displacement of people fleeing areas where fighting is taking place. The efforts made by the State are commendable and to be encouraged. However, targeted measures should be taken and existing programmes adjusted to better address the challenges of internal displacement. Article 3: General obligations

The Commission commends the Republic of Cameroon for the presentation of its Initial Report under the Kampala Convention and the various measures taken within the framework of its implementation, including all the laws and regulations that were adopted and aimed at ensuring the protection of the population. The Commission also notes the establishment of several entities to address the needs of internally displaced persons (IDPs). Recommendation: - Continue submitting periodic reports under Article 14 of the Convention on a regular basis. Article 4: Obligations of States Parties relating to protection from internal displacement

The Commission notes the following: - Creation, by the Minister for Territorial Administration, of a Working Group in charge of the legal and institutional reform of the civil protection system; and - A draft legislation establishing the general framework for civil protection in Cameroon as well as a proposal for a new institutional and operational architecture adapted to the requirements and contingencies of present-day civil protection. Recommendations: - Finalize the draft law establishing the general framework for civil protection in Cameroon; and - Finalize the proposal for a new institutional and operational architecture to meet the requirements and contingencies of present-day civil protection. Article 5: Obligations of States Parties relating to Protection and Assistance

The Commission notes the measures taken to address the assistance needs of IDPs: - Development of humanitarian response plans by UN agencies; - Development of the 2017-2020 humanitarian response plan for the Adamaoua, East, North and Far North Regions; - Establishment of a Coordination Centre for Emergency Humanitarian Assistance in respect of the situation in the North West and South West regions; - Assessment of the needs of displaced persons, refugees and host communities, relating to the protection of civilians, education, health, food insecurity and acute malnutrition; - Existence of two sets of mechanisms for evaluating assistance, i.e. administrative mechanisms and specific mechanisms implemented by humanitarian organisations; - Damage assessment by administrative mechanisms and census of displaced populations to determine health, nutrition and first aid needs; and - Multi-Sector Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA), which is carried out as soon as the disaster occurs and focuses on identifying basic needs. Recommendations: - Allocate adequate funds to support these different programmes over the long term and not just on an ad hoc basis; and - Involve IDPs in the evaluation of these different programmes in order to better identify their needs and also to allow them to be actors in their rehabilitation. Article 6: Obligations relating to international organisations and humanitarian agencies

The Commission notes the following: - Implementation of mechanisms, at both the Government and humanitarian actor level, to monitor the compliance of humanitarian actors with their obligations; - Supervision of assistance operations at the local level through regular (monthly) consultations, and at the central level to monitor humanitarian assistance operations; - Organisation of joint Government/partner operations; - Internal code of conduct for humanitarian actors; - Establishment of a Coordination Centre for Emergency Humanitarian Assistance in respect of the situation in the North West and South West Regions; and - The inclusion of support plans into local development plans as recommended by the Strategy for Recovery and Peacebuilding in the North and East Regions of Cameroon (2018-2022). - Continue ongoing efforts; and - Adopt measures to ensure sustainability of the various initiatives. Article 7: Protection and assistance to internally displaced persons in situations of armed conflict

The Commission takes note of all the measures adopted by Cameroon in the context of the ongoing socio-political crisis, including the assistance provided to IDPs as a result of the crisis. - Continue ongoing efforts; and - Work actively to resolve the conflict. Article 8: Obligations relating to the African Union

The Commission notes: - The mission dispatched to Cameroon in July 2018 by the Chairperson of the AU Commission to assess the situation in the Far North Region and the two other crisis- ridden regions to determine the support that the AU could provide; and - The proposal for the organisation of an International Donors’ Conference as part of efforts to implement the Emergency Humanitarian Assistance Plan for the populations in the North West and South West regions.
However, the Commission notes that information is not provided on the outcome of the AU mission and the organisation of the donor conference.

Furthermore, the Commission notes that despite the adoption of the Common African Position (CAP) on Humanitarian Effectiveness in January 2016 at the Heads of State Summit, the establishment of the African Humanitarian Agency is yet to be effective.

Finally, it would be fitting to create a continental fund for assistance to countries facing large-scale internal displacement in Africa. Such countries would be supported through the Humanitarian Agency. − Provide information on the findings of the AU mission and proposed solutions (Cameroon); − Implement the Common African Position (CAP) on Humanitarian Effectiveness adopted in January 2016 at the Summit of Heads of State and Government, including the establishment of the African Humanitarian Agency (African Union); and − Provide Cameroon with support to mobilise resources for assistance to IDPs (African Union). Article 9: Obligations of States Parties relating to protection and assistance during internal displacement

The Commission commends the Republic of Cameroon for the measures taken to implement Article 9 of the Convention on the obligations of States Parties relating to protection and assistance during internal displacement. The Commission notes the measures taken for protection against summary and arbitrary executions, kidnappings, genocide, crimes against humanity, including: - Both preventive and repressive actions carried out with the support of humanitarian agencies as well as awareness-raising campaigns on peace; - Establishment of monitoring mechanisms such as watchdog and joint committees set up by the local authorities and UNHCR in some Divisions of the Far North Region to ensure the protection of refugees, IDPs and asylum seekers; and - Legal proceedings against perpetrators of violations of the right to life and physical integrity of displaced persons.

Protection of internally displaced women against violence (Art. 9 para. 2 d) - Definition of an integrated and multi-pronged assistance strategy for women and girls, built around “social cohesion spaces for women” in the camps, the setting up of call centres and gender desks and multi-disciplinary support for survivors; - Awareness-raising activities carried out in communities and sites hosting refugees and IDPs, with a view to influencing and changing social norms that promote GBV. Using a community-based approach, 142 community relay workers carried out these activities which reached more than 351,218 men and women, refugees and nationals; - With regard to guaranteeing the right to security (right to seek safety in another part of the State – Art. 9 para. 2e) and settlement of IDPs in safe places – Art. 9 para. 2g), the Commission notes the measures taken by the State, including: - Accommodation facilities for some displaced people while others were taken in by host populations; - Assistance and support from local administrative authorities such as the reception and resettlement of displaced persons and the distribution of bedding, toiletries, food items and basic necessities; - Measures to enrol students in schools that are in the regions hosting them; and - Construction of water points, health care delivery, rehabilitation of classrooms, distribution of health kits, school supplies and food items.

Concerning the protection of the right to family life (Art. 9 para. 2h) - The adoption of a multi-year humanitarian response plan for Cameroon (2018- 2020). A strategic area of this Plan is to address the issue of displaced persons returning to their places of origin. The aim is to: ▪ Enhance the alternative support provided on a temporary basis to unaccompanied children or those separated from their families and facilitate family reunification for unaccompanied children; and ▪ Provide psychosocial and psychological support to all children and adolescents affected by the crisis.

The Commission notes, however, that there is still progress to be made with regard to family reunification, which is made difficult by the security context, the loss of identification documents and the weakening of the birth registration system. Recommendation: - Adopt measures to establish an automated system for the registration of displaced persons with disaggregated data that will facilitate family reunification. Article 10: Displacement induced by projects

The Commission notes that measures have been taken to reduce the negative impact of large-scale projects on local populations, in particular: - Conduct of environmental impact assessments; - Compensation and/or resettlement of those whose properties were expropriated; and - Implementation of socio-economic support projects. Recommendations: - Ensure that information campaigns targeting affected populations are effectively carried out so that they know their rights; - Provide statistics on those compensated in the context of large-scale projects, indicating the method for determining the amount of compensation; and - Provide further details on the resettlement programme for persons whose properties were expropriated. Article 11: Obligations of States Parties relating to sustainable return, local integration or relocation

The Commission notes: - The creation of the National Committee for Demobilization, Disarmament and Reintegration pursuant to Decree No. 2018/719 of 30 November 2018; - Assistance provided for the return of displaced persons to their places of origin with the support of humanitarian agencies; and - Income-generating projects, at the initiative of humanitarian agencies, for IDPs who have decided to settle permanently in their places of relocation. Recommendations: - Continue efforts and allocate funds, at the national level, to implement the rehabilitation and reconstruction component of IDP assistance plans; - Strengthen programmes for the resettlement of IDPs or their integration into their host communities, initiated by humanitarian agencies; and - Adopt measures to ensure the rehabilitation of areas abandoned by IDPs when this is due to natural disasters. Article 12: Compensation

The Commission notes the absence of a legal framework establishing specific mechanisms for compensation to IDPs. Recommendation: - Adopt measures to develop a legal framework governing compensation to IDPs. Article 13: Registration and personal documentation

Measures taken to facilitate the issuance of birth certificates to internally displaced persons, including: - Ordinance No. 81/002 of 29 June 1981 on the organisation of civil status and various provisions relating to the status of natural persons, as amended by Law No. 2011/002 of 6 May 2011; - Establishment of a Divisional Commission for the Determination of Status by the Prefect of Mayo-Tsanaga to address the documentation needs of IDPs in February 2017; - Issuance of birth certificates to 310 returnee children and 58 children of the host populations of Mozogo and internally displaced children in Mozogo, i.e. a total of 368 birth certificates, after court-issued declaratory judgment. The beneficiaries include 200 boys and 168 girls, with the support of UNICEF; and - Implementation of the Emergency Humanitarian Assistance Plan for the North- West and South-West Regions to reconstitute civil status documents for displaced persons. Recommendation: - Improve the system for the registration of IDPs and issuance of birth certificates or substitute birth certificates (declaratory judgements) in order to avoid situations that could lead to statelessness.

The Government of Cameroon is expected to submit its next Periodic Report on the implementation of the African Charter, the Maputo Protocol and the Kampala Convention in November 2024, i.e. two years from the date of notification of these Concluding Observations. Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu une plainte de la famille (victime indirecte) de feu Banombi Sylvain (victime directe), représentée par l'Observatoire Congolais des Droits de l'Homme (OCDH) et l'Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) ci-après dénommés les Plaignants ; sur fondement de l'article 55 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (Charte africaine).
La Plainte a été introduite contre la République du Congo (Etat Partie à la Charte africaine et ci-après dénommé l'Etat défendeur ou le Congo).
La Plainte expose que le 18 juin 2008, le parking où travaillait Feu BANOMBI Sylvain a été le théâtre d'une rixe entre un agent dudit parking et un contrôleur de bus.
Les Plaignants indiquent que l'intervention de la police sur les lieux a été soldée par l'arrestation et la détention de trois agents du parking dont sieur Sylvain BANOMBI.

Les Plaignants exposent que les prévenus, à leur arrivée au poste de police de Kombo, auraient été dépouillés de leurs biens, déshabillés, torturés puis enfermés avec d'autres détenus dans une cellule sans aération, sans nourriture ni soins médicaux.

Les plaignants déclarent que le cinquième jour de la détention, sieur Banombi, qui ressentait d'atroces douleurs ouvertes sur sa tête et au bas ventre du fait des coups et blessures reçus, n'a pas été autorisé à recevoir des soins médicaux.

Les plaignants rapportent qu'au 8ème jour, réalisant que sieur Banombi était mourant, ses codétenus ont fait beaucoup de clameur jusqu'à ce que le chef de poste en service ce jour vienne extraire Banombi de la cellule. Les Plaignants indiquent que ne pouvant plus marcher, le chef de poste en service a abandonné sieur Banombi devant le poste de police à la portée de vue de tous les agents du poste de police.

Les Plaintants exposent que le soir, aux environs de 17h30, Banombi a été amené au domicile de son grand-frère grâce à l'aide de deux femmes, puis conduit au dispensaire du quartier, avant d'être transféré en urgence à l'hôpital de Talangaï sur instruction des agents de santé. Le 26 juin 2008, tôt le matin, il a été transféré au Centre hospitalier universitaire de Brazzaville où de simples examens ont permis aux médecins d'affirmer qu'il y a eu un blocage du système d'évacuation des urines et des selles suite aux conditions de sa détention.

Les plaignants soumettent que l'opération chirurgicale qu'il lui fallait n'a pas pu être faite par manque de moyens financiers car l'intéressé devait payer une caution avant l'opération. Les Plaintants soutiennent que le grand-frère de la victime l'a ramené au poste de police, l'y a laissé et a exigé sa prise en charge et ce après que le chef de police de Kombo eut refusé de le recevoir.

Les plaignants rapportent qu'aux environs de dix heures, le grand-frère de sieur Banombi a reçu un coup de fil lui annonçant sa mort. Le corps du défunt a été transporté à la morgue de l'hôpital de Talangaï mais suite aux difficultés financières, la famille de Banombi n'a pu procéder à son inhumation qu'après quatre mois et demi après l'exonération des frais d'inhumation par le directeur de pompes funèbres et ce sur instruction du maire de Brazzaville.

Les Plaintants indiquent que l'acte de décès délivré par le médecin légiste sur réquisition du service d'enquête criminelle de la direction départementale de la police de Brazzaville a établi que la mort de sieur BANOMBI a fait suite aux coups et blessures volontaires.

Les plaignants allèguent la violation des dispositions des articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 (1) (a) et (d) et 16 de la Charte africaine. Les plaignants demandent à la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Commission) de déclarer la Communication recevable.

La Plainte est parvenue au Secrétariat de la Commission le 22 mars 2017. Lors de sa 62 Session Ordinaire tenue du 25 avril au 09 mai 2018 à Nouakchott, en Mauritanie, la Commission a examiné la Plainte et a décidé de l'admettre. Le 18 mai 2018, le Secrétariat a informé les parties de cette décision et a demandé aux Plaignants de soumettre leurs moyens sur la recevabilité de la Communication.

Le 23 juillet 2018, les Plaignants ont transmis au Secrétariat leurs observations sur la recevabilité. Le Secrétariat en a accusé réception le 20 août 2018 et les a transmis à l'Etat défendeur le même jour et requis sa réponse dans un délai de soixante (60) jours, conformément à son Règlement Intérieur (2010).

Lors de ses sessions successives tenues entre mai 2018 et décembre 2021, la Commission a examiné la Communication et décidé de renvoyer sa décision sur la Recevabilité pour défaut de soumission par l'Etat défendeur. Les correspondances requises ont été adressées aux Parties. Des rappels ont été adressés à l'Etat défendeur, notamment les Notes Verbales CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/1234/18, CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/618/19, CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/1138/19, CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/1357/19, CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/605/20, CADHP/COMM/687/18/RDC/439/21, par lesquelles le Secrétariat de la Commission l'invitait à soumettre ses observations sur la recevabilité de la Communication.

Le 27 août 2020, le Secrétariat a informé l'Etat défendeur de la décision prise par la Commission, lors de sa 66 Session ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 13 juillet au 7 août 2020, de rendre une décision sur la base des éléments en sa possession, en raison de son défaut de soumission du mémoire sur la recevabilité.

Lors de sa 68 Session Ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 14 avril au 4 mai 2021, la Commission a décidé de renvoyer l'examen de la Communication en vue de préparer une décision par défaut sur la Recevabilité.

Se fondant sur les observations qu'ils ont soumises à cet effet, les Plaignants soutiennent que la Communication respecte toutes les conditions de recevabilité prescrites à l'article 56 de la Charte africaine. Ainsi, les Plaignants soutiennent que la condition posée à l'article 56(1) est remplie puisque l'identité des auteurs de la communication est indiquée. La communication est présentée par deux organisations non gouvernementales (ONGs), à savoir IHRDA et OCDH dont les adresses physiques et les coordonnées de contact sont bien précisées dans la plainte ainsi que leurs domaines d'action.

Ils soutiennent également que la Communication est conforme à l'article 56(2) parce qu'elle est compatible avec la Charte de l'UA et la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples. Ils indiquent que la présente Communication remplit toutes les conditions exigées par la Commission dans l'application de cette disposition. Pour les Plaignants, la Communication est dirigée contre la République du Congo, un Etat partie à la Charte depuis le 09 décembre 1982 ; les violations alléguées dans la Communication enfreignent les droits garantis par les articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 (1) (a) et (d) et 16 de la Charte et sont survenues à partir de 2008, répondant ainsi au critère de postériorité à la ratification de la Charte par l'Etat défendeur.

Pour prouver le respect de l'exigence faite à l'article 56(3), les Plaignants soutiennent que la Communication est dépourvue de tout langage insultant. Ils font observer qu'ils ont beaucoup d'estime vis-à-vis de l'Etat défendeur, ses institutions et celles de l'Union Africaine et ne prétendent pas manquer de respect à leur égard.

Concernant la condition posée par l'article 56(4), ils indiquent que les informations diffusées par les médias n'occupent aucune place dans la présente Communication. Ils rapportent que les allégations y contenues sont basées entre autres sur des documents émanant des autorités policières et administratives ainsi que des services médicaux, notamment le procès-verbal du commandant d'enquêtes criminelles de Brazzaville et les certificats médicaux.

S'agissant des prescriptions faites à l'article 56(5) de la Charte africaine, les Plaignants rappellent que la Charte Africaine pose la règle de l'épuisement des recours internes s'ils existent, à moins qu'il ne soit manifeste à la Commission que la procédure de ces recours se prolonge d'une façon anormale. les Plaignants indiquent qu'il est clairement établi dans la jurisprudence de la Commission que les recours existant dans l'État défendeur doivent être disponibles, efficaces et satisfaisants.

Les Plaignants exposent qu'aux termes des articles 34 et suivants du code de procédure pénale congolais, soit le juge d'instruction, soit le président du tribunal de grande instance est chargé de mener l'instruction d'un dossier criminel sur saisine du ministère public. Ils indiquent que la police judiciaire territorialement compétente aurait dû d'office porter les circonstances entourant la mort de Banombi à la connaissance du procureur de Brazzaville et ce dernier aurait dû lui-même déclencher l'instruction parce qu'il ne pouvait ignorer la mort de Banombi. Ils soutiennent que face à l'inertie des institutions concernées, Camille Balbota (représentant la famille de feu Banombi Sylvain) a déposé une plainte au tribunal de grande instance de Brazzaville le 07/05/2010 conformément à l'article 70 du code de procédure pénale.

Les Plaignants s'indignent qu'à quelques jours de la prescription de l'action publique fixée, aux termes de l'article 7 du code de procédure pénale congolais, à dix années révolues à compter du jour où le crime a été commis, le ministère public n'avait pas encore initié des poursuites contre les personnes impliquées dans la mort de Banombi Sylvain. Ils exposent que les organes judiciaires internes saisis n'ont fait preuve de diligence voulue dans l'instruction et la conduite dudit procès.

Les Plaignants notent en outre que la Charte Africaine admet une exception au principe d'épuisement des voies de recours internes, celle de leur prolongation anormale. Les Plaignants observent qu'à travers sa jurisprudence constante sur le caractère illusoire et futile de l'épuisement des recours internes lorsque la procédure s'était révélée anormalement prolongée.

Les Plaignants s'appuient sur cette exception tirée de la prolongation anormale de la procédure des voies de recours internes pour prier la Commission de les exonérer de leur épuisement et de déclarer la Plainte recevable. Au soutien de cette demande, les Plaignants font observer que dans la présente communication, huit ans se sont écoulés sans que le procureur ou le tribunal de grande instance de Brazzaville ait commencé l'instruction de la plainte introduite par la famille de Feu Banombi.

Les Plaignants concluent qu'outre que le recours interne s'est anormalement prolongé, la passivité des autorités judiciaires dresse un obstacle infranchissable pour la famille de feu Banombi, rendant le recours interne théorique ou pratiquement inexistant. Ils prient la Commission d'exempter les victimes du devoir d'épuiser les recours internes et de considérer que la condition posée par l'article 56 (5) est remplie par la présente communication.

En ce qui concerne la condition posée par l'article 56 (6) de la Charte africaine, les Plaignants rappellent en s'appuyant sur la jurisprudence de la Commission, qu'en l'absence de l'épuisement des recours internes, la date de notification au plaignant de l'indisponibilité et de la prolongation anormale est prise comme point de repère dans le calcul du délai raisonnable. Ils indiquent que dans la présente affaire, le tribunal de grande instance de Brazzaville n'a pas encore notifié aux plaignants l'issue de la plainte intentée en 2010 ; ce qui implique que jusqu'à la date de la saisine, le délai raisonnable pour saisir la Commission n'avait pas commencé à courir.
